1.1: Logic, a lot of fun, but also a lot of work. Applied, can be very theoretical and abstract, too. I want to start with the question of why bother with dealing with all the hard abstractions, doing all of the sometimes difficult work involved in logic, mastering it and then being able to apply it? I'll make a claim that, for human beings, logic is the most practical thing one can master. That's a very strong claim, and it's a controversial claim, even within pro-logic circles, but I'm going to make it.
1.2: Some of the reason for this is for thinking about what makes it possible for us human beings even to survive, but beyond mere survival, flourish and to accomplish wonderful things that human beings can accomplish. It has a lot, of course, to do with our bodies, learning how to use our bodies well. But for human beings, what matters more is how we use our brains, how we use our minds, and that brain-mind combination, however we sort out what that is.
1.3: We are not particularly fast in the animal kingdom. We're not particularly hardy in the animal kingdom. Our range of comfort and temperature is pretty narrow. But we do have extraordinarily powerful brains, extraordinarily powerful minds, compared to others. The amount of information that we can take in and our capacities for sorting, differentiating, noting similarities, noting differences, repackaging information, drawing inferences, building enormously complex understandings of the world makes us amazingly powerful human beings.
1.4: Now, that takes work. And part of the work is that our brains and our minds, they come as a set of capacities. But a big part of what we need to do is become self-conscious about our capacities and learn how to use them—what they can do, what they can't do, and how to use them properly and improperly. This is going to be primarily a course on logic methods, logic techniques, increasing our sophistication, and being able to understand and evaluate arguments.
1.5: At the end of each lecture, where we go over a certain body of important material, I want you to step back for a few minutes and be philosophical and identify either a point of controversy; because while this is a course that the premise of it is that logic is great and wonderful, not everyone believes that, and there are, in some cases, important controversies within the philosophical traditions of logic or people who are outside of that tradition. So I want to flag, in each case, what those are, or give credit to the giants in the history of logic who developed the important things.
1.6: On that latter score, I want to turn for a few minutes, rather, to Aristotle, who is almost always the person who gets the lion's share of the credit for founding the discipline of logic. This is 2400 years ago in ancient Greece, ancient Greece being an amazing place where all sorts of things were happening in the development of early sciences, literature, political developments, artistic developments, and so forth.
1.7: Aristotle was a student of Plato who was in turn a student of Socrates, and these individuals had already elevated thinking, and to some extent, thinking about thinking, to a higher art. But typically, the lion's share of the credit for founding logic goes to Aristotle to be the one who is making it most explicit. This is what we are doing, developing axiomatic or foundational principles for logic, why logic is the right way for us to use our thinking. Then over the course of several books, developing an impressive array of logical techniques.
1.8: Collectively, those books that Aristotle wrote that are devoted to logic and logical techniques are called the Organon. And as a Greek word, this means a tool. So these are tools of thinking and different tools for different kinds of circumstances. So the first passage I want to draw our attention to is this question of, why is logic so fundamental to human thinking? Our answer can't just be that, "Well, I happen to like being logical." The answer has to be, from this perspective, that logic is what keeps our minds connected to reality, on track with reality, no matter how complicated our thinking is.
1.9: If we push that, this is where it gets controversial, it's the only way that we can be sure, particularly in our highly abstract, highly complicated thinking, that we are being connected to reality. If our goal is to know the real world, know being, know what exists, then we need to have a certain set of techniques, and that needs to be justified. An important historical passage is from one of the books that's typically in the Organon, called the Categories. The statement might not be too impressive to us, but there's a lot built into this.
1.10: "What is makes statements true or false." The idea of an axiom as a founding principle. Where do we start? Where we start on this Aristotelian phrase is with what is, a recognition of reality, a recognition of existence. We might emphasize it, what is, is. Reality is real. Facts are facts. Existence exists. That's where we start. And if we're interested in truth and falsehood, we are making statements and claims and abstract propositions and so forth, we know sometimes those are true and sometimes those are false. It is reality that is the determiner of truth and falsity.
1.11: So statements have to be connected to reality; that makes them true. If we can't connect them to reality, that's a mark of their being false. So, start with what is, and our job is to make all of our statements connected to, or in reflection to that. And that's a very pithy statement, but a lot built into it. As an axiom, we have one that is called the principle of non-contradiction, as it comes through. We have our minds, it gets very complicated, and the rule of logic, the operative rule, is don't contradict yourself.
1.12: If you have a contradiction, you've made a mistake, and that means you need to go back and do a whole lot more work of whatever it is. Aristotle argues that this principle of non-contradiction is also axiomatic in our thinking. Then as mature thinkers, we want to bring it to our conscious, explicit attention. I'm not going to contradict myself in my thinking. The idea is that what is, is. Reality is what it is. It works the way that it does, and that there's some consistent causality.
1.13: Things have an identity, or things have a nature, or certain patterns emerge as a result of reality doing whatever it is that reality is doing. But reality doesn't contradict itself. It is what it is. And that means, in our thinking, we can't come up with contradictions; or we can come up with contradictions, but that means we have made a mistake. So here is Aristotle's formulation of this, for the historical record, from his Metaphysics.
1.14: "Such a principle is the most certain of all; which principle is this? Let us proceed to say. It is that the same attribute cannot at the same time belong and not belong to the same subject in the same respect." So whatever we want to say about reality, reality is X, then we are committed to saying it is X, but it's not also not X. And if I find myself ever saying, well, this thing is X, and then a little bit later, it's also not X, that's where the mistake has happened. Non-contradiction. I need to go back. Is it X, or is it not X?
1.15: And that's the point of the third one, drawing our attention to this principle. Sometimes it's called a principle of either-or. "To hold equally to the opinions and seemings of those disputing against one another is foolish, for clearly one of them is mistaken." So it might be in your own thinking, or it might be in the thinking of two people who are disputing with each other. But if they have a dispute, there's a contradiction, this person says it is, this person says it is not, this person says it is X, this person says it is not X, they can't both be true. It's either this one, or it's that one. And this is the either- or principle.
1.16: So what we have then is Aristotle enunciating what you might think of as four foundational principles or four axioms for logic. First, what is. Start there. Reality comes first, and that's a commitment. It's a fact and it's a commitment. Reality comes first. Our minds, our statements about it, what we come to believe is true, what we come to believe is false, takes its bearings from and has to be connected to what is. That's number two. Non-contradiction. Things are not both having a certain property and not having that property. Then number four, either-or.
1.17: Now, this is historically foundational, and this puts Aristotle, what we call philosophically the small-O objectivist tradition. Objects are what they are or objective reality is what it is. The commitment to logic is the commitment then to being objective. My thinking as a subject is trying to stay in connection with objects or objective reality as it is. And logic is the set of tools increasingly that enables me to do so.
1.18: Now, in the philosophical tradition, there are various challenges attempted to these as axiomatic. If you are interested in the history of logic, that can also be a lot of fun and rewarding reading. There is an analogy here. We are partly physical, partly mental. There's a mind-body integrate of a sorts. But if you think about logic by means of this analogy to physical fitness, one healthy human goal is to have the best physical body you possibly can. And a part of that then means you start to pay attention to your body and you learn its capacities.
1.19: And then at various points, you decide, "I'm going to work out." And what we then do when we are working out is, we're using our body for day-to-day life, but we are self- consciously setting the project of attending to our bodies. And we say, "I need to work on this, that, or the other thing." I want, for example, to have, say, more strength of body. Then I do exercises that will build my strength. I want to have more flexibility in my body. We do exercises to increase the flexibility of our bodies.
1.20: I want to have more endurance to be able to do things over the long term. I do exercises to develop the endurance of my body. By analogy, and slightly metaphorically, the same holds for the use of our minds. We want to have strength of mind. And what that means is to be able to take up difficult problems, ones that require heavy lifting, intellectually hard challenges, not easy problems to solve or things to deal with.
1.21: I also want to have flexibility of mind because one of the things we know is, things change. Sometimes I need to think and rethink and be able to think quickly in a different way and look at things from different perspectives. So the flexibility of mind is also something that we need to practice and train. Then there's an endurance issue as well, so that carries over. Sometimes we don't need to think about something for very long. We can make a decision and act on it. Other things require a lot of thought.
1.22: They require that I have developed my mind so that I can stay with a problem, stay with a challenge, or stay with whatever it is that I'm thinking about for minutes, hours, sometimes days, weeks, before I've done enough thinking to be able to figure out what it is that I want to do. So just as I might say I want to have a lean, mean, powerful body and design workouts and commit myself to a life-long working out to keep my body as healthy as I possibly can, the same thing holds for the mind, and that's what logic primarily is—self-consciously attending to the development of one's mind's capacities over the course of one's life.
1.23: Now, the analogy breaks down a little bit because a lot of what we do physically, in terms of internal processes, is done automatically. I take some stuff into my mouth, I swallow it, it goes into my stomach, hopefully it's mostly nutritious stuff. But at that point, my stomach and the rest of my physiology more or less automatically sorts out what's good for me and what's bad for me. It sorts the good stuff, uses it in various ways automatically, and then automatically gets rid of the stuff that we don't need.
1.24: When we take information in, observations, ideas, suggestions, and we have other things kicking around in our minds, it's not automatic that we are going to sort what's good from what's bad. We have to pay attention to it. One of the things that we do know is sometimes we make a lot of mistakes. We let too much false stuff in, or we can take perfectly good information but combine it in weird ways. And so we end up, as a result of our thinking, not in a place where we want to be. We are fallible in our thinking.
1.25: And this is where logic, in addition to being an enormously important set of exercises, needs to be self-consciously directed. And there's great value to sorting out and learning explicitly what kinds of thinking processes work to preserve truth, to extend our understanding of truth, sometimes to enable us to tease out new ideas and new truths that are not very obvious, and distinguish those from the ways of using our minds. Sometimes they're pretty easy and seductive that lead us astray, so that we can then self-consciously apply our mind.
1.26: Let me give you a couple of examples here. We'll start abstractly, just to make this point here. In this case, it appears in the subject position from our grammar. In this case, over here, both times, it's in the predicate position. The point of this is, and we laugh because it's a ridiculous conclusion to me, but what it tells us is, we started with perfectly good information. Humans are mammals. Pigs are mammals. 1.36: And that tells us, this pattern of reasoning is not a good pattern of reasoning. We'll say it's an invalid pattern when we get to the terminology. 1.37: Some of it we can do by memorizing. So, as I've indicated here, always look for duplication in the predicate. That should be a sign that maybe something is wrong, and then I'll take that one away. Now, logic is also useful in discovery mode. Sometimes we're taking existing information and just repackaging it in a way that's not particularly revelatory. None of you were particularly surprised when I said, "Oh, by the way, humans are mortal beings."
1.38: But logic is useful not only for tidying up our existing knowledge and structuring things in a way perhaps that's more economical, but in figuring out brand new things. And this is where one of its greatest strengths comes along. Let me give you an example from the history of science, and it will sound childish when I tell you the example initially, but it's the way we make progress.
1.39: So one of the questions in ancient societies was, an observant guy noticed that when people work out, we've all noticed this, their skin will get wet. We start to perspire. And this is ancient times, though. They don't have microscopes. They haven't been able to look at the skin very closely, so they're not able to see that human beings have pores through which moisture can pass. So there's a question here, perhaps even a little bit of a mystery question. Where's this water coming from?
1.40: It doesn't seem necessarily like, if you're in some places, as coming from the air; I didn't splash water on myself, but my skin seems like it's pretty solid. So how could water be coming from the inside of me? So question, puzzle. But then this person noticed that one night he had a bucket and he filled the bucket up with water and he would leave it outside for his animals to drink during the night. And then the next morning, he got up, and the bucket was completely empty of water, and there was just a big puddle around the empty bucket.
1.41: So how did the water that was in the bucket get out of the bucket when the bucket is supposed to be a solid, impermeable container? And then he takes the bucket that's now empty and he holds it up to the light and he looks really closely. You can see there are some very tiny holes at the bottom of the bucket. 1.42: This question of water on the skin, maybe it's the case that, on our skin, we have little tiny holes that we can't even see, but they are big enough for water to get through. Now I've got a scientific hypothesis. But how did I get to that scientific hypothesis? By an act of reasoning, I observed a bucket of water that had water in it, that then emptied, and I observed that it had holes. I observed that somehow water is appearing on my skin. And so, by analogy, I'm drawing the conclusion that maybe skin also has holes.
1.43: So we do a lot of analogical reasoning. We have lots of information over here, lots of knowledge over here. Then the way you make that is by making an analogy to the dinosaurs.
1.45: The dinosaurs didn't survive, and why didn't the dinosaurs survive? 1.46: But the point then is, then we need to study lots of analogical patterns, lots of patterns like this, to develop a good sense, sometimes an explicit sense, of what are the good ones and the bad ones. 1.64: So, suppose you go to the island and you say, all right, I'm going to get this figured out. Then I want to be able to study these people, to get lots of information about them to write my new anthropology book or whatever it is. So I go to the island and I get off and I start going along and I encounter a native. And this native comes up to me, and now I want to communicate with this person. So I can start asking him or her questions. Let's suppose it's a him. Start asking him questions. And sometimes he says dal and sometimes he says bal. But I don't know what that is.
1.65: I point to a rock. "Is that a rock?" He says, "Dal." I point to something. "Bal." Do I know what those words mean? No. I don't even know if I can trust this guy to be saying truthfully what it is. It might be that, yes, there's a certain word for rock, but he's a liar. He's trying to mislead me. He'll tell me something else. What can I do to get past this language barrier? Now suppose you're a very clever anthropologist. You've taken some logic. You sit down and you think about it, and you come up with this question that you're going to put to the native.
1.66: You say, "Is your word for yes, bal? Is your word for yes, bal?" And suppose, so this is you, as the anthropologist asking this question, and then the native responds, "Bal." OK. You look at that and then you say, well, he's saying that the word for yes is bal. If he's a truth-teller, it is, but if he's a liar, then it isn't. I don't know if he's a truth-teller or a liar, so I'm stuck. I don't know if I can trust this guy or not.
1.67: But suppose we say, let's do a little logic work on this. We say, well, here we have two things that we don't know. We don't know what bal means. Does it mean yes or no? I don't know if this guy is a liar or a truth-teller. I've got two things that I don't know, and both of them have two possibilities. I've probably taken some math classes or logic classes, and it tells you when, if you have two variables and each of which has two possibilities, there's four overall possibilities. But what are those four possibilities?
1.68: Now, it's just an abstract rule, right? Back from 10th grade math class, it just popped up into my mind, but let's work it through. We could say, well, I don't know if he's a truth- teller or not, but suppose he is a truth-teller. And suppose that bal in their language does, in fact, equal yes. So that's one possibility. This guy's a truth-teller, and bal does mean yes. It could also be that he's a liar and bal means yes. It could also be that the guy's a truth-teller, but bal means no, and so forth. So we figure out what the four possibilities are.
1.69: But this is one possible situation. The guy's a truth-teller and the word bal means yes. So when you ask him that question, "Is your word for yes, bal?", what is the true answer to that question? According to this assumption, "yes" is the right answer that question. And this guy is a truth-teller, so he's going to tell you the right answer to the question. And in his language, the right answer is yes, and that word is bal. So he's going to say, "Bal."
1.70: Now, that was a lot of "if this and this that," with a couple of assumptions built into it. You have to hold all that in your mind to say, yeah, he's going to say bal. Now, on the other hand, suppose the guy is a liar. Another possibility, he's a liar. But in their language, the word bal still means yes. Now, in this case, what's going to happen? You ask this guy, "Is your word for yes, bal?" The correct answer is yes, but he's a liar. So that means he's going to say no. He wants to trick you.
1.71: And in their language, if ball means yes, how do you say no? You say "dal." So he's going to say "dal." Now, that's only two of the possibilities. Suppose we have truth- teller. But in fact, we don't know this guy is a truth-teller, bal means no in their language. So you ask this question, "Is your word for yes, bal?" Well, it isn't. And this guy is a truth-teller. So how is he going to say "no, it isn't," in his language? Well, if bal means no, the right answer is no. So he's going to say "bal."
1.72: And then this is actually the hard one. So once the guy's a liar, you don't know he's a liar yet, you ask him, "Is your word for yes, bal?" And the other assumption is, bal, in fact, means no. So, "Is your word for yes, bal?" It isn't, but he's a liar. So he's going to say it is. And how do you say it is, yes, if the word for bal is no? You will say "dal." Now, we just ran through that pretty quickly. On your own time, double-check, triple-check a few times, see if my reasoning is correct in each case. But if this is correct, and this is some work, we've learned something. What have we learned?
1.73: The guy said to this question, "Bal." That was the response this particular native gave to this question. And the only time someone is going to say "bal," two times that popped up, in both cases, the guy was a truth-teller. So to that question, liars are always going to say "dal," and truth-tellers are always going to say "bal." So now you know at least one thing. You know this guy is a truth-teller.
1.74: Now you've got something to go on. You can say, "I like you. Come with me. I want to do my anthropological research," and you can start learning from him. You can ask him other questions, and you will know that he's a truth-teller. You also now know, since he is a truth-teller, that what he said was true, and that the word for yes is bal. So anytime he says "bal," you've got information. Anytime he says "dal," you've got information.
1.75: Now, this is not obvious. You're only going to get to that and break through this language barrier if you go through that process of logic. This is one of the great values of logic, is the capacity of learning more tools and learning more methods of structuring and restructuring, and in some cases torturing the information to get unexpected things to pop out. And the more of it you do, the better you become at it.
1.76: One of the things that's very common in social circumstances is, the people involved will all have access to the same information. But some people, partly because they've practiced a lot more, they know how to see further implications and repackage the information to get unusual ideas, creative ideas, and new information to pop out. It's enormously valuable.
1.77: Now, another great value for logic is not only learning methods of extracting new kinds of information, but the flexibility point. This takes a certain amount of endurance to be able to go through this and stick with it all the way through. But another thing that's important that logic helps you is learning how to adjust to new information. This is something that's very common with us as human beings. We have lots of information come in. We have a hypothesis or an idea about what it all means. Sometimes because we came up with that new idea, we want that idea to be true.
1.78: But then more information comes in, new information comes in, and you recognize that there's a tension between your earlier hypothesis or your earlier interpretation of this new information. Now, some people, if they're lazy, they don't want to do the reinterpretation work or the rethinking work. They'll just block out that new information. But if you're a good thinker, if you're a careful thinker, and if you are committed to the truth and you say, "Well, this is new information. It seems like it's true information. I have to find a way to make it work with my existing hypothesis, and that might mean changing my hypothesis and doing a certain amount of work."
1.79: Just to take a silly, not really a silly, if it's a cold winter night and your car is dead, but example of this, suppose it is a cold winter night, you go out to your car and you put your key in the ignition, you turn it and your car doesn't start. And then not only that, it doesn't start, it doesn't even crank. So it's not that it tries to start but fails to do so. It's just completely dead. Now you're a person of some experience with cars. So immediately you're going to say, all right, with all of this new data, cold night, car, probably the battery is dead. Chances are very good that's the first hypothesis that comes to mind. And you'll think, probably the battery is dead.
1.80: Then you might remember immediately, "Wait a minute. Just two weeks ago, I had a new battery put in." That's a new piece of information. You're going to then almost instantaneously then rethink, "Well, maybe it's not the battery, or it's less likely that the battery was dead. New battery shouldn't be worn out after two weeks." But then you might remember, you watched the guy putting the battery in, and he seemed a little tipsy, maybe even a little bit drunk.
1.81: He didn't say anything at the time, but maybe he didn't fasten the new battery as tightly as he possibly could have and should have. So something has come loose in a couple of weeks. So now we're back again to thinking, "Oh, tipsy mechanic, cold night, battery, we're probable now." Then you remember maybe your dad, when you got home, checked everything, and your dad said, "No, no, everything looks really good, tight," and so forth. So then you're back saying, "Well, it's not likely the battery again."
1.82: Then you have new information comes in. Finally, you look at the light switch on your dashboard and you see that you left it on. And then you went away for some hours on a cold winter day, so again, the battery. So the point is, new information coming in, hypothesis, weak, strong, weak, strong, back and forth. And all of that is a certain character of mind. You're willing to go through that process, but then also being able to know what to do with the new information and how it affects your previous thinking.
1.83: Now, in more serious cases, if we think about what detectives do, where they go into an enormously complicated situation, they want to figure out who the murderer is, and immediately, it's just overwhelming the amount of information. They have a huge amount of sorting to go through. They're constantly coming up with new hypotheses; new information comes along. This is actually the way, if you read Sherlock Holmes or Agatha Christie or all of these very popular detective shows, they set this up intentionally, where all the initial evidence that they draw your attention to points in a certain direction. This guy is the suspect.
1.84: And then they let you dwell on that for a little while, and then they give you some new information. Then you realize, "I have to rethink everything, go back to the beginning, and now it's like, maybe it's her. She's really the suspect." And it's only through the commitment of that process and the willing to be flexible and to take into account all of the information and look at it at different ways that eventually the detectives figure out whodunnit. Now, we're interested in justice. Justice can only happen in complicated situations if we have people willing to go through that process of logic and are trained, as we want detectives to do so.
1.85: Now, other value questions with respect to logic. I'm going to say that logic is absolutely important to all of us as individuals. Just as we want our bodies to be as healthy and strong as they can be, we want our minds to be as healthy and strong as they can be, and logic is indispensable for doing so. But lots of life involves dealing with other people and the extent to which the parties involved, whether it's just two people or more, are committed to a logical process, those social relationships are going to go well.
1.86: We all know, from often bitter experience, that a lot of people are not committed to logic. That's in many cases why those relationships break down. There might be other factors at work, but they just make stuff up, or they make all kinds of logical leaps, or they don't listen to your reasoning. Of course, sometimes you don't listen to their reasoning because it's often hard to do. There's a complex situation. They've packaged it a certain way, and it seems reasonable here. You've taken the same information but packaged it in a different way.
1.87: But you need to be able to step outside of your framework, see how this person has packaged the information. That person has to also be able to do the same thing. And that's hard. And it requires a commitment. And so it's partly a character issue, but also partly a learning issue. That's in friendships, it's in romantic relationships, it's when you're dealing with kids, when we go out into the business in this world, and we're doing negotiations, when we're talking about very important things in our lives, like politics and what laws are going to govern all of us, what we think about our religious beliefs and how important those are to how we're going to conduct our lives.
1.88: To the extent one is able, on those really complicated things, to use logic effectively in a social context, those things are going to go well. A big part of it is self-defense. Let me give you a hopefully fun example of self-defense. Most of the examples we've been working through is, I gave you a certain amount of information, and there was all of the information available at that moment, and it was a question of, what can we do with this information? In many cases, though, in human reasoning, we don't have all of the information available, that an important part of what we to think about is left implicit or unstated.
1.89: Now, a lot of times this is consciously done because, by the time we are adults, we have a huge amount of knowledge. And in most social circumstances, we know other people also have huge amounts of knowledge and there's lots of shared knowledge, so we don't need to belabor the obvious. So I can say things like, you're heading out the door, and I'm your friend, and I say, "I saw that it might rain; you might want to take an umbrella." That makes perfectly good sense to you.
1.90: I'm not going to say, "You know what? It might rain, and when it rains, water falls out of the sky. If you are outside when water falls out of the sky, it will fall onto you, and then you will get wet. Chances are good, maybe you're going off to work, you don't want to get your work clothes wet. So, if you have an umbrella, what umbrellas do is, they open up and they block the rain from falling onto you, so you'll stay dry and then you'll be comfortable at work."
1.91: Now, all of that is true and all of that is relevant, but we've learned all of that. And so all of that remains explicit, or implicit rather, by the time we become to be adults. And we just say, "Hey, it's going to rain. Take an umbrella," and you fill in automatically all of the rest. We're very powerful minds in that capacity, for being able to assemble all of the relevant information and bring it to bear on a particular case.
1.92: But at the same time, in a social context, while that's useful, people will do these things in sneaky ways. People who know the logic and know the assumptions, they will put you in a position where they want you to answer a question or respond in some way, and they've given you some information, but the most important information has been left out. So standard examples in logic courses, lots of these ones are, people who are hostile, they will ask an attacking bundle question, as we call it.
1.93: So we're at our high school reunion, and I come up to you—we didn't like each other in high school—and I say, "Are you still that jerk you used to be, back in teen years?" Now, immediately you're going to be on the defensive, and that's the right thing to do so. But part of the issue here is that that is a bundled question because the guy is asking you for a yes or no answer. It's an interrogative. Yes or no? "Are you still the same jerk you used to be back in high school days?"
1.94: But the problem is, if you say yes, then what are you saying? You're saying, "Yes, I used to be a jerk, and I'm still a jerk." And he likes that answer. But if you say no, which is the other logical possibility, then what you're saying is, "No, I'm not a jerk anymore, but yes, I used to be." You're implicitly granting that assumption. In that case, what has happened is, in a social context, the person has bundled a certain amount of information, but assumes something as given. He doesn't even need to state it or defend it explicitly. "You used to be a jerk back in high school."
1.95: It's only to the extent that you recognize complex bundles of information, and you're able then quickly to unbundle those pieces of information, say, "Well, wait, there's two issues here, the past and the present. Which one do you want to take up first?" And so you immediately push it back. But also at the same time, going back to our analogical reasoning, chances are good you've dealt with other people who are obnoxious and verbally attacking and so forth in your life.
1.96: And so you've learned some lessons from them, and you say, "Oh wait, this guy is acting like all of these other people over in the past. Those were problem people. Those relationships didn't work out. I probably don't want to deal with this guy." So then you say, take all of that, apply it to this case, and you set the guy aside. Very useful logic as a tool of self-defense. One more motivational thing, that's in individual social context. If we elevate this to very important issues, where logic and a commitment to logic becomes absolutely crucial, not only to individual relationships, but legal principles, the conduct of law, and so on.
1.97: I like always to reflect on the example of John Adams before Independence, when John Adams was a lawyer, and the British and the colonial Americans, there was tension between them, borderline riots, and some British soldiers had shot into a crowd of Americans who were getting a little uppity. It's not quite clear who instigated it, who was in the right and who was in the wrong, but British soldiers shot, Americans ended up dead.
1.98: There was then immediately an outcry among the early Americans and beginnings of a lynch mob. "We're just going to storm, take all the British soldiers, and just basically kill all of them." That likely would have happened. It didn't matter which one did the shooting, it didn't matter who started or not. But the police were able to defuse the situation. The British retreated, things tempered down, and then there was going to be a trial. At this point, with tempers running high, the question of taking this to a trial is already a commitment to logic, and the logic commitment is bundled with a commitment to civil decency and justice.
1.99: The only way we are going to figure out in this situation, even though someone has died, what the right thing to do, who is guilty and who is innocent, is to put it before a court of law. And what we're going to do in the court of law is, we have two possible positions. The British acted wrongly or the British acted correctly. And we're going to gather as much evidence as we possibly can, and that's going to be a lot of evidence, including all of the eyewitnesses' testimonies.
1.100: We're going to cross-examine them. We're going to see if the arguments can be put together for guilty, for not guilty. The best way, put them in collision with each other. Then and only then, when we go through that process, will we have a best, just verdict. We'll probably get the right answer, but just by committing ourselves to that logical process of evidence and argumentation and counter-argumentation, are we showing what our commitments are?
1.101: One of the things that made John Adams' reputation was that he was willing, even though he was a colonial American, to be the defense attorney for the British and to make the best arguments possible for the British defendants in that case. It was a matter of principle for him. It doesn't matter my American loyalties or my British loyalties. Those are not relevant to the truth and the justice of the matter. The logic matters. We're going to go through this logical process.
1.102: That's logic and why it matters. What I want to do next is turn to more formal methods and start from the beginning and do logical analysis from the ground up. Some technical terminology and some foundational nuts and bolts with respect to the logic. One of the things that we do in reasoning, of course, is we take the existing facts on the ground or the ones that are available, and we've got them organized in a certain way, is try to break them down to as far as we possibly to their component parts.
1.103: But then also we take this chunk that we've integrated and we put it together with another chunk over here to build a larger structure. By analogy, I often think of a car and mechanics. You can look at the car engine, and it all works together. If you know what you're talking about, and this is not necessarily me, you can say, "Ah, that's the fuel injector, that's the break fluid, that's where the transmission is. Those are the pistons and spark plugs." There's all of those elements, and you can see how they are working together.
1.104: But one thing you do want to be able to do, if you're a good mechanic, is get really into it and say, "This is the transmission," and be able to take it apart and see all of its moving parts. A certain amount of what we will be doing is looking at relatively simple arguments, like the ones we've had on here. How do we take them apart, look at their component parts, and see how they are put together? Another part of it, this is typically more advanced, is then how do we deal with more complex arguments and networks of arguments all the way up? We'll work our way through this course as much as possible in there.
1.105: Now, the first thing is the word argument itself. In logic, we use argument precisely. If two people are just yelling at each other, that "you're an idiot," "no, you're an idiot," "no, you're a bigger idiot," "no, you're an even bigger idiot," that's not an argument as far as the logicians. That's just people yelling at each other. An argument is a structure of propositions where you take one piece of information and you make the claim that something else follows from that.
1.106: So if the one person had said, "No, you are an idiot because," and then gave a reason, then we've got two things. There's the reason, and now we have the conclusion, "you're an idiot." Let's try to come up with something a little less insulting if we possibly can. That then is to say, an argument is always going to have two components. One is the conclusion. What is being argued for? What are you trying to establish? What are you trying to prove, either for yourself or, if it's in a social context, what do you want the other person to come to agree to?
1.107: The argument has a conclusion. It also has a premise or premises. The premise or premises, those are the reasons that are given in support of the conclusion. Think of the conclusion as, what am I supposed to believe? And the premise is, why should I believe that? Now, that's the nuts and bolts, but that's how we'll be using these concepts throughout the course.
1.108: Here, let's read through this first argument. I just took it straight out of Aristotle's Politics. "In a democracy, the poor have more power than the rich, because there are more of them, and the will of the majority is supreme." Now, in this case, we have three claims. First, in a democracy, the poor have more power than the rich. We have another claim. We say there are more of them. And the" them", this pronoun refers to the poor, so we might substitute the word poor. There are more poor people in society than there are rich people.
1.109: And, that conjunction, the will of the majority is supreme. That's how democracies do what they do, by means of the will of the majority. To say that it's supreme, that's connected to the word power. The will of the majority, that's connected to the word democracy. We have a nice tight connection, but sometimes the verbal formulations are a little bit. Now, this is an argument, three pieces of information. Which one is the conclusion and which are the premises?
1.110: In this case, we would say, well, what he's trying to prove is that in a democracy, the poor have more power than the rich. I'd like to just indicate that with a little c. That's what I think the conclusion of the argument is. It makes sense to say that that is the conclusion. Well, why should I believe this, Aristotle? And he gives us some reasons. He says, "Well, there's more people who are poor in a democracy, and whoever is the more, the majority, they are the ones who have the most power."
1.111: So I reconstruct this in my mind. We say, there's more poor people than rich people, and in a democracy, the poor people have the power, then it follows that poor people have the most power in a democracy. Now, another thing. One thing that's useful is that, in English and various other languages, we have developed concepts or words that we use to indicate whether something is a premise or an indicator. Surprisingly, we call these indicator concepts, conclusion indicators and premise indicators.
1.112: You've got these largely automated as adult thinkers and conversers, but it's worthwhile to highlight explicitly the various kinds of concepts and which ones they are. In this case, I would, when I'm learning logic, circle that word. That word is a premise indicator. And anytime you see the word "because", it tells you that the person is now going to give you the reasons. They're going to indicate the premises. And it almost always means that the thing just before that is the conclusion.
1.113: So in a democracy, the poor have more power than the rich. Well, why should I believe that? Well, Aristotle says, because, or by the cause of, for these reasons. There are various other words that we might use that would be synonyms at this point. I could, in this case, instead of the word because, I could have put the word "since." The poor have more power than the rich, since there's more of them, and blah, blah, blah. Or I could say, for the reasons that, really just belabor the point, for the reasons that, or as, or for, and there's a whole number of them.
1.114: So what I recommend is, when you're practicing this method initially, and it's good to practice it this way, start to mark things up when you are looking at various arguments. Sometimes it's a little bit obvious in the easier cases, but it's a useful skill to have when you're starting to deal with more complicated pieces of reasoning. In many cases, you'll read some long passage and you know there's an argument in there, but the passage is kind of confusing, and it might not be your fault. It might be that the person is not a very clear writer, or it just might be that this is a complicated amount of information.
1.115: If you can identify that's a premise, and just put a little p next to it, that's a premise, that's got to be the conclusion, put a little c at it, and then go through that way, then reread it with that information in mind, your comprehension oftentimes will go up a lot more. In this case, we have the will of the majority. That's a premise, and there's another premise there.
1.116: All right, let's try this one. Doctors should never lie to terminally ill patients, for one ought never to lie, and patients have a right to know their condition. What would we say in this case? Well, I've got this piece of information. Doctors should never lie to their terminally ill patients. You might be tempted to. You don't want to hurt the person's feelings. Then we have this claim here. One ought never lie. And we have this claim here. Patients have a right to know their condition. This one seems to be speaking about an obligation that one has, as a physician or as a doctor. This one is talking about patients and a right that they have.
1.117: We have this word in the middle, for. I would circle that. That is a premise indicator. If we read that, then to say, well, this is probably the conclusion. The person wants you to say, "You shouldn't lie to terminally ill patients." Well, why not? It makes sense to say, well, for these reasons. You should not lie, in the first place, and the patients have a right to know. If I reconstruct it, one should never lie, therefore, follows that physicians should not lie to their patients. If it's the case that, the other premise, patients have a right to know about their condition, then it follows that doctors should not lie to them about their condition. So it follows. This is a conclusion indicator.
1.118: Try this one. We can't go to the concert and clean up the apartment tonight. But as we are hosting that dinner tomorrow, we've got to clean the place up tonight. So the concert is out. We can't do both of these things. New information. We're hosting a dinner tomorrow. We've got to clean the place up tonight. Concert is out. We can't go to the concert. Now, in this case, I would circle this word, so. When we use the word so, we're almost always indicating a conclusion. This is what we're trying to get to.
1.119: In these cases here, I gave the conclusion first, then the supporting reasons. Conclusion first, supporting reasons. In this case, I'm laying out my reasoning, and then at the end, we get to the conclusion. How does this one work? Well, we have an option here. We can go to the concert or we can go to or stay home and clean up the place. Then, as I said, this one I have to give priority to, cleaning up the place.
1.120: Why? I give a reason for that. I've got these two options. I'm going to give this one a priority. Why? Well, because tomorrow we're having a dinner, so we have to clean up the place tonight, but we can't do that and this other thing here as well, go to the concert. So, big conclusion, concert is out. We're not going to the concert. End of that chain of reasoning.
1.121: Now, let's try this fellow. Rabbits are a type of fish. Since fish have fuzzy ears, it follows that rabbits have fuzzy ears. I'm glad to see smiles. Rabbits are a type of fish. Oh. Word since, what is since? It's not a conclusion indicator, it's a premise indicator. I could put the word because here. Then I've got this other claim, fish have fuzzy ears. I've got this little phrase here, it follows that. This is a conclusion indicator. It follows that. Well, something follows, logically follows. This is going to be a conclusion indicator. This is what I'm trying to argue for or prove. Rabbits have fuzzy ears.
1.122: Now, this is puzzling because when we see an argument like this, and we do see lots of arguments like this, not as blatant as this typically, we start to get confused because there's obviously some bizarre information in this argument. But nonetheless, it is an argument, even if it is going to end up being a bad argument for obvious reasons. What we do need to do is develop our habit of being able to see what the argument is and not let the distracting falseness of this particular piece of information confuse us and lead us not to do whatever.
1.123: Good argument or not, nonetheless, the argument is, the person says rabbits have fuzzy ears. Now, interestingly, that's a true piece of information. Rabbits do have fuzzy ears. But that piece of truth is largely irrelevant to the truth of the premises here. We've got false information. Rabbit are not a type of fish. Fish don't have fuzzy ears, but nonetheless, somehow we still end up with a good conclusion. That's illuminating right off the bat then, to say, well, I've got false information, but somehow I ended up with the truth. Was it a coincidence, or is there something else at work here as well? But at least I know what the argument is, and I can put it in standard form.
1.124: Let me read through a few examples. As I want to say my hometown, Toronto, is going to win the championship because they have the best field goal kicker in the league. Train your ear to pick out the word "because." That's a premise indicator. He's claiming that the reason why Toronto is going to win is they have the best field goal kicker, therefore, they're going to win. The indicator concepts, what I would recommend is, for further self-study, is make yourself a list of premise indicators and conclusion indicators. Any good logic book will include those. You can also have lots of online sources that will do so.
1.125: Just make them part of your mental furniture. So you know premise, conclusion, argument, and you have a whole list of indicator concepts, more or less automated. This is very useful because the very first thing we always need to do is learn how to take arguments, however they come at us, and put them in what we call standard form. There's this premise, this premise, and then the conclusion, or however many premises they are. But that's not typically how arguments come at us. And knowing what the indicator concepts are will immediately do a lot of the sorting for you.
1.126: It's very common, particularly among adults, for people just to give information in any particular order. I can say, for example, Socrates is a human, and humans are mortal, so Socrates is mortal. Now, I give a little boost to the word "so" there. You know the conclusion is, so Socrates is mortal. But I can give you that same argument. It is the same argument, same information, but in a different order. I could say, since humans are mortal, Socrates must be a mortal, as he is a human being. That's exactly the same argument, different order in this case.
1.127: But I've got some indicator concepts that help you out, as he is a human being, since humans are mortal. So then you know what you're looking for. Or I could give you the conclusion up front. Socrates is mortal. After all, he's a human being, and human beings are mortal. In this case, "after all" is another kind of premise indicator. After all, here's all of the other information, and after that comes the conclusion. So the more you practice this, the more automatic and the more fluid your thinking is going to be.
1.128: Next complication. We've indicated this before that, very often as adults, people do not give you all of the information. But what we want to do, if we're going to do logical analysis, is get the argument out fully and completely. We could do that very laborious thing about umbrellas and the rain and not getting wet. If we are, for example, going to be talking to a computer, we have to have all of that information out and feed it into the computer to put it together, at least in the beginning.
1.129: When we were little children, we had to go through all of that process and have a certain amount of experience to put all of that information together, so that we know about making umbrella-taking a habit under certain circumstances. This is another thing to start practicing. Almost always when you have one premise and one conclusion, there's almost always a missing piece. In that case, technically, we call the argument an enthymeme.
1.130: So if you're up on winning Trivial Pursuit-type games and knowing the terminology, the word is enthymeme, an enthymematic argument. That is to say, arguments that are incomplete are common, and they're not necessarily a bad thing. Sometimes we are saving people's energy. So I might say, Socrates is a man. Sorry, I might say Socrates is mortal because he's a man. It doesn't follow, he's a man, therefore he's mortal. I need to have a connection between the man concept and mortal. But then there's that obvious piece of information. Human beings are mortal, and we just fill that in.
1.131: When I was a young faculty member, I was at a party, and there was a woman who was making a joke from a feminist perspective. We were talking about another colleague who had said something a little bit off-color, and she said, "Well, of course he's a chauvinist. He's a man, isn't he?" Now, that's an argument, but it takes a little bit of massaging. So this is where I want to take a moment. Suppose I say, "Of course he's a chauvinist. He's a man, isn't he?" Now, in this case, we have two pieces of information. Claim that he's a chauvinist and that he's a man.
1.132: Now, we start to do the analysis. We start to say things like, well, what's she trying to get us to believe? What does she want us to believe? He is a chauvinist. I'll just abbreviate the chauvinist with C, that's the conclusion. There's no conclusion indicators here, no premise indicators, so we have to figure it out from context in this case. Well, why? The argument is, he's a man. This is actually put in the form of a question, but this is a rhetorical question.
1.133: One of the things we learn is, often rhetorical questions are to be translated into a declarative statement. But if you're trying to make a joke, or sometimes if you're trying to be sneaky, rhetorical questions are useful because you know that people have to do the additional work to figure out, what does this rhetorical question mean literally, and what other assumptions are involved? Now, in this case, it's not particularly complicated, but what you look for is, we have he here, we have he here, he is connected to M, he is connected to C here. We need to connect M and C somehow, to make this logical tightness work.
1.134: Then the claims are going to be something like, men are chauvinists. That's the general claim. If men are chauvinists and he's a man, then it does follow, logically, that he is a man. That's the argument that we are dealing with. But then we would say in this case, probably this is the overstatement question. But you're not going to get to the overstatement, a claim, rather, that's being made, unless you do this initial work, or you can pull out, "Wait a minute. There is this assumption here. Your argument was an enthymeme." Now that we make this explicit, we can talk about this. Now, this is not what you want to do at the party, but this is the logical work that will have to be done.
1.135: All right, how about this joke? I hope it's a joke. "Every fourth child born in the world is Chinese. Mrs. O'Reilly is expecting her fourth child..." Now, good. That's a little bit of humor. But what makes it funny? Well, in order to get the joke, you have to do a certain number of things. You have to take "every fourth child born in the world is Chinese" and interpret it a certain way. One of the things that we learn as adults is that some formulations are somewhat ambiguous.
1.136: We could say every fourth child in the world who's born might mean, well, this one, then this one, then this one, then there's the fourth one. There's a sequence way of using that. But sometimes we say "every fourth child in the world" is to use percentages. All we mean is, not in sequence, which is 25% of all the children who are born in the world are born to Chinese people. We deliberately misinterpret that one to make it a sequence thing.
1.137: Then we make it more ridiculous by choosing an obviously Irish ethnic last name. Mrs. O'Reilly is expecting her fourth child. If she's Irish, she's not Chinese, then it makes it absurd, the inference, but also notice the inference is not made. The inference in this case is, this argument is an enthymeme, but we just use our logical sense and we say, "Oh, so the person is trying to say, Mrs. O'Reilly's child is going to be born Chinese. Ha, ha, ha."
1.138: All of that is going on, but what was interesting, if you monitor your own reaction, is that that happened in half a second. All of that happened. That's good. That's a sign that you are a mature reasoner, but we need to start at the beginning. Suppose we were explaining this to a computer or a four-year-old. A huge amount of information, go slowly and carefully. That's what we are in the habit of doing.
1.139: All right. Final thing, piece of terminology for breaking down arguments and putting us in a position to evaluate them. We know what the premises are, we know what the conclusions are, we have the ways of filling in any missing pieces that are there, so it's no longer an enthymeme, we have the complete argument. We have indicator concepts for conclusions, for premises, to help us sort out which one is which.
1.140: The next thing is going to be the terminology that takes us into evaluating arguments. Once we've got the argument in front of us, it's complete. We know what the premises are, we know what the conclusions are, any missing pieces, we have added them. It's complete. It's before us. Our next question, of course, is, is this a good argument or is this a bad argument? In many cases, this is important to go through these steps ruthlessly and train yourself always to go through these steps.
1.141: Because as we know, one of the things that happens in social conversations that don't go very well is that people are not careful in figuring out what the argument is before they launch into criticisms. They're very quick to start evaluating, but in many cases, they miss some subtlety that's in the argument or misinterpret it in some bad way. So at least at the very beginning, be careful, be careful, be careful all the way through.
1.142: So I've got three arguments out here. They are complete, but they're all basic arguments. So Aristotle is human. Aristotle, humans are mortal, so therefore, Aristotle is mortal. The concepts we want to introduce for evaluating are two concepts. One is the concept of truth, and the other is the concept of valid. These two concepts pick up two different aspects of evaluating an argument.
1.143: By analogy, suppose you were on a shopping trip, a little mathematics example. You went on a shopping trip, you bought a whole bunch of things, and then you get home and you say, "How much did I spend?" And then you start to write down all of the things you bought and how much they cost. Then you add all of that up and you get a certain number. Is that the correct number of how much you spent? It could be true. Sorry, it could be the right number, but that would depend on all of the things that you bought, you remembered them and you got the right amount.
1.144: And it would also depend on that you did addition correctly, with respect to all of those numbers. There's two possible sources of error. One is that you got a number wrong, the other is that you made an addition mistake. By exact parallel, truth and validity are capturing the same thing in logic circles. In this case, with respect to truth, we can apply, say, the truth filter. We would just say, well, here's a premise that the argument depends on. Is that true or not? Look at that premise in isolation and ask that one question. We'd say, yeah, that's true.
1.145: Humans are mortal. Look at that premise in isolation. Is that true or not? Say, yes, that is true. Now, the follow-up question, since we're doing an argument, and the point of an argument is to take some information and draw an inference from it or make an inference from it, if this is true and this is true, we put these two pieces of information, does it follow logically that Aristotle must be mortal? If our answer to that question is yes, if that's true, and if that's true, this has to be true, then the argument is valid.
1.146: What we are attending to is not the truth or falsity of the individual components, but the form of the logic or the structure of the reasoning that we engaged in. In this case, we would say, this follows logically. That's the same thing in logic as saying it's a valid argument. Truth, do the pieces of information correspond to reality? Validity, have you structured that information and drawn an inference in a way that preserves truth? And both of those are important.
1.147: So in this case here, Aristotle is human. Humans are mortal. Therefore, water freezes at zero degrees celsius. Well, this is true, this is true, the same true information. But in this case, obviously, the conclusion bears no relationship whatsoever to the premises. It doesn't follow. If this is true, that water freezes at zero degrees, this is not the reasons why. So this is a bad argument. So in this case, we say this is an invalid argument. You can have perfectly good information, but not do good stuff with it. You end up with something that's not relevant.
1.148: In this case, rabbits are a species of fish. False. Fish have fuzzy ears. False. Rabbits have fuzzy ears. Well, we're supposed to see if the conclusion follows from the premises or not. If it were the case that rabbits are a species of fish and fish had fuzzy ears, would it follow that rabbits have fuzzy ears? The answer to that question is yes. This is the same pattern as that first pattern over there. This is a valid argument. The premises are false, but using that information and structuring it to draw this conclusion, this follows.
1.149: This is probably the first mental barrier that one has to get past. You have to be very comfortable with saying perfectly valid argument, even though the information is false. With that, we will pause on this first unit. We now have some skills under our belt, separating premises and conclusions, knowing what premise indicators are, knowing that we have to make sure we're filling in some missing pieces to have the entire argument before us, practicing, putting things in standard form, listing all of the premises, followed by the conclusion, then starting the evaluative work.
1.150: Go through all the premises and ask, given your knowledge, does that seem true or false? Whatever your state of knowledge is. Then the logic part that we especially are going to be, if that information is true or false, we set that aside for the moment. Does this conclusion follow, logically, from those premises? We'll go on to do more sophisticated stuff in the next lecture. Lecture 2: Concepts & Our Cognitive Hierarchy At a glance — Concepts and our cognitive hierarchy.
2.1: The 18th century thinker Voltaire, he of the razor-sharp logic and razor-sharp wit, once said, "When enlightened men go on arguing for a long time, there's a distinct possibility that the question is not clear." This is an occupational hazard for us as thinkers about abstract things and complicated things. It's very easy for our thinking to get fuzzy, in our own thinking, but also for people to be using words in overlapping but sometimes distinct ways.
2.2: So one of the important elements of logic is paying attention to the concepts that we are using to build up our propositions and make sure that we are, in our own thinking, clear how we are using the words that we are using and certainly in a social context. Now, one way of approaching this is to say, well, if you think of a standard argument, "All human beings are mortal, Aristotle is a human being, therefore, Aristotle is moral, or mortal," well, already in there, I've got a number of abstract concepts, mortal, mortality, human being, a concept of all human beings.
2.3: And then relationships between those concepts start to develop. And we have a proper name. Aristotle is a particular being whom we've assigned a proper name. Do I know what all of those concepts mean? And in a social context, will we be using those concepts univocally? So your thinking is mapping onto my thinking as well. That's an important part of the logical analysis process, but it's also a part of seeing logic as an integral part of what is actually a broader human cognitive apparatus. I want to spend a little time putting logic in that slightly broader context.
2.4: Here, logic develops tandemly with developmental psychology. If we imagine for the moment a baby that has just been born, and we tell a story about likely human cognitive development, from just being born all the way up to mature adult thinker, it really is an impressive process. Partly, what makes this process impressive is that we typically think of humans coming from infancy to adulthood as being a process that takes a dozen years or more. You're not really an adult until you are significantly into your teens, and maybe not even then.
2.5: If you contrast that with the cognitive development of all most other animal species, even intelligent species like, say, dolphins and dogs and so forth, it's usually a matter of two years, three years, or four years until they have reached their cognitive peak, so to speak, and they are ready to function fully as adults. But then if we look at our three- year-olds and our four-year-olds, they're just getting warmed up. They're already impressive in a lot of ways, but they still have a lot to do.
2.6: I want to start by putting some developmental structures and some claims about them along the way. The first thing that we start off with is by having sensations. A child is born, the child is born fully healthy, you have five sense organs, and they immediately start giving us information about the environment. So light energy, chemical energy, sound energy, tactile energy, more chemical structures with respect to tastes and so forth. So all of this information starts, say, impinging upon the baby fresh out of the womb, so to speak.
2.7: Fairly quickly and almost automatically, the child rises to the level of perception. What we mean by perception is integrations of sensations. So again, I'm appealing to some developmental psychology claims, but you take a fresh baby, born baby, looks, eyes, and there's just all this stuff impinging upon the eyes. But very quickly, babies are able to recognize their mothers, because obviously the mother has a vested interest in getting to know her child as soon as possible.
2.8: But at the beginning, there's just all these color patches and things moving around in the visual field. But at a certain point, that face with the two eyes and the mouth integrated as a unit, that's now a perception. It's not just a bunch of sensory stimuli happening. If the mother's face goes away but comes back, the child recognizes it as the same integrated unit. If the mother's face moves across the infant's visual field, it's not just changing visual fields all over, it's, there's background, visual face, and you can see the child tracking the mother's face.
2.9: Now, this happens also with the other sensory modalities. We start to integrate bundles of sensations into what we call percepts, and we are aware of objects now out there in the environment. Now, this also happens with most other animal species. What seems to be largely distinctive, this is another developmental psychology claim, it may not be that we are unique, but we are among a small group of beings that have the next cognitive power, which is what we call conception. That is to take a bunch of percepts and bundle them and integrate them into a new mental unit, but one that is now abstract, and we start to learn words.
2.10: So this happens immediately. This happens within minutes and then, with increasing sophistication, typically over the course of the child's life, even on into adulthood. This typically starts to happen when kids start having their first words. Because then what we know when they start using the first words is, they are using those words to designate classes of things.
2.11: So it might be the case that there's the mom and the dad, maybe they have a family dog, and maybe the neighbors have a dog. So at some point, the kid is going to learn the word dog, but then you might be out riding or the parents might be out riding with the kid, and there's another dog out on the street, and the kid will say dog. And that then is not a proper name for that particular percept. And dog is not the name for this particular percept. It's that there's this category that's more abstract, of a certain being, and the one at home and this one and the other one down the street are all members of that particular category.
2.12: Now, there is some evidence that some dolphins have some concepts, some chimpanzees have some concepts, and that's an open-ended question in animal psychology and human psychology. Human beings definitely have it, typically kicks in seven, eight, nine months, and then it's another open-ended process where we start to have all kinds of categories until, these are some estimates by linguists, the average high school graduate in North America has about 10,000 such words. Those words stand for concepts that he or she all understands. The average college graduate has about 25,000 such words kicking around.
2.13: Now, just a couple of examples about the difference between the conceptual level and the perceptual level, because this is very important. Standard examples we use is, you take a hen, a chicken, the female chicken. There's one species of chicken that is a speckled hen. And these ones, characteristically, are not all white or beige like a lot, but they have lots and lots of speckles on them. We can, as other animal species can, look at that hen and we can perceive the hen as a unit, as an integrate, and we can see distinctly all of the speckles that are on it.
2.14: But we have no idea how many speckles the hen has, just by looking at it. But we can, if we learn this, we can learn to count. Then we could take the chicken, probably against its will, and then say, I'm going to count every single speck on here. We end up, it's not going to enable me to perceive the chicken any better, but I might then reach the conclusion, because I have these mathematical concepts, there are 872 speckles on this chicken, and that's different from 871 and 874. The math is going to be different. I am thinking now conceptually about the nature of that chicken.
2.15: This is learned, and it's important to understand that it is learned, because this is where we have to start doing extra effort to figure out what we're doing with all of these bundled concept categories that we are using, what's included, what's not included, to make sure we're in a position to build more sophisticated structures. This is learned. There are some fascinating experiments that have been done.
2.16: So we use the example of counting. It might seem like counting is pretty basic and it would come more or less naturally to human beings. But there is some evidence that it is not something that comes naturally, that it has to be discovered and then transmitted by learning to each of the next generation. There were some anthropologists who were studying a tribe in one of the Indonesian islands, there's thousands of them, and this was a tribe that was still Stone Age in its technology and quite remote. So they just went and they started to study them. And the tribe, they were perfectly fine with this.
2.17: And they had some fairly sophisticated things, sophisticated buildings, so to protect them from the elements. And they were at the stage of agricultural because they had goats, and they had built enclosures to keep their goats at night. But they had a job assigned to the young boys of the tribe, which was, every morning, take the goats out of the enclosure and take them out into the meadows and forests where they could feed, and at the end of the day, bring the goats back in. But it's important. Goats are valuable. These are an important animal, to keep track of all of your goats.
2.18: And so there would be a boy who would be assigned, when the goats were coming out of the enclosure. There's a big pile of pebbles there. Every time a goat came out of the enclosure, take one of the pebbles off this pile and start a new pile here. So that kid would just stand there doing this, and then all of the goats would be gone. And if you asked, how many goats does the tribe have? The answer would be this many. This pile of stones represents. But they did not have counting concepts. It wasn't for them, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
2.19: And this became very apparent and became important because, at the end of the day, the goats would all come back, the boys would bring them back, and one of the boys would have the job, take all the stones here. Goat comes in, goat comes in, goat comes in. It's a good day if you have no stones left over at the end of that process. But what happens if there are stones left over? In some situations, the anthropologist would be in, where they would say, oh, there are eight stones there. That means there are eight goats missing. We have to go out and find eight goats.
2.20: The problem was, there could be eight stones there, but the boys had no idea how many goats were still out there. It's like the speckled hen. There's just a bunch of stones there. If it was 15 or 13, so they wouldn't be able to go out, for example, and say, "We know we are looking for eight goats. Find the eight goats and bring them back." Or they go out there and they only find six goats. We've counted them, we bring them back, but now we know, even before the stones, that we still have to find two more goats.
2.21: So the point of all of this is, conception, abstract mathematical concepts, which is one important category, it's learned, and the precision of being able to use those kinds of concepts, logically, is an important learned skill. One other famous experiment that I'd like to talk about, it wasn't formally an experiment, it was actually a semi-formal experiment. It goes back to the 1880s, about the difference between perception and conception. There's still an ongoing question about how intelligent crows are, and they're pretty smart for birds.
2.22: But this guy was Sir John Lubbock. He was a hunter, and what they did, I'll draw a little picture here, there was some sort of a clearing here. There's a bunch of trees over here. So a little bit of woods. Then there was a path that came out of some other woods over here. Over here in the woods, right at the edge, there was a little cabin. And what typically would happen is that these crows, I suppose I should draw the trees in green and the crows in black, there's the crows that would come down and hang out here in the evening, to do whatever crows do in the evening, but there's a whole flock of crows.
2.23: So what Sir John noticed was that he would come through here. The crows would see him when he appeared, and then they would fly up into the trees for safety, and then he would go into the cabin, and the crows would not come out until he left this cabin. Let me make it more clear that that's a cabin. That's the chimney. When he left the cabin and went away, then the crows would say, "OK, fine, it's safe for us to come back," and they would come down again.
2.24: So he was curious how smart crows are. So he got a buddy, and the two of them would come through here. Crows would fly up into the trees. They would go into the cabin, and they would try to trick the crows. So just one of them would leave, go back along this pathway here, and then what would the crows do? They would stay up in the trees. They would not come down. They know that there's two, only one left. There's some rudimentary—I don't know if I want to call it arithmetic yet, but they're able to perceive the difference between one and two, and remember the difference between one and two, and then that matters.
2.25: Well, let's try it with three. Three guys come in, three go into the cabin, and after the crows have flown up, two of them leave. What do the crows do? Big mystery, the crows stay up in the trees. They don't come down until the third person leaves. Then the crows know it's safe, and then they come down. Next iteration of this semi-formal experiment, four people come through, crows fly up, they go four of them into the cabin. Three of them leave. There's still one in there. What do the crows do? The crows come down and they start to feed again.
2.26: So, from their perspective, it's like their math is one, two, three, many, and it just becomes undifferentiated at that point. So when it was four, it was more like, many came, many left. End of the story. All right, now human beings, of course, we can operate at that level in our thinking as well, but we can be four, five, six, and we have these open-ended processes. The point is that that is all learned.
2.27: Now, the next thing that we start to do is, once we have words, if we go back to a developmental thing, children typically build up an arsenal of single words—blanket, food, drink, mommy, daddy, dog, etc. But then at some point, they start putting the words together. There's a further integration. So the sensations are integrated into percepts. Percepts are integrated into concepts, and we start to speak in sentences. And a sentence will be an integration of concepts.
2.28: So, Aristotle is mortal. So I know who Aristotle is. I know what mortality is. Probably not when I'm one year old, but Aristotle is tall. I know what tall is. I've got some height and some length concepts. Aristotle is tall. So I know tall, I know Aristotle, but I put those together as a new unit. Or the mother can say, "Where is your blanket?" And the child might then be able to say, "My blanket is in my room." Blanket, a possessiveness, room as a certain place, my room, relationship between the blanket and that particular place. That's pretty sophisticated. That's five or six mental elements all being integrated into one sentence.
2.29: And so then we know we are increasingly able to make more complicated sentences as we mature. So we can say things like, read in a story, "The quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog and escaped from the henhouse with the prize clamped firmly between its jaws." So what was that? Sixteen, eighteen words, and it's easy even when you're four years old. That's how sophisticated we have become.
2.30: And then we start to do more sophisticated things, individual sentences. Parents, when they start reading to their children, we start to have storybooks where we'll take individual sentences and we start stringing them together to tell a little story about what happened to Peter Rabbit or whatever the story is. So we start to do what we call narratives, and we have complexes then of sentences that are connected in various ways, and we want them to be connected logically, so that the causal events of the story fit together and everything ultimately makes sense.
2.31: We also go on, since often narratives are fictional, then to develop more sophisticated theories, which are whole networks of propositions about the way the world works. Just as an example, I always think of at this point, because all of the younger kids that I know have gotten to this stage quite sophisticatedly, usually by grade 2. I remember growing up in Canada, even in grade 2, then when I moved to the United States, kids were doing the same thing. So there must be a universality about this.
