2.32: But the weather cycle, and at some point, every kid in grade 2 comes home with a picture he or she has drawn of the weather cycle. And what it does is, just put it up here, is, I'll say, here's the sun, and here is a lake, and then here's a little stream, and then on it, there will be some water and there will be some squiggly lines that say this water from the heat of the sun evaporates and it goes up. So we put a little arrow here, and then it forms clouds. I should have paid more attention in art class instead of logic class.
2.33: But as it goes up, it also cools. So we build in this knowledge about cooling, and the clouds get heavier and heavier, and then it's going to fall down as rain, and then this is going to flow into the sea. Then there's going to be the ocean, and the same thing is going to be happening here. Sometimes there's the wind that blows the clouds over here, so sometimes it's raining. We have this sophisticated drawing. But we have lake, rivers, oceans, sky, heating, cooling, water in various states, and the kid gets it. This is our little theory about the weather cycle at age six or seven years old.
2.34: But that's a theory. That's a lot of abstractions, a lot of sentences based on certain concepts and observations and so on. And it's open-ended, so as we grow to adulthood, our theories get more complicated. We start off reading just short little books, three, four, five pages, mom and dad with the kids. We progress to chapter books, which might be as long as 30 pages or so. And then by the time we are young adults or into adulthood, we're hopefully reading novels or even multi-novel series, and we are keeping the story arc going and so on. So it's an open-ended, extraordinarily complicated process.
2.35: Now, logic is built in at all of these levels, keeping track of everything. But this is the level we are focusing on right now, at the concept level, making sure that we are clear in what these concepts are. So suppose we are now adults and we are comfortably working our way throughout, and we get into adult-level issues, and we want to have arguments about religion and politics. So does God exist, for example? We all bump into this question at some point, and we reason about it, and we want to reason about it; we want to make up our mind about it.
2.36: From the logic perspective, the first question would not to be, to start plunging into the arguments for and against the the existence of God. The first question is going to be, when you say the word God, do you know what you mean? That should be a deeply personal question. I should be able to identify, in a clear statement, sometimes it might be in a formal definition, what I mean by God. It's going to be important for my own thinking, but then as we know, it's important for social reasoning as well, because that is one of those words that, by the time we enter into the discussion, there are dozens of major religions and thousands of historical religions, and how they use God is not univocal.
2.37: So the first question will be, before you and I, say, start having a discussion about, do we believe in the existence of God or not, what are we talking about? Can we get this concept clear? If we were going to argue about important things in politics, I want to say, that guy is a socialist, that guy's a conservative, then we immediately plunge into all kinds of arguments for and against socialism, arguments for and against conservatism, and so on. Do we know what those concepts mean?
2.38: We should, in our own thinking, know what we mean by the word socialist. But of course, we know, as soon as we enter into social context, different people mean different things by socialist. Again, there's a big history of socialism, as there is for conservatism. The logicians always want us to slow down, and they're always going to say, "Clarify the terminology first before you start the argument." If you're really serious, give your definitions of your key terms up front, so that everybody knows what you are talking about. You also know what you are talking about.
2.39: The models here would be things like in geometry, where we can say, what is a square? When we are young, so there's a square, there's a triangle, there's a circle. And your geometry teacher, in introducing these concepts, you have lots of observational experience of each of them. But before we can go on to do more sophisticated logical derivations of theorems when we're doing our geometry, what is a square? Then we look at the square, we measure the square, we figure out its important attributes.
2.40: We say, well, it's got four sides. The four sides are supposed to be enclosed. These angles are supposed to all be the same. If we measure the angles, they should add up to 360 degrees. We take all of that as raw material. Based on my observations, I've got all of the constituent concepts, and I'm going to try to define this more abstract thing. I might say something like, a square is a quadrilateral, four-sided thing. The interior angle is adding up to 360 degrees. Or we might say with four right angles as interior angles. That would be my rough draft. Go to work on that, fine-tune it, and so on.
2.41: What about this one? Well, three sides enclosed. The interior angle should add up to 180 degrees because this also is a triangle. Three sides, the angles will add up to 180 degrees. Having done that preparatory work, a triangle is a three-sided figure, interior angles adding up to 180 degrees. That's precise. This one, a little bit tricky. How do you define a circle? It doesn't really have sides. It seems like it only has one, or it has one line, but this is also just one line.
2.42: We want to differentiate the circle from the one line, but it's hard to figure out this angle stuff that goes on in here. We might say it all adds up to 360 degrees again. So a line, blah, blah, blah, blah. So how do we capture this, the fact that it's not a straight line and so on? We might try a device like saying, well, imagine a central point. So it's a line, all of the points of which are equidistant from a given point and adds up to 360 degrees. Again, that's my rough draft. Continue to work. But the point of this is, before we can go on to do serious work in the geometry of mathematics, this definitional work has to be done.
2.43: In business, if you're going to talk about investment, almost all business textbooks will define their investment terminology, and that's very important. What's the difference between a stock and a bond? Well, they're both investment devices. Then you start to think, well, let's see, in stocks, what's important about stock? Well, it's an investment thing, but you own a chunk of the company. There's a certain amount of risk because the stock might make money, it might not make money, and so you might lose your initial investment or you might not.
2.44: By contrast, you can say, here's a bond. Well, it's another kind of investment, but in this case, it's a loan. You're loaning money to the company. You don't actually own it, but you have a guarantee from the company that they're going to pay you a certain amount of money each year. You're looking at these devices and what's going on in the relationship, and you have all the constituent concepts. This now puts you in a position to make something that would be a more formal definition. Stock is an investment vehicle or an ownership investment vehicle that carries risk. By contrast, a bond is an investment loan vehicle with a guaranteed rate of return. Again, rough draft, clarification, now we're more ready to go on.
2.45: One of the ones I like to think about a lot because this is one that's commonly confused in common distinction is the distinction between envy and jealousy. Suppose we are, I'm just going to use this as an abbreviation for psychology, the Greek symbol, psi. We're figuring out what goes on, and one important part of psychology is all of the emotions that we have, as well as all of the thoughts and conceptions that we have. There's a whole bunch of emotions that are out there.
2.46: But if we are trying to sort out our own mental furniture, what's going on in me, we're dealing with our children, and children are having all kinds of emotions, and we want the kids to describe how you are feeling, so I can figure out what's going on with you; or even if we're going to become professional therapists and psychologists and so on, all of this territory, we need to get sorted out before we can do sophisticated theorizing about it.
2.47: So one of the very basic distinctions is the distinction between these two, but often they are used interchangeably with each other, even though there is an important distinction here. So, in thecase of jealousy, for example, what do we mean by jealousy? We start by saying, well, here's some examples of cases where we would use the word jealousy.
2.48: Suppose my wife, she's gone out for the evening, and I remembered I needed something at the mall, and so I went off to the mall and, walking through the mall, and then I see, oh, that's my wife, but she's with another man, and that man is hugging her, and she's hugging him back. This is a nightmare. This is totally made up. But what am I feeling at that moment? Am I feeling envious or am I feeling jealous? The right answer is to say, no, I'm feeling jealous in that case. So, I'll say, well, that would be an example of jealousy.
2.49: Then I'll try to unpack a little bit more what's going on there. But what would be an example of, say, envy? There's another made-up example. Suppose I drive a really old car and it's breaking down, and each day I get a new, I'm not sure if it's going to start up or not, but I don't have enough saved up to get myself a newer vehicle. And then I see one of my buddies, with whom I've always had a little bit of rivalry, drive by, and he's got some $100,000 vehicle. It's exactly the kind of vehicle, I would just love to have that vehicle. At that point, what am I feeling? Well, I'm not jealous in that case. In that case, I am envious. He has this beautiful, say, new car. I'm feeling envious.
2.50: Now, those are some working examples. We might get some other working examples, but then we start to analyze and we would ask, well, what's the difference between these two? Well, in the case of jealousy, these are actually both involving possessions. I say, "Well, this guy has a car, and I have a different kind of car; and I have a wife, but it maybe seems like somebody else has her right now," so these are, we might say, both involving possessiveness, or possessions.
2.51: But what's happening in this case is, I think that I have this possession. She is mine, hands off. I think she belongs to me. I have no idea what's going on. I think I have here, but I fear, with this new evidence—there she is, hugging some other guy—I fear that I am losing her. I have her, but I am fearing the loss of her. That bad emotion is the fear of loss and the unexpectedness, given what you thought was the reality.
2.52: Over here, in this case, when I see the guy driving by in the beautiful car, well, I don't have a beautiful car. So this is an issue of, I don't have. I'm responding to something that I don't have. I think of myself as not having that. I have this old beat-up, not- working-very-well car. And I would say that I fear that I won't get that. Because given my current budget circumstances, I can't afford a car like that. It's not very realistic that I can, we're going to get the money anytime soon. So this guy gets this great car, I don't have it.
2.53: So these are both about possession, where this is the fear of losing something that you have. This is the fear of not having or not getting something that you would like to have. And now we're in a position, I think, to come up with, say, a rough draft of a definition of the distinction between fear and jealousy, and then we can go on more explicitly and do serious work.
2.54: This would be important because, suppose you become a professional psychotherapist and you have a patient you've been working with, but you want to refer this patient to another psychotherapist. If you send it, well, the person has severe jealousy issues, but really you mean the person has severe envy issues, that's going to be destructive of the process when it picks up with the other psychotherapist as well.
2.55: All right. Carrying on, we should be able to do this in politics. If we are serious thinkers about politics, what are the important concepts? Well, starting in the American context, liberal, conservative, socialist, libertarian, fascist gets thrown around a lot; communist gets thrown around a lot, Democrat, Republican, etc. It should be part of your serious enterprise, before you enter into any decisions about what your views are or start to argue them, that you've got it all worked out, what the proper definitions of those concepts are.
2.56: I want to give an example of human beings. It's because this is an interesting one and a fundamental one. When we are working through these sorts of things, we are doing it somewhat case by case, working our way up from examples. As we start to deal with things that are increasingly complicated, we'll start to find all sorts of things that we are putting on our rough draft list, as I think of them here.
2.57: Then the important thing is to figure out from that rough draft list, this is a complicated situation. It's got all of these elements over here, and I'm trying to distinguish it from this situation, which has all of these elements over here, what's similar, what's different, and so on. But also there's an essentiality judgment. So one thing that is fun is to say, what if we try to say "human being"? And we'll often see this when you read more serious, shorthand, for definition, you're trying to try to define human being. And let's just go through this exercise a little bit.
2.58: So suppose we might say, well, what makes a human being a human being? Well, they have a body. They have a mind. Then we start talking about this part here. Should we call it a spirit? Should we call it a soul? Should we call it something more neutral, like the psyche? And what's the relationship between these sorts of things? We notice if we look at the body, the human beings, we can list all of the various body parts. But we might then say, one of the things we want to be able to do, just as we're trying to distinguish envy from jealousy, distinguish conservative from liberal, is distinguish human beings from other animals.
2.59: We might notice that human beings are the only beings that have an opposable thumb. Now, I think that's true, but I'm not a human biologist or animal biologist, so let's just take this as a working example. But apparently, it's either very rare or it's exclusive to human beings that we have a thumb that we can oppose to the other fingers. That gives us more manual dexterity, and we can grip in various ways. Others, they can grab like this, but they can't quite make that opposing thing happen.
2.60: We might be listing all sorts of traits, right, out there. Human beings have an opposable thumb. Human beings, we might then say, are the animal with opposable thumbs. Say, well, it might be true, and it distinguishes this from other ones. Another candidate that was offered was to say, well, actually, the important thing about human beings—this goes back to Plato and Aristotle times—is that human beings are, more importantly, bipedal. If we look at other species, so gorillas are mostly on all fours, cows, horses, dogs, cats, squirrels, and so on, on all fours.
2.61: Some of the apes and monkeys can, for a short period of time, rise up, so there might be a judgment call. Then someone said, well, what about chickens? We might be willing to say chimpanzees or whatever are a borderline case, but chickens are also bipedal, and so this one doesn't seem to be able to work very well. Then suppose we then say, well, we are not only bipedal, but we are featherless. So we introduce this negative thing. So human beings are animals that are featherless bipeds.
2.62: And then the joke was, in history of philosophy, that someone took a chicken and plucked all the feathers off it, and then just threw it in the philosophers who are arguing about what it is to be a human being. So then you have a featherless bipedal thing, this featherless chicken in there. But obviously, we haven't done our work. So what else do we have to add here? We can work the body side of the equation. Sometimes we will get over to this side of the equation.
2.63: People will say, the thing we need to focus on is that the human being is not a body primarily, but more primarily, it's something on the psychological side of things; that we have a part of us, a spirit or a soul, that is different from physical stuff. And so what differentiates human beings from all other animal species is that they are animals who also have a soul or animals who also have a spirit. That, of course, takes us into arguments about whether souls and spirits really exist.
2.64: Others, they'll want to say, there's not really a differentiation between body and mind, they are two aspects of one integrated being. Nonetheless, what differentiates us in our minds or in our psyches is that human beings have the capacity for rationality. We might have the opposable thumb, and maybe there are beings that are pretty close to that. But in terms of our capacity for rationality, doing math, doing logic, thinking about history, projecting the future, designing scientific experiments, complicated jokes, theatrical productions, and so on, all of these things that are expressions of our rationality, maybe that's the thing that differentiates us from all other beings.
2.65: Now, at this point, we are just working our way through four definitions, or four proposed definitions, and I don't want to terminate the process, where the point is that this is how it has to be done. It has to be done more, the more you're dealing with more complicated beings. The point then might be that we're trying to look for things that are meeting two creatures.
2.66: One is that they differentiate. That is to say, whatever it is that you're interested in focusing on, this is my concept, this differentiates it from all of the other ones. So does bipedal do it? Does opposable thumbs differentiate? Does the lack of feathers, does the rationality, does the possession of the soul? We have to think hard about whether, in fact, it does it.
2.67: And the other is the essentiality. Whatever it is that you are trying to explain or talk about, what are the most important things about it? The essential things that, if you didn't have that, you wouldn't have those anymore. On this kind of score, the way this next level of argument would be to go, would be to say, well, suppose you took a human being and instead of making it featherless, you took a human being who had suffered some accident and lost their thumbs.
2.68: You would say, well, if our definition of being a human being is that it's an animal with opposable thumbs, and then here you've got this guy who no longer has any thumbs, do we want to say, well, therefore, he's not a human being anymore? And that seems a bit harsh. It also seems wrong because human beings do have them, but these are not as essential to what it is to be a human being compared to other things. So we might not want to put that in the example.
2.69: By contrast, we can make a better case for rationality. Our rational capacity enables us to do language, get jokes, do math, think about our lives, be morally responsible agents, and so on. We might say, if we're trying to understand what it is that makes a human being a human being, rationality is a lot more important and a lot more explanatory than, say, having thumbs. We might then do the same thing and say, well, look, what happens if you lose your rationality? If someone has some severe brain damage or some severe Alzheimer?
2.70: We do start to say, well, it seems like the person isn't there anymore, or he's lost his identity or her identity, or something important is missing. Still human, but we are more likely to say this person is not able to do the things that are essential to human beings as before. That would then be a sign that maybe there's something more to that definition.
2.71: Now, other cases where these distinctions are important and being able to do the conceptions, all this definition work, is discovery. One of the things that we do is, then we take our concepts and we have organized them definitionally and we see relationships between the various ones, is that they enable us to make a connection between things that we otherwise would not be able to observe.
2.72: An example I want to use here is from the history of medicine, involving the condition of scurvy. The historical story here is that the British Navy, early in its days when it was off exploring the world, trading with the world, conquering the world, and building up the British Empire into something fairly significant, was running into a problem that, when the sailors were at sea for a long time, they started to develop scurvy.
2.73: This would have a number of symptoms, one of which would be that your teeth would start to get loose and then start to fall off, and there would be other physiological symptoms as well. It was a serious problem, and they had no idea what caused the scurvy. But then almost accidentally, they discovered that limes cure scurvy. This is partly why the British then acquired the ethnic nickname of being Limeys, because the British Navy, once they discovered that limes cured scurvy, everywhere that they went, that was almost like their first question is, "Do you have any limes? Do you have any limes? Give us your limes. We want limes." So they became the Limeys.
2.74: This was an accidental connection. But if you add limes into the diet, then the scurvy symptoms go away, and so they start to do it more systematically. Now, the follow-up question, though, is, well, why? What's going on in the limes? And there you need to do some biological research, some chemical research. What nutritional needs do human beings have? What are the biochemical structures of limes? And so all of that project considers.
2.75: But also, sometimes it's pretty hard to find limes, because limes don't grow everywhere in the world. They don't even grow everywhere in the tropical world. But if we have, say, observed other kinds of fruits, for example, we notice that some of those fruits are somewhat similar to limes. Then when we are forming this concept of limes, and now we're adding to limes as part of that concept, limes cure scurvy, if we have perceived and categorized some other kinds of fruits that seem similar to limes, we might then ask the question, "Maybe those also can cure scurvy?"
2.76: They would start to say, limes are green and round and small. And lemons are typically a little bit bigger and yellow, but they seem to be in that same tart sweetness category when you taste them. So maybe it's the case that limes and lemons, while we have different concepts for them, and maybe we've organized them into yellow fruits and green fruits over here, that nonetheless, they are part of a broader category.
2.77: And that whatever it is up in this broader category, it's not the greenness of the limes that cures the scurvy, it's not the yellowness of the lemon, that it might be some common ingredient that they both contain. And so with this conceptual structure, what we then say is, we know the limes work to cure scurvy; what if we see other things in this more abstract category, whatever we call this? We might call this category citrus fruits.
2.78: That will then lead us from our lime discovery to this abstract move to the case of lemons. Then we go get a bunch of lemons, we give them to our sailors, and we see if they cure the scurvy or not. Then it turns out, yes, they do, they work. Then we also then will say, well, what else is in this category? Then we might say, well, what about oranges? What about grapefruits? And so on. The point then just is that paying careful attention to our conceptual structure, and defining it and organizing it explicitly in this way leads us to more scientific discoveries that lead to better health and medicine results.
2.79: OK, as an example of generalizing on this issue of citrus fruits, and we know also we take fruits and we put them with vegetables, and then we will put those in as things that grow on plants, and so we have a higher abstract concept. But then we have all of the animals that we've learned, dog, cat, cow, horse, goat, human being, and so on. Then we have mammals. Then we've got other beings that we've learned, birds and so on, fishes and so on. We put those all together in hierarchical trees.
2.80: We might all say, then we take the plants and the animals. We have this very abstract category, living things. We have this entire hierarchical structure. The more sophisticated we are in our thinking is, if we know where things are in that hierarchical structure, we can get there very quickly. And then when it's important, formally, we can specify its location in that hierarchical structure and communicate that to other people.
2.81: So just as an example of an exercise that one would do, and this is something that I think it is fun to practice on a regular basis, anytime I am learning about something new, some new area, I will typically spend some time in this area. Most textbooks that are introductions to new areas, the important concepts that need to be learned by the incoming students are defined. In many cases, there are charts and hierarchical tree structures and places to get that person up to speed.
2.82: But just as an example, what would we do to make a hierarchical structure that enables us to then define each element's place in that structure? So these are all modes of transportation. And we might say they are all automobiles. We might notice that there's also going to be trains and boats and planes, and so then we would have an even more abstract category of modes of transportation that would be possible. But we're just focusing in here.
2.83: So what do we want to do? We start looking at the list, and some things seem to go together, some things seem to differentiate from each other. Sometimes it requires specific knowledge, so you might not know exactly what that means. You might have to go and look up, what does that word mean? So one word that strikes me as a sticking- out word here is this word, import. Those are cars or automobiles that are brought in from foreign countries. And I know that the contrast to that is export, but export is not on the list here, so chances are good that I'm going to have to put export on the list as well.
2.84: Suppose I say that maybe that's what's governing this approach here. We have imports and, I'm going to put this in brackets, exports, or perhaps it is domestic, ones that are made inside this country. I don't know yet. I put the square brackets here because there's a good habit to get into, that whenever you're adding something to an argument or a conceptual structure that's not in the original, put that in there to indicate "I'm adding this." It's a standard device because of course, if you want to be fair to someone else's argument, you don't want to be putting words in their mouth that don't necessarily belong there.
2.85: If you find the person, you've reconstructed their argument, and it ends up making them seem like they're saying something ridiculous, it's always worthwhile to go back and make sure you're not adding something that has made it ridiculous. So, I'm adding this as a possibility. Then I would say, well, I know from personal experience, Expedition and Ford, that Expedition is a kind of Ford, but I know also that Ford is made in the United States, so I would put then Ford here, and then say the Expedition as an example here. And now I've got import covered, I've got Ford covered, I've got Expedition covered.
2.86: I know also Chrysler is made primarily here, and it's different from Ford, it's a different company. So I would put that there and cross that one out. I might say Toyota, and I know that Lexus is the luxury brand of Toyota, and that Toyota is not made here. So I would put, say, Toyota over here, and Lexus as a luxury sub brand of that one. That crosses out those ones, that crosses out those ones. Tesla, made mostly here, so I would then add that one in the domestic production. That looks after that one.
2.87: Volkswagen, BMW, and Accord. I might, from my knowledge, say, well, I know Toyota is made more over in Asia, in Japan. These ones are from Europe. If the geography matters, I might make a distinction—imports from Europe, imports from Asia, imports from wherever. Doesn't necessarily seem important here. So, at least in this first draft, I won't do that. So VW, I would put it here, BMW here, and now I've got Accord. I'm saving that one for last. What about Accord? BMW.
2.88: Here what I would say is, I know that Accord is a sub brand of Honda. It's the Honda Accord. Honda seems to be at the same level as Toyota, Volkswagen, and BMW. Those are different companies, but I don't have Honda on this initial list here, so I would consider doing this. Honda, equal level hierarchically with those ones, and then one of their variations is the Accord. OK, rough draft, but that's the exercise to go through, and one clarifies in one's own thinking, one can communicate, and one can leave things open for further additions of knowledge as they come along.
2.89: Now, this issue of definition is important work, but one of the things that's always very interesting is the connection between humor and logic and how, in many cases, the best humorists have not only a wicked sense of humor but a wicked sense of logic. They have very keen insights into how we use words, how we think, how we set up people's thinking; where you take them along this direction, you know they're going to carry along in that direction, and then you switch and you take them in this direction suddenly, and it's very funny. But it requires that they have a very sharp logical brain in order to be able to do so.
2.90: It also holds at the level of forming definitions. One of the strong versions of humor, of course, is word humor with respect to definitions. I want to give you some examples of this, and we can talk about these definitions. A committee. Well, what is a committee? "A cul-de-sac down which ideas are lured and then quietly strangled." Now, this is put in the form of a formal definition, but it's meant to be humorous. It's also, I think, meant to draw on our knowledge of having been on committees.
2.91: What's the idea of a committee? A committee is where we're supposed to get together as a group, share ideas, and then decide what we are going to get done. And so what makes this humorous is, he's aware of that, and he's aware that we're all aware of that, but then he sets up your expectation for something like that, but then subverts it. This is partly a dark truth because we do know that what often happens, against the purpose of forming a committee, is the exact opposite happens. Anybody with a creative idea gets stifled, or the good ideas don't get acted on, hence the bitter humor in this definition.
2.92: Cult. What is a cult? "A cult is a religion with no political power." OK. Now, this is an interesting one. It's a witty point but it's got an edge to it. There's some criticism of existing religions that seems to be built into this. Why so? Because typically, we know when we use the word cult, it's meant as a bad word. "Oh, he's joined a cult. We need to get this person out of the cult and remove the brainwashing from this person, get the person back to normal."
2.93: So the suggestion then here is, well, what's the difference between those crazy brainwashed people who've lost control of their lives and real religions that aren't cults? The suggestion here is, there's not really an important difference, except that ones have power and the other ones are marginalized and taken unseriously in our society. Then, of course, that means, wait a minute, not my religion, whatever that is. My religion is better than that. But it forces me to then say, well, in what way is my religion better than that?
2.94: Can I say, it's not just that my religion has captured a bunch of people and brainwashed them to believe certain things from youth, and we just happen to have a lot of power in society and nobody really questions us? If that's all I've got to go, then this definition has some traction. But if I don't want that definition to have some traction, I need to up my game in terms of figuring out what makes my religion better than that religion. So it's humor, but with an edge, and it's a clever edge.
2.95: "Shaving is a male ritual that consists in spreading a potion across one's face and scraping it off with a sharp implement." See, my fellow guys are not with me right on this one because I shaved. They haven't engaged in this ritual, and maybe they have not engaged in this ritual because they agree with this definition, because the point of this definition is to reduce shaving to triviality and something that seems irrelevant. What's the point of putting some potion on your face and scraping it off?
2.96: Of course, the interesting thing is, he's making fun of people who shave, and he's trying to say, "This is why I have my beautiful beard," or whatever it is, because it seems kind of pointless. But for the joke to work, he has to, I've already erased it here, but eliminate the essential thing that really would go into a definition of shaving, which is to say, it serves a certain function of removing unwanted facial hair. That's not in there, but it's, of course, meant to be humorous with a joke.
2.97: One more. "Junk is something you throw away three weeks before you need it." Again, in the form of a definition, it's true; junk is stuff that we throw away, but then he's just reflecting on that wry experience that no doubt we've all experienced. I don't think I need this. My judgment was wrong. Ha, ha, ha. So good connections there. I always like to end with this quotation from Confucius.
2.98: While it is fun, if you are nerdy and geeky and you just like to have a clean and tidy mind, these exercises are important. They're always very important foundationally, in learning any new discipline. But especially if we want to protect the things that really matter to us, when we get up to talking about religion and politics and relationships and family structures and so on, there, when the stakes are the highest, it's equally important that we have our concepts at their highest level of clarity.
2.99: In this lecture, we have been talking about concepts and concepts as abstractions, and then as building blocks for later propositions and then logical structures in theories and narratives. There is an ongoing philosophical and psychological controversy over the nature of these concepts. And built into that controversy is whether our concepts are still keeping us in connection with reality, or if there is something subjective and arbitrary about them, that means we are engaging in a disconnect from reality, right at this level of concepts.
2.100: So for example, we would say all of us in this room are human beings, and we would say that we are all equally human beings. I've got this abstract category. I can see each of you as discrete, distinctive individuals, but nonetheless, we share something or we're all part of this broader abstract category, human being. Then the puzzle might be, well, if I then look at you more carefully, what is this abstract thing that we are talking about, this humanness or this humanity? Then I would notice that your hair is all equally, or unequal, so to speak. You have different hair, different lengths, different colors, and so forth.
2.101: You are different shapes, different sizes. You have different weights. I won't do this, but we all have different smells, if we get close enough to each other. We make different sounds. In terms of every thing that we can possibly sense and/or perceive, we are all individual, unique, and different. Then suddenly we are going to this abstract level where we are saying, this one label "human" fits all of you equally.
2.102: There is a bit of a mystery, or at least a philosophical and psychological issue, about what we are doing when we go to that level of abstraction, and whether we are maintaining an objective connection to reality. In the history of logic, and the history of this part of logic, there have been three main positions that have developed about this issue, and logicians and psychologists continue to debate them.
2.103: One of the most famous individuals is a guy named William of Ockham. He was a brilliant late medieval logician and an epistemologist. But here was his position, and his position was to maintain that there is something subjective about concepts and that they are not objective. So the phrase is, "I maintain that a universal is not something real that exists in a subject, but that it has a being only as a thought-object in the mind."
2.104: So that then would be to say, the universal human, it doesn't exist in you. So if I say humanness or your being human is out there in you, that's wrong. He doesn't think that's true. What's out there is a unique particular individual with his or her own unique particular traits. This human, this abstract that we're all equally human, whatever goes into the definition of being human, that's only something in the mind, and we've made it up inside the mind.
2.105: That then is to say that we have a gap between the words we are using, as we go on to use these words, and reality. In some sense, we are being false to reality in using these concepts. That takes us in a certain more skeptical direction. This position is usually called nominalism, from the Latin, which is to say, these things are just names, they're not realities, just a bunch of names.
2.106: Now, an opposite position is often ascribed to Socrates and then most explicitly to Plato, which is to say, it can't be right that all we are is different names or different objects with different dimensions. We just have these subjective names that we've slapped on to things that are more or less similar to each other. You really are human. You really are human. You really are human. And you are just as human as she is. And you are human in exactly the same way that she is human. That's real. I didn't just make that up.
2.107: But Ockham and the others are right that when I perceive you, I don't perceive this abstract humanness floating around. I perceive particulars. So the answer then that Plato came up with is then to say, it must be the case that we have two levels of reality. We have the level of particular physical reality, where you have your body and your features and so on. And when we are talking about humanness, there is an alternative reality in which there are these perfect abstract, what he called forms or templates, and that we have a mental ability to intuit these perfect abstract forms in the other dimension and see how they apply to their particular entities in the physical world.
2.108: We might, if we go back to examples of triangles, we might say, well, here's a triangle, here's another triangle. But if we actually took a really precise protractor and measured all of the angles, is it going to equal 180? Well, the Platonic answer is going to be probably not. This one might only measure 179, and this one's 180.5 degrees. You're never going to find a perfect triangle in this world. Everything has little bits of imperfection.
2.109: But there is a perfect triangle, perfection. The definition is perfect. So there must be triangularity in this higher world of forms, and that we have a cognitive capacity for seeing it or perceiving it or intuiting it that works with our perceptual capacities and so on. Now, this position is sometimes called realism, the idea being that abstract things are real and independently out there in reality, just not in the lower physical reality, in a higher physical reality.
2.110: Then the third position, more contemporary, Ayn Rand, wants to argue that neither that realist position nor that nominalist position is correct. And this is her description of it from her work in epistemology. "None of the traditional theories of concepts regard concepts as objective, i.e., as neither revealed nor invented." Let's just pause right there. So the Platonic position where we say abstract concepts are as an act of revelation to us, they're out there and they are revealed to us, the nominalist position is to say, no, we just make them up. They are inventions. Our position is to say those two traditional theories are wrong.
2.111: "But as produced by man's consciousness in accordance with the facts of reality, as mental integrations of factual data computed by man, as the products of a cognitive method of classification whose processes must be performed by man, but whose content is dictated by reality." So that's a lot of words, and we're just introducing what the issue is. But what she wants to argue is that it is objective, but when we are observing, and I see all of you in your particularity, and I'm sorting similarities and differences, all of that is objective, and you all have the features that you have.
2.112: But nonetheless, it's not just revealed to me. I have to engage in a certain process of abstraction. She wants to make a distinction between the process that the mind engages in and the nature of the reality that one is abstracting from, and that's the proper understanding. Now, that's just to describe three positions that smart philosophers continue to debate over the nature of concepts.
2.113: But I want to have that as a part of the record for the course in logic, because how do we think about these concepts? Did we just make them up? Should we strive to be intuiting perfect forms more better? Do we need to attend to these conscious processes that we are engaging in, in a way that keeps us connected to reality or not? The further research and thinking about concepts stems from what position one takes on that controversy. Let's pause there.
2.114: As far as, we talked about the concepts of reality in this debate, does postmodernism fit into that concept, as far as logic? Because they don't really think of reality as—
2.115: OK, good. That's a great question. I used Plato from the ancient world and Ockham from the medieval world, and then Rand from contemporary times. But it is interesting that you find all three of those positions articulated in each of those eras. So the postmoderns whom you are mentioning would be in the shoes of William of Ockham. They are nominalists in that conceptual sense.
2.116: So Derrida, Foucault, and the others, they don't say, yet the words that we use, all of the language that we use is subjective. We're just arbitrarily carving up the world however it is that we want. Although typically they want to say that we ourselves, the way we're trying to carve up the world has just been conditioned into us by power structures who themselves have just arbitrarily decided to carve the world up in certain ways for their own value agenda. They are extreme nominalists, extreme subjectivists. Lecture 3: Logical Fallacies At a glance — Logical fallacies and good versus bad reasoning.
3.1: In logic, we like to emphasize the positive, good reasoning, valid reasoning, sound reasoning, keeping our minds in connection with reality, and figuring out the truth. But also, of course, we know we are beings that can make mistakes, all sorts of mistakes, and particularly on things that are complicated and things that push our emotional buttons. It's customary in logic courses, and I think for very good reason, to spend a certain amount of time looking at common patterns of invalid reasons.
3.2: Typically in logic textbooks or logic courses or wherever one gets one's material, these will go under the label of informal fallacies. They're called informal fallacies because they are fallacies, which is to say they are mistakes in reasoning, where the premises seem to provide some support for the conclusion, but they don't provide any support for the conclusions at all. So it's fallacious reasoning. But informal because there are different kinds of logical forms.
3.3: You can be doing deductive categorical syllogisms. We'll get to those in a little bit. You can be doing propositional logic, you can be doing inductive statistical, whatever form of reasoning you are doing. There are some common patterns of bad reasoning that pop up all over the place. So it's worthwhile to isolate them since they are so common, assign them names, and then just the act of going through that and doing some practice examples puts you in a position of intellectual self-defense.
3.4: Sometimes, with respect to yourself, it's very easy for us all to slip into certain patterns of reasoning, but also in social context, so that other people don't slip one past you. In many cases, there are people who are con men, the lawyers who have the bad reputation, who know certain tricks of the trade, so to speak, how to use illogic in a way that seems to be persuasive. So it's worth being on one's guard against those.
3.5: So the basic idea of logic is to maintain an objective connection. That is to say, our minds are trying to attend to the objective reality. So what goes on inside the subject, I'm not just making up the truth or just believing whatever it is that I want to be true. I'm not being subjective, in that sense of subjective; I'm trying to be objective. But subjectivism is the first one that we typically give a label to.
3.6: So subjectivism and, in its crudest form, is just to say, I want something to be true, and so I'm going to believe that it's true, or I'm just going to will myself into believing that something is true, even if I don't have good evidence for it. Even if I know there are some evidence that militates against it or leans against it, I'm just going to not pay attention to that evidence because, ultimately, I want this to be true.
3.7: Now, if we put that in standard form, it would just be looking like this. I want X to be true, and so therefore, I will believe X is true. Obviously, we call that subjectivism. The reason for that is to say, well, what is the evidence for X as being true? It's just my wanting. That's just something that is with respect to me. Now, almost never does this happen so clearly. Even people will try to deceive themselves that this is the policy that they are operating on. But nonetheless, you can detect in yourself and in other people when this is happening.
3.8: Let me give you some examples to work on. Sometimes we have something with respect to our bodies, something acts up as one gets older or whatever, and something in the back of your mind says, "Maybe I should go to the doctor to get this checked out." That's a reasonable thing. Evidence something is wrong, doctor is expert at fixing things, I should get this checked out. I don't know what it is.
3.9: But if what's going on is, I don't want to go to the doctor; maybe I'm too busy or I don't feel like going to the doctor, or it might turn out that the doctor gives me bad news, and I don't want to hear bad news from the doctor. So what one will then do is just going to push out of one's mind the pain that one is suffering or whatever the symptom is, or whenever the idea of, "Go to a doctor," no, I'm not going to let myself think, "go to the doctor." And that's a policy of subjectivism.
3.10: In that case, it's like, I don't want there to be something wrong with me, so I'm going to act and believe as if there is not anything wrong with me, when the proper policy would be to pay attention to the evidence. If the evidence is that there's something wrong, get it looked after by someone who has the qualifications to do so. Now, very interestingly, there's an interesting connection between the logic and psychology here. Just put this out that women are much better at being objective on these issues than men are on these issues.
3.11: There are some studies that seem to indicate, keep the symptoms similar, women have those symptoms, they will get themselves to the physician much more regularly. Guys will be more likely to shrug it off. It's just a flesh wound. Maybe it's an issue about male ego. "I'm a tough guy," and you don't want to think of yourself as someone who gets damaged, for whatever the reasons are. There might be psychological sex differences that lead to subjectivism being easier or more difficult for us as individuals.
3.12: If I can be in true confessions mode, for example, I can look back and laugh on this, but when I was a college graduate student, I went on a road trip with a buddy, and we were driving across the United States, and we were in the middle of Nebraska, which I always think of as the state that never ends. You just keep driving and driving, and there's more and more Nebraska. And as poor college students, we had a car that probably should not have left the original city that we were in, so it was not clear it was suited for going that far.
3.13: But sure enough, we're out in the middle of nowhere in Nebraska, and there starts to be a sound happening from the engine. And you know that's not the right sound. What I did, I was driving at that point, was reached over and turned up the music. So this is a policy of subjectivism. In this case, I don't want there to be anything wrong with the engine; and if I can't hear anything wrong because the music is so loud, then I don't have to think about it, I don't have to believe it, and so on. OK, so kind of a ridiculous example, but that's an example of it.
3.14: More serious cases of relationships, and we all likely have had failed relationships, and in many cases, after the relationship has failed, we say to ourselves, "I should have known better." There were lots of red flags or lots of indicators. But we do know at the same time, as part of human psychology, when we're in the early stages of a relationship, everything is easy, everything is wonderful, and you want the relationship to work. You're always looking for the good in the other person. It's very hard to get yourself to be critical and notice possible weaknesses, possible red flags.
3.15: If some of those do start to arise, it's very easy for us to not pay attention to them, shut them down. Even in the case of well-meaning friends or parents who might say, "I know some things about this person," trying to be gentle, you will shut that person down because you don't want to know certain things, given that you are in a certain psychological state. Now, again, some people are better or worse at it, but it's a set of skills that happen, and subjectivism is dangerous.
3.16: Relationship issues, religions. People often know there are issues in their religion they should think about, perhaps tidy up their religious beliefs, but they don't want to, or their political candidates or their political philosophies. "This matters to me. I really want my politics to be the right politics. I want this to be the right person. I want this to be the right religion because I'm already invested." And so, subjectivism is an occupational hazard constantly in all of those issues.
3.17: In business cases where you are trying to make a big decision, you're going to be putting a lot of money out there, but you came up with an idea, and it's your idea, you worked out the business plan, you really want it to work, it's easy for you not to take criticism well in that situation, and so you lose a lot of money. So the policy is, while emotions are wonderful, emotions are important. There's a huge place in our lives for emotions.
3.18: But deciding what's true and false, that's not the job of emotions. Since we are subject to strong emotions and we want to be subject to strong emotions, we have to manage our internal dialogue to make sure that we're not letting our subjective desires interfere with our objective assessment of the evidence. Ongoing challenge.
3.19: Now, second fallacy that commonly gets put on the list is the appeal to large numbers of people who believe something. So the label for it is the appeal to majority. And in its crude form, it is, I'm going to believe that something is true because lots and lots of people believe that it is true. Sometimes it's a little narrower, and that's a lot of people in my peer group believe that it's true. So I'm going to believe that it is true as well.
3.20: And this is a fallacy for the most important reason that, if what you have only is that other people and lots of them believe something to be true, that doesn't tell you in your own mind whether it is true or not. You don't have access to whatever thinking they did or did not do to make up your own mind whether the thing is true or not. So many people believe X, therefore I believe X. So it is a failure of independent thinking.
3.21: Other people believing that something is true can be a clue that maybe there is something to it. You might ask them, why do you believe that? What's your evidence for that? What's the reasoning for that? Why did you come to believe whatever it is? Then you go through the same process and see if you reach the same conclusion of it. Or, of course, if you disagree, you have to, have to disagree.
3.22: Now, if you don't do that, then another reason why it's obvious this is not a good policy of mind is we just look at all of the historical examples where lots and lots of people throughout history have believed lots and lots of things that are wrong, ridiculous, crazy, destructive, and so on. So one of the lessons of history should be, it might be, if it is the case that there's just a huge mob of people suddenly latching onto some idea or it's very popular, it might very well be wrong.
3.23: So the famous examples are ones that we laugh about now, or at least we roll our eyes about, involve things like people believing that the Earth is flat. And for many people, it would be just something they picked up by osmosis. Everybody else seems to be suggesting it, but they've not actually spent any time thinking about it, asking what would count as evidence for or against the Earth being flat or not. They're just carrying on someone else's belief.
3.24: How do we find out if a woman is a witch, if we up the stakes a little bit? Well, what you do, everybody believes this, and there are dozens and hundreds and thousands of trials conducted along this way, is you take a woman to a body of water, you tie her to a long pole that has a fulcrum, and you dunk her so that she goes underwater for a long period of time. And if she is not a witch, this is partly in a certain kind of religious context, God will intervene to show her innocence, and he will protect her while she's under the water.
3.25: On the other hand, if she's a witch, she will also engage in various witchery type of things to protect herself. So if she can survive this repeated dunking, it probably shows that she's a witch, in which case you have to burn her at the stake because you've proved that she's a witch. And unfortunately, if she doesn't survive, maybe God didn't just choose to intervene. She was innocent and just a normal woman and not a witch. Well, too bad. But that's a destructive practice based on just following a practice and a belief that seems to be widespread in that cultural atmosphere.
3.26: But my favorite historical example involves the early days of electricity and magnetism, back in the 1700s, when you can take this thing that just looks like a piece of rock and then take some iron, and then somehow they attract each other. We don't know what the causal mechanism is. It seems a little bit mysterious and magical. But many humans, being what they are, they then start to ascribe all sorts of things to these magical powers. It's like the crystal bracelets and this, that, and the other thing of our own time. But one of the very common beliefs that started to sweep through early America at the same time was that the magnets had the power to determine and tell you if your wife was cheating on you or not.
3.27: So the test was, you would take one of these magical magnet things, and of course, you have to pay me a lot of money for this, but you take this home, if you were worried about your wife, and put it under her pillow at night. And if she is an adulterous, the magnet will know, and it will drive her from the marital bed, and then you can take the appropriate consequences. Everybody else is doing it. Where's my money? I need to get one of these magnets. The fact that lots of people believe it doesn't provide any support at all. Let me put a box around this one, so I can put another box around this. This is the appeal to majority.
3.28: Now, as with the subjectivism, when you start putting it out clearly and logically like this, it seems ridiculous, and it is ridiculous. But there is the question why so many people seem to commit the appeal to majority so frequently. Peer pressure, going along with the crowd, and just saying things like, "Well, you don't want to believe that. Nobody believes that anymore. Everybody else is doing this." There does seem to be a psychological element that makes us prone to believing whatever the majority of people want to do.
3.29: Now, it might be just laziness. I don't want to have to think about these things. These other people seem to have thought about it, so I will just rely on their judgment. But it might be something else. There's some very interesting psychological experiments that have been done on this issue of committing the appeal to a majority for conformist reasons. The most famous name associated with this is a psychology professor named Solomon Asch. I want to spend a little time just showing this experiment.
3.30: There's lots of variations on Asch-types experiments over the subsequent decades. I believe these were first done in the 1960s and different types of constituents and variations on the theme. But the bottom basic variation was this. Professor Asch was teaching at a university, has lots of students, and he uses his students as subjects in these experiments. He says, "I'll pay you a couple of bucks." He would tell them a story.
3.31: He says, what we want to do is bring you into the lab and do tests of visual acuity. We're going to show you some lines and shapes of different shapes and sizes. What we want you to do is tell us whether these, say, two lines or two shapes are the same, or if you can see that there's a difference between them. Sometimes the differences will be really blatant, but sometimes they will be quite subtle. We're testing people's ability to discriminate subtle perceptual differences.
3.32: Here's a big whiteboard, say something like this one here. It's on a stand. We're going to bring the—that's a chair. We're going to bring the student in. Years of art lessons paying off right there. Just imagine that the guy's head is facing that way. Then we got some projector back here, and we're going to put projected images. This guy just has to say, "Same, different, same, same, different, different," right, and so on.
3.33: But we have two other students. We say, well, we're going to do this so that we gather more data at the same time. Also here, so these guys will be sitting here as well. This person is the test subject. We're not really interested in visual acuity. These two people look like students, but they are working with Professor Asch, and they are told to make mistakes in their answers at certain key times.
3.34: What we want to do is see when this person can see whether they actually are the same or actually are different, but these two say something else, what does this guy say? Does he go with his own independent judgment? I can see. Or since there's two of them and only one of him, and they're saying something different, will he say what they are saying? So, I'm going to say, I don't know, we have a secret Professor Asch commitment there.
3.35: So on the board, we start, say, putting two lines. I'm just going to keep it as lines to keep it the same. So we have two lines. Are those lines the same or different? These people can see, everybody can see, they are basically the same. These guys say the same. This person says, "Oh, they're the same." And then we do the same lines, different orientations, some shapes, things are the same.
3.36: Then we start to mess with the guy a little bit. We make this one just a little shorter, but we know that people from this distance can see that difference. These two people are quick to say at this point, "Oh, they're the same." The question is, what does this person say? Majority of cases, this person will say, "They are the same." He will agree with these two test subjects, but you know that he can see that there's a difference. Majority of people, and sometimes it's girls, sometimes it's boys.
3.37: There are later experiments where you have people of different age groups who count as being part of your peer, different racial groups or ethnic groups, and so on. The common data is that in the early stages of this experiment, this person will say something he or she knows is false. The only reason seems to be that to say something true would put him in a position of disagreement with the majority of people. Most people are not willing to express disagreement with the majority, at least in this experimental setting.
3.38: These are standard American kids, most of these initial experiments, but a lot of them have been duplicated around the world. It makes it even more pointed if you start to bring in cultural issues, because typically Americans have a culture of saying, "No, just believe whatever you want, think for yourself, be your own person," and so on. We don't have a culture that, on the face of it, compared to many other cultures, encourages conformity in going along. We seem to have a culture that encourages being independent and so forth.
3.39: But even in such a culture as that, a majority will still do this. All of this is being filmed by some hidden cameras. You'll mess around even more. You'll make that line even shorter. At some point, the line gets short enough. These people will start to defect and say, "No, it's different." Even those two continue to say that it is the same. The interesting thing is, when you look at some of the films, you see the people's faces, looking at the screen, the images. "I can see that clearly they are different. I'm ready to say different. Then I hear this guy says same, this guy says the same."
3.40: There's that whiplash head. "What am I hearing?" Then you can see the face change, this anguish. "What do I say?" Then at the point where they are willing to defect, they apologize. They'll say things like, "I'm sorry, but they're different." So something psychologically is going on. Again, this is not just isolated individuals. You're at the point where you have to apologize for stating something publicly that is really obviously true.
3.41: If it's difficult for many people in these cases, then when we get to the more complicated cases, the more controversial cases, that might be then part of a psychological explanation for why the appeal to a majority is such a popular fallacy, and we see it all over the place. Which then means, by implication, if our goal as logicians or people who are committed to logic is, monitor this in myself, of course.
3.42: But if I'm a parent, if I'm working with other people, how can I encourage them not to be lemmings or conformists, such that they are willing to speak the truth when they see the truth for what it is and not to start lying publicly, which, of course, sabotages your own psychological states as well?
3.43: Next fallacy I want to turn to is a variation on the appeal to majority, and it is called the appeal to authority. As the name suggests, the crude version of this one is to have not just your peer group or lots and lots of people, but one or a few people who are authorities or have some reputation. They have a PhD in something, or they are the CEO, or they have some fancy title or claim to fame. And this argument then says, well, this person believes X or says that X is true, and then, therefore, I believe that X is true.
3.44: So often it will be the case, an English literature professor will say, "Here are the five books that are the greatest books ever written, and you ought to read those books." And so many people will then say, "Well, I want to be considered an educated person just like this professor, and so I will make a point of reading those books, or at least saying that I've read those books, or know what to say about those books because I want to be in the more elite crowd."
3.45: Or the president believes a certain piece of legislation will pass, or in some versions of parenting, parents will encourage this: "Children, don't think for yourself so much. I'm the parent. You should believe what I tell you as the parent." Now, in that case, it's not a willing obedience to the authority person. It's an enforced obedience from the higher authority.
3.46: Let's put it formally on the board, the appeal to authority. All of these fallacies also have Latin names. This one is ad verecundiam, but we'll just stick with the English, appeal to authority. The blatant form of it is, some expert says X is true, and then I believe, therefore, X is true. Obviously, it's a fallacy in one respect because it's a failure of intellectual independence. The fact that the expert might properly know that something is true does not put you in the position of knowing why it is true. You're just taking it on faith that this other person says so.
3.47: Other obvious reason why this is a fallacy is that almost all important controversial issues, again, we can appeal to history. People who are experts have been wrong, believe all kinds of ridiculous, crazy, sometimes not ridiculous or crazy, but nonetheless, wrong things about various important matters. If everyone's policy is just "whatever the experts of our generation say, that's what we're going to believe," then we're setting ourselves up for stagnation.
3.48: It's also the case, as we know, even in our own generation, on almost every important controversial issue, there are experts who disagree with each other. And so, appealing to experts is going to be a nonstarter strategy for you actually figuring out what's going to be true. Nonetheless, this one is a favorite of the advertising agency. There's a whole genre of advertisements where they'll have experts in one field, but they will bring them in nonetheless to promote something in some other field.
3.49: So I don't know, you get some, what would it be? I don't know. You get a famous actor to say, "This is the best beer in the world," holding a glass of beer and looking satisfied. Well, this person might have expertise in acting and be a famous actor, but that does not translate into expertise about beer-making and the quality of beer. Certainly from the perspective of the audience, say, "Well, I don't know why this person thinks it's the best beer, but I'm just going to buy that beer." In that case, it's an appeal to authority, but it works on lots and lots of people.
3.50: We'll come back to, in a moment, what might be going on psychologically, but we'll flag that just for a moment. Now, that then is to say, sometimes the appeal to authority happens in celebrities, movie stars, or famous people endorsing things or believing things. So whatever the global issue is, you bring in a famous musician who's on some side of a political issue on the other side of the world—the idea being, this famous musician has lots of people and is an authority for those lots of people who like that particular music. And so their opinion on this foreign policy, politics issue, is supposed to have influence with those people.
3.51: Now, the more complicated cases, where ad verecundiam or the appeal to authority happens frequently, is though when it's an expert who has authority in his or her field, making a pronouncement in his or her field. So it's not the celebrity endorsing deodorant. It is maybe a celebrity telling you about acting techniques or a musician telling you about their creative process and what you can do to become more creative in your music.
3.52: Or you go to people who are experts because you know they have knowledge that you do not have. You get sued on some matter of a business issue, and there's lots of complicated law at stake. You don't have time to get a law degree. You go to a lawyer, you pay that person the money, and you ask that person for expert advice. So, that lawyer might then say, "X is true. This is the best strategy. This is what we should do. These are the arguments that we should use." It is, of course, tempting and to some extent understandable why so many people will say, "OK, fine, you're the expert. I will just do whatever it is that you say."
3.53: Other analogy, or other example rather, is, again, there's something wrong with you. You don't have time to get a medical degree. You can poke around online to get some information, but you go to the physician, and the physician says, after examining you, "This is what's wrong with you. This is what I think we should do. Here, take these pills or have this surgery or whatever." You know that person has expertise. It's understandable then to say, "OK, I will take those pills, I will get that surgery," and so on.
3.54: But even here, I want to say it's still a fallacy if you act as described so far, that what logic will say, as a matter of intellectual self-defense, as a matter of self-responsibility, is even when you are talking with your lawyer, talking with your physician, you should ask them why. It can't simply be, "My doctor said that this is the case." The doctor says, "This is what you have. This is your condition." You should ask, "What makes you think, or what symptoms are you saying?"
3.55: The doctor should be able to, in ordinary person's language, say, "Well, you have this symptom and you have this symptom and you have that symptom. 94% of the time, people who have that symptom, this is the condition. But it might also be this other thing, and we might want them to check it out. Since you have this problem, we are going to do this surgery." You say, "Well, why that surgery? What are the other alternatives? Or what are the other options at this particular case?
3.56: The physician should be able to say, "Well, there really only are three options that we can do here. I settled on this one because it has an 85% success rate. This one only has a 40% success rate. This one has a 30% success rate. Here's the literature you can go and have a look at and so on." Now, at that point, you are still going to be trusting your physician up to a certain point, but he or she has explained a huge amount and is putting you in a position to make a much better independent judgment about whether the policies are appropriate or not.
3.57: But even then, in a lawyer, if it's a really big case, or in a physician, if it's a really important issue, a part of responsible self-thinking and self-decision-making might be to say, "Well, I am going to get a second opinion. That makes sense. I can see where you're coming from, but I still have some questions. I know sometimes things are cutting-edge. Sometimes people have narrower understandings of the literature, even if they are experts in that field. I'm going to get someone else."
3.58: Maybe your doctor is 60 years old. I'm going to get a 30-year-old doctor. Maybe the 60- year-old doctor isn't keeping up with the newest literature, but the 30-year-old doctor is more likely to have read that. On the other hand, the 30-year-old doctor doesn't have as much experience as the 60-year-old doctor. So maybe the best on this very serious medical issue is to do a compare and contrast of both of them. That's to avoid ad verecundiam.
3.59: Now, obviously, that's a lot of work, and it requires that you absorb a lot of information, a lot of information processing, making some important decisions. Maybe one of the reasons why people appeal to authority a lot is just a laziness. They don't want to do that work. Maybe it's a matter of social issues. You don't want to seem critical of this person in authority, like you're being a little bit rude by asking them hard questions, asking them to justify themselves. So it might be some social pressure, but override that. You can always find a diplomatic way to ask the important questions that needed to be asked.
3.60: As with the appeal to majority, there do seem to be other psychological issues that might be involved, aside from the certain kinds of emotional issues or the laziness issues that we've studied or mentioned so far. This also has been subject to psychological study in the form of formal psychological experiments, to try to test this appeal to authority. The most famous name in this area is another psychology professor whose name was Stanley Milgram. Again, experiments done back in the late '50s or the 1960s, subject to a certain amount of replication, lots of variations.
3.61: These ones are trickier because they start to run afoul of human ethics experimentation boards. They have to be more subtle now about how we're going to be testing for appeals to authority. But nonetheless, let me give you a picture of the kinds of experiments that Milgram did to illustrate that, in addition to this being just a strictly logical independence of judgment issue, there might be other psychological factors at work.
3.62: Now, in this case, think of a two-chambered room. Perhaps a close analogy would be a police interrogation chamber. We've seen them in the TV shows, in the movies, where you put the prisoner or the suspect in this room. And then here you've got, let me see if I can draw it very lightly. Imagine that's a two-way glass, where people in this room can see into this room, or it's actually one-way glass. You can see into that room, but people in this room cannot see back into this room. They just have a mirrored image. So I'll put a little arrow just to say that that's only that way.
3.63: In this room, what we have is a chair, and we've got a machine. On this machine, we've got a big electrical dial and, in big letters, say the word volts. This part of it is all in red, and there's danger if the voltage gets up to that point. There's an indicator of what your level of voltage is.
3.64: What Professor Milgram does in this case is, again, he has a large student body, he says, "I'll pay you a few bucks if you come and you work with me in the lab. I want you to be my laboratory assistant." And what he tells them is, "We're going to bring people in and we'll sit this guy here and we're going to attach him to the machine." So there's wires that come out, and they hook up to this guy with the electrodes at various sensitive points of the guy's body. There's also, one more color, there is a switch here for on, and then if you put over there, it will be off.
3.65: What we're going to do is, "I'll explain that we have good reasons why we're going to do this," I'm Professor Milgram right now. But we're going to turn this on and give him electrical shock sometimes, and other times we'll turn it off. But what we're trying to do is, we're trying to see if people's learning abilities, their memory, their attention improves through exposure to mild amounts of pain. So we give people tests, we ask them all kinds of questions, and we see how well they do on those tests.
3.66: And then we give them a very similar test, but every time they get the wrong answer, we give them a little electrical shock, and we see if that causes them to pay more attention and to do better on the test. So I want you to work with me to do this test. So we have some observers over here. OK. And that's going to be, say, Professor Milgram. And he's got to, I'll give him a hat because he's an important guy. And there's his clipboard, right, with all of the questions. And he's going to be speaking through some loudspeakers and so on.
3.67: But what I want you to do as my student assistant on this is to be in the room with this guy, and I want you to be in charge of the switch. So your job is to control the switch. And we'll have a microphone hooked up, so I'll tell you when to switch or when not to switch. We're going to ask this guy a bunch of questions. When he gets the answers correct, no problem. But once in a while, when he gets the answer wrong, I'm going to ask you to turn the switch from off to on and deliver a little shock to this guy.
3.68: Now, initially, it's on very low setting. It's going to be mild shocks and so on. Now, full disclosure, behind the scenes, I would not tell you this if you were this person here, but this person is an actor who has been hired by Professor Milgram to give wrong answers at prescripted times, get the right answers at various times. And in fact, there is no voltage at all going along here. But this person, you don't know that. And so our question is going to be, when I give you the instruction to turn that switch on, what will you do? So we've controlled all of the variables, and that's what we are interested in seeing.
3.69: So let's start the experiment. Professor Milgram asks, and the voice comes over, what is, let's just do some warm-up questions, what's 2 plus 2? This guy says 4. What's 13 plus 8? This guy says 21. What's 16 times 47? 184. Professor Milgram says, "Sorry, that's wrong. Please shock him. Or just please turn the switch on." What does that person do? Vast majority of cases turns the switch from off to on. And this person is the actor who knows it's coming. You can see he gives a little twitch.
3.70: Let's turn it back off, carry on the test. Who was the author of Moby Dick? Herman Melville. Who wrote House of Seven Gables? James Joyce. Wrong. Shock, please. Shocks him again. Now, we play around with this. At one point, Professor Milgram then says, "Would you turn the dial up? We want to have more." People will continue to shock the person who gets wrong answers.
3.71: Now, as you might expect, as this goes up and more and more, these people start to defect. "I don't want to do this anymore." But there are a significant minority of people, again, mostly young Americans, but adults, this will get into the red zone. This person is crying. This person is saying, "Ouch, that really hurts." This person is saying things like, "I don't want to do this anymore. I want to stop." And Professor Milgram will say, "I just have a few more questions," and asks those questions, and a significant minority will continue to shock.
3.72: Now, why is this? That's the question. And it's not because they are sadists. They've just been waiting their whole life for a chance to shock people for getting wrong answers to trivial questions. We've isolated as many things as we possibly can, and it seems to be, "This guy's the professor. He's running the lab. He's my superior on this order, and he said I should do this." So I, in a way, stop thinking. Stop thinking I'm a responsible agent, the one who's making the decision here.
