I am a, maybe overstating, I'm a robot, just doing what the real power and the real decider makes.
3.73: So very disturbing set of experimental results from Stanley Milgram. And this is on the psychological side of things, because anybody, if you just stop them on the street, all of these people, if you said, "If someone doesn't know who the author of the House of Seven Gables is, do you think it's appropriate to run electrical current through their body?" All of them will say, "No, absolutely not. That's sick. What are you, a weirdo? I would never do that." But put them in this situation, and significant numbers of them would. These are not bad people, but under this set of circumstances, authority is seductive in some way.
3.74: These all have English names. They do have Latin names behind them, but there is one of the very common fallacies that the Latin name has stuck, and we don't use English variations of it very often. When you hear people talking about ad hominem, it's this particular fallacy. The Latin simply means that, instead of attacking the person's argument, you attack the person. Or instead of attacking the ideas, you attack the man, or you attack the woman, you attack the person. Ad hominem is the argument.
3.75: Again, this is something that happens very frequently. Someone will say, "I believe that X is true, and here are my reasons for it." And then the person who is responding will not attack or pay attention to the reasons. Instead, they will attack the person personally. There's lots of versions of doing so, like old-fashioned sexism, for example. If it's a woman who's making an argument, you don't want to have to deal with it, then the old sexist response is, "Well, she's just a woman." And so you just dismiss it on the basis of that, when obviously as a woman, she can have really good reasons for her argument, and you have an obligation to attend to those arguments.
3.76: One of the very frustrating things we all know on social media these days is how quickly people will say, "Well, you're a member of this race, or you're a member of that religion, or you believe in that politics." And even though the person is making a point that's a point worth paying attention to, has data, has arguments, and so on, the person is not willing to address those. They want to just dismiss them by dismissing the person.
3.77: So, the way this argument goes in its crude form, ad hominem, is, just to say, X says that Y is true, but X is fill in the blank with whatever thing you don't like about that person. Therefore, Y is false. It might be that older people want the kids to shut up. So they'll say, "Well, you're just a kid. Wait until you are older." Even if, as kids, as we know, can have good ideas, good arguments, be thinking through various things. So just dismissing their say-so on the grounds of their age is another form of ad hominem.
3.78: Now, the way this often happens is in charged areas, as we might expect, politics discussions, religion discussions, family debates that get out of hand and various so on. But let me give you a couple of examples from business. Here's one. We're arguing over taxes. Should they be raised, kept the same, or lowered? Here's an argument that says, "Business professionals say the economy would improve if taxes were lowered." Presumably, they've given some arguments for that. "But of course, people in business just want to make money, so they would say that." And so we have that sarcastic tone in there.
3.79: Now, presumably, there are arguments about the taxes. If taxes were lowered, this is what would happen to the economy. Maybe it's good data, maybe it's good argument, maybe not. But if all we're doing is saying, we're not paying attention to your argument, we're saying you have a motive, you're a business person and you want to make money, and that's supposed to discredit your argument, well, it doesn't. It's irrelevant to the argument.
3.80: Nonetheless, we do know that, and this might be part of the reason why this argument is so common, if you have a constituency of people who listen to you, who don't like business people, who are already on the other side of the taxation argument, if you can find a way as to attack this person, get them not to pay attention to that person, it might work, but it's not working logically. It's working through cheap and dirty tactics.
3.81: Another example I hear a lot in philosophy, one of the great giants in the history of philosophy is Friedrich Nietzsche. Everybody reads Nietzsche and gets excited by reading him. Just so that everybody finds some things in Nietzsche that are incredibly outrageous, but other things that are incredibly penetrating. I would agree with most philosophers that he's worth spending some time with.
3.82: But he was famous for being harshly critical of religion in general, but particularly the forms of religion that were extant in the 1800s during his time. There's a lot of really interesting arguments there and a lot of really important arguments for religious people and non-religious people, too, to pay attention to. But it will be a mark of a person who's not interested in the issues seriously to find various ways to say, "I don't want to have to read Nietzsche. I don't want to have to be dealing with counterarguments of Nietzsche. It makes me too uncomfortable."
3.83: Maybe it's subjectivism. I want to just believe what I believe, without having to deal with this philosopher as well. So, the mark of that kind of person pops up very regularly in social media, and even in semi-professional philosophy discussions, is the biographical fact that toward the end of Nietzsche's life, he did go crazy. He became intellectually dysfunctional. One of the leading theories was that he contracted syphilis at an earlier age, and syphilis can do nasty things to you because there wasn't a cure for it at that time. That's not the only hypothesis.
3.84: But the faulty argument, or the ad hominem, then would be to say things like, "Well, yeah, Nietzsche has all of these arguments about religion, this, that, and the other thing, but he went crazy. So we don't have to pay attention to that guy." And so his later craziness, which is not relevant to his earlier arguments, and the arguments stand on their own, and even independent in the Nietzsche case, we know that sometimes people who are a little bit eccentric or a lot out there can nonetheless still come across things that are interesting, important, and you have to attend to them on their own grounds.
3.85: Another common version of this one is, and this might explain part of the psychological attraction of ad hominem, is pointing out hypocrises in other people. So someone might be making an argument for something, but then you notice that in their behavior, currently or perhaps in their past, they've not been saying things or acting in a way that's consistent with what they are arguing for right now. And you will then notice that and then say, "Oh, you're just a big old hypocrite. Therefore, this argument is no good."
3.86: For example, it might be, say, that I'm running for political office, and we're having big debates about public education. Should we reform public education? Should we have more private schooling? But suppose for whatever reasons, I am an advocate of public education, but I'm approaching it seriously as a politician. I'm saying I'm doing these studies, I've got these arguments for public education. I'm not necessarily opposed to private education, but I'm running on a platform of strengthening the public education sector.
3.87: Now, this happens, but you might then say, "Oh, well, you, 20 years ago when your kids were going through school, you didn't send your kids to public schools. You sent your kids to private schools. So you're saying you're in favor of public schools, but you sent your kids to private schools." So there's an inconsistency there that is worth raising. Why did you send your kids to private schools?
3.88: It might be that it was 20 years ago, different context. Maybe I had different beliefs, back 20 years ago. But if the cheap shot is just going to be, "Well, there's an inconsistency in what you say now versus what you said then, therefore, I'm going to ignore your arguments now on the benefits of public education," that would be to commit ad hominem.
3.89: But we're going to see in political campaigns when people are emotional and they're looking for the cheap shot, why an argument like that would be attractive. There also, I think, is something about the human condition when we are monitoring ourselves and certainly monitoring others, that we seem to be very attuned to hypocrises or inconsistencies in what people say versus what they do, what they say now versus what they say then.
3.90: Even in little children, if you have any parenting experience, they're very quick to pick up on the slightest inconsistency in policy, as announced or practiced by their parents. It might be that this is something that we are wired, psychologically, to be especially attentive to and to be especially irritated by it, which makes this argument very attractive.
3.91: Another example might be, I don't know, suppose you go to your physician and your physician says, "Really, we weighed you and this, that, and you seem like you're carrying a few extra pounds. You should go on a diet." But then your physician is sitting there, belly hanging out right over the belt. And you might then say, well, you know what the temptation is going to be. But don't give into that temptation because it may very well be the physician is exactly right to say you are carrying a few extra pounds, and there's good reasons why you should pay attention to this medical advice.
3.92: Whether I am doing a good job of maintaining my weight is an important issue for me, but it's not an important issue for you. The fact that I might be overweight does not undercut the value and the legitimacy of my arguments for you being there. I want to do one more in this session, and then I want to turn to a controversy and a historically relevant controversy.
3.93: This other important fallacy is called the appeal to force. In Latin, ad baculum, an appeal to a stick. So, metaphorically, the idea is, you're engaged in a discussion, you're engaged in an argument with someone. I'm supposed to be presenting my reasons for my belief. You're presenting your reasons for your belief. That's the right way to go. But I introduce a threat into the discussion, or I introduce some force element into the discussion. The idea then is, since I am threatening you, you will start to say different things or you will start to behave differently.
3.94: This is a "might makes right" approach to argumentation, or saying that rather argumentation doesn't matter, rather who has the power matters. That's how we are going to decide socially. The appeal to force, or ad baculum, it's just X is true because I say so, backed up with threat. Sometimes the threat is veiled, sometimes the threat is explicit.
3.95: Organized crime, one of the standard things, we see this in the movies. A shop person opens up a new shop, and then some tough guys come around and they engage in conversation with the new shop owner, saying, "This is sometimes a bit of a dangerous neighborhood. It's always good to have some extra security to make sure nothing bad happens to your shop, particularly when you're not here, or even if you're here or your kids are helping out in the shop. Wouldn't it be awful if something bad happened to the people in your shop? If you slip us some money on a regular basis, we will make sure that none of those bad things happen to you and your shop."
3.96: Now, in that case, that's an appeal to a threat. If they were to say, "You should give us money on a regular basis," they don't really have a good reason for that independently. They said, they are manufacturing. They are the threat. "We will mess you up and mess up your shop if you don't buy us off." So that's an appeal to force, and it's obviously inappropriate.
3.97: Parents will say, the kid says, "Why should I eat my vegetables?" "Because you will get a spanking if you don't." Now, typically, we don't make that argument so much anymore. It's a generational shift, but parents are tempted sometimes to appeal to force, because at that point, saying the kids said, "Why do I need to eat my vegetables?", to get into a discussion about nutrition and so forth, you don't want to go there at that point. You just want to tidy up and go watch TV or relax. So this is a short- circuit of the reasoning process, but it still is a fallacy.
3.98: Much of terrible education. This is a scandal in some higher education faculty, where we're trying to train young people to think for themselves and to be aware. Lots of controversial issues and arguments on both sides and to present all of that, but many professors we know are less interested in education and more interested in indoctrination.
3.99: "I'm the professor. I have my views, say, on these political issues or these religious issues or whatever it is that I am teaching, and I want you all to believe what I believe. I will make it clear in various ways that if you say the wrong thing in class or you say the wrong thing on the test, you will get a worse grade." Now, I'm obviously going to be sophisticated enough not to come out and say this explicitly, but savvy students pick up on this.
3.100: So part of, I think, professional education responsibility, given the stakes that are involved here, young people, we don't want to be teaching them less than that. What they should say is just whatever the authorities want them to say, and to say it out of fear, which is what the ad baculum or appeal to force argument is.
3.101: If I say, this would be even too crude, "I know you're all writing your essays on the French Revolution. But in the course of this lecture, I've made it clear what my views on the French Revolution are and what the right political lessons are. It's almost the end of the semester. Don't forget who gives the grades in this class." That's pretty naked, but people know that that's going on, and so that's going to short-circuit the thinking of the students over the course of whatever period of time that they are writing the lesson.
3.102: We know some religions, when children start to ask pesky questions, challenging questions about the religion, will threaten various sorts of things. The big one is, "You will go to hell if you ask questions like that." So ad baculum is built into some forms of religion that are not trying to encourage independent thought. Same thing occurs in political discussions. "I'm the father, and around in this house, we vote this way." Election season is coming and to make it very uncomfortable for anybody to articulate a possibly critical political opinion about my views because I am the dad and I've got power over you.
3.103: So, obviously it's a temptation. If you want to get people to believe what you want, the hard way to go is, you have to present your evidence. You have to present your data. You have to present your reason. You have to be patient with the person as they process through all of that. You have to handle their uncomfortable critical questions, their offbeat questions, their critical questions, and have good answers to all. That's very hard.
3.104: In many cases, if I'm not very committed to objectivity and independent reasoning of the people I'm dealing with, just using my power to force in the short term the result that I want, it can be tempting. And then on the other hand, a lot of times, unfortunately, people, when they are on the receiving end of that, they also learn the lesson, particularly when they are young, "I shouldn't think for myself. I shouldn't raise hard questions. I should just do what they tell me in order to get through this process." But that ends up being hard on their character, submerging yourself in that way, and has the damage of turning into a habit.
3.105: All right, in the case of all of these fallacies, what we have are extreme ways and a lot of different ways of not paying attention to the connection between evidence and/or the premises and the conclusion, short-circuiting that process by means of various kinds of devices. All of them are illogical, but some of them have some psychological power because human psychology is very powerful.
3.106: The lesson of all of them is to resist all of those temptations and all of those cheap tactics, and make sure that, in your belief formation, whatever you are believing, your belief is tied as tightly as possible to the available evidence and the available data, making that your policy of action. Now, that policy, historically, is controversial because many philosophies, many politics, many religions have found logic uncomfortable when they sort through their positions. They have inconsistencies and/or things that they don't have good data for.
3.107: So the policy of having to be reasonable in that logical sense, they will try to subvert it in various ways. Some famous historical examples of this controversy. Thomas Henry Huxley in the late 19th century stated it this way. "In matters of the intellect, follow your reason as far as it will take you, without regard to any other consideration." At some point, there will be other considerations. You have to take them in, your emotions, how they affect on other people, what other people believe and how they feel about things. But first obligation is, what does your reasoning intellect teach you?
3.108: "And negatively, in matters of the intellect, do not pretend that conclusions are certain which are not demonstrated or demonstrable." So we all would like to be certain in our beliefs, but sometimes the way it is, is we only have a certain amount of data, and something is suggested as a hypothesis. I'm considering it as a hypothesis. It might be that I'm in a situation where I know I've got inconsistent data and a couple of possible hypotheses. Well, that's where I am in my thinking, and I face that squarely.
3.109: I might have a lot of data, but I know it's not certain yet. But I really want the closure on this. Well, resist that. Say, "This is very compelling. I'm not yet certain." And only let yourself feel that certainty and make that commitment until you've got the certainty. Always be ruthlessly honest about how much support you have for whatever beliefs that you have. No contradictions, or if you have contradictions in your thinking, face them up and then back away from believing either side of the contradiction until you get it better sorted out in your thinking.
3.110: Now, the most famous historical antagonist to that viewpoint is represented by Tertullian, one of the early church fathers. Back in the times when the Roman Empire was still strong but starting to go into decline, Christianity was an ascendant force; and there was a lot of tension between the Greek and Roman schools of philosophy that thought Christianity was not true—some of them thought it was ridiculous—and some of the early defenders of Christianity who recognized that it had some serious possible inconsistent and outright contradiction problems, but nonetheless wanted to be committed to it.
3.111: So, Tertullian is one who went on the offensive in response to that, against the idea that logic matters, assessing the evidence matters, or worrying about contradictions matters. So on issues, for example, that are parts of faith, here faith meaning things that you don't necessarily understand, might not even seem reasonable to you, but nonetheless are part of the belief system that you want to commit to. If you're going to maintain your belief, it seems like you can't be logical and rational at that same time.
3.112: So was Mary really a virgin? Did an infinite God become a finite being in time and space? Could Jesus really have died and then really have come back to life? Can we really say that God is one, that we're really serious about monotheism, but then start talking about God and Jesus in different language, and also have the Holy Spirit somewhere in the mix as another element as well?
3.113: The point of all of this is not to say that, if we are smart theologians, that we can't address these issues and maybe find ways to overcome what seems to be tensions and inconsistencies and perhaps contradictions. But should we have to do that in the first place, particularly if we are the average person who wants to believe in this doctrine? Are we going to sell people, "No. Be super logical about everything in Christianity and don't believe it until you've got all of those things worked out for you. You've got all of those possible contradictions solved in your own mind"?
3.114: So Tertullian's strategy is to say,"No, logic is not for religion. Logic and faith are opposite. I'm on the side of faith, and that means I'm going to critique logic fundamentally." So the famous lines are these ones: "The Son of God died." How can God die? He's supposed to be immortal. "It is immediately credible," that is to say, believable, "because it is silly." It is silly, but I believe it. "He was buried and rose again. It is certain because it is impossible." It's impossible. But it's something that I have a psychological attitude of certainty to.
3.115: Now, this is not logic, this is faith. We have a huge then controversy over human cognition, whether the Huxley position of faith—no, you don't believe stuff, particularly if it seems inconsistent in contradiction to you—and Tertullian taking the position, no, you have to have faith, and if that means you have to set aside logic, you set aside the logic.
3.116: Another variant on the religion some thousand years, most famously perhaps represented by Galileo, who—Huxley was an agnostic, probably didn't believe, but thought we should be rational. Galileo was a believer in a god, but thought one should be rational. Tertullian wanted to believe, but on non-rational grounds. The essence of Galileo's argument is to say, look, if you're going to be a good believer in God, then you have to believe that God made the world. He made it a certain way, so that scientists can study it using logic and scientific method.
3.117: God made us, and he gave us certain faculties. He gave us our senses. He gave us our concept faculty. He gave us our reason. He gave us the ability to do logic and mathematics. So he wants us to use those things. He wants us to use our God-given faculties to study nature, logically, rationally, scientifically, to come to know him and his creation. So believing in the doctrine should ultimately be consistent with being logical.
3.118: And so, now what we then have is a three-way debate—Huxley thinking, if you are logical, you're probably not going to be a believer; Tertullian arguing or stating rather, if you want to be a believer, you have to be illogical. And Galileo arguing that we should be able to reconcile being logical with belief. We'll pause there. Lecture 4: Fallacies & Cognitive Biases At a glance — More fallacies and cognitive biases.
4.1: All right, more fallacies. We're in the midst of looking at a pattern of argumentation that is fallacious. It has the appearance of premise leading to a conclusion, but there is no logical connection at all between the premise and the conclusion. Instead, what seems to be going on is people are pushing each other's psychological buttons and trying to manipulate a certain conclusion or get it for free in a way.
4.2: So, appeal to majority. Lots and lots of people believe this doesn't mean anything for the truth of what it is that they believe. Authoritative individuals believe or are urging something. That fact alone does not provide support for the truth of the premise. The fact that you want something to be true, that you would really like something to be true, provides no evidence for it actually being true and so on.
4.3: The fact that you don't like a certain person making an argument—your dislike of that person or disapproval of that person does not mean there's anything wrong with the facts or the argument that that person is pressing. What we need to do is just train ourselves to recognize when that pattern of linguistics or arguments is happening and red flags go up and one is less likely to do so.
4.4: There's another common family of argumentation called begging the question. There's a whole family of them. There's a lot of variations on this fallacious mode of reasoning. It is really like empty calories, but it has the appearance of taking you where you want to go. Now, the name begging the question goes back to some old Latin, "petitio principii," where the idea of begging the question is—the question is the thing that you're supposed to be proving, what's your conclusion—but you're trying to get it for free in a way, and that's the begging part.
4.5: Or you haven't really earned the right to that conclusion; you've begged it in some way. Almost always what it means in a simple or more complex form is whatever it is that you are trying to conclude, you assume that in one of your premises. Having assumed it in your premises, you've already got it in your conclusion, so it makes the work of argumentation a whole lot easier.
4.6: In very crude form, it would be—when you reduce all of the manipulations out of the way—X is true, and at some point in your premises, you've got X is true. Now, almost always, though, it's not that crude. Instead, what happens is people do various machinations or linguistic manipulations.
4.7: Now, one form of that is just restatement. We know in English and in most languages, there's lots of different ways of saying the same thing. We have lots of synonyms, we have phrases that stand in for particular words. Sometimes we use metaphors and clichés and so on, and they stand in for a particular concept. A restatement would simply be to say whatever your conclusion is, you just said the same thing, but in different words in the premises. When you cancel out the differences of the words, it ends up being the same content.
4.8: Got some examples here on the board to get us started. Capital punishment. Take this first one. Capital punishment is justified because there are good reasons for putting people to death. Now, this looks like an argument. It is an argument. We have the because here. That's a premise indicator. We know this is the premise. There are good reasons for putting people to death. Before the because, almost always is the conclusion: capital punishment is justified.
4.9: So the argument is: there are good reasons for putting people to death. Therefore, if we're putting it in standard form, capital punishment is justified. But when we look a little more closely, we say, well, what is capital punishment? This phrase, capital punishment just is the legal system putting people to death. It's the same thing. It's a restatement of what capital punishment is. Then this one here, it's justified. Then we have this phrase here, good reasons.
4.10: Well, what is something to be—well, you have good reasons for it. If you have good reasons, then you have justified. This is two sets of phrases that are saying the same thing. This is one word, but then a short phrase saying the exact same thing. In this argument, I've just said the same thing repeatedly, and that then is begging the question.
4.11: Another example here, switching to democracy. Let's read it. Democracy is the proper social system as society should adopt majority rule. I've got a "should, proper," so normative concepts here. But then, let's look at it a little more closely. Actually, we have an "as" indicating. This is a premise indicator. This is my premise, "as" giving my reasons, and then this must be my conclusion.
4.12: We say, "Well, what are we talking about here in my conclusion?" I'm talking about democracy. Then we say, "What is democracy? Normally, we say, "Well, it's majority rule." Majority rule and democracy are the same thing. It's a synonym. What is it to say that something is a proper social system? It's a social system with this normative evaluation concept, proper.
4.13: Well, is that not the same as saying society should adopt? Should adopt the proper thing. Society, social system is proper, what you, society, should adopt, that's just a restatement. It seems like I've got an argument here. These are all nice words, but these are empty. These are begging the question.
4.14: So restatement. One thing, then, when you're dealing particularly with matters of some complexity is to make sure that it's not simply restatement, that the premises and the conclusions, the premises have more information. The conclusion is drawing an inference, not simply saying the same things in different words.
4.15: Now, another form of this is a kind of redefinition that we can do. What we can do in an arbitrary way is take a concept that we know people ordinarily use in a certain way, and then in the course of argument, substitute a different definition that takes you to where you want the argument to end up.
4.16: Now, that's an abstract formulation. Let me give you an example here. Suppose we're arguing about religions and morality and whether some religions are more moral than other religions and so on. So this is a made up example, but I'll be Q. I will say, "All Buddhist are virtuous. That's a very strong claim. And then you can be Z. You would say, "Wait a minute." You know a Buddhist, this guy named Singh. You say, "Well, he does such and such," various unvirtuous things, whatever those are. "Look at Singh's behavior. He's a Buddhist, but he isn't virtuous."
4.17: And then I say, "Well, obviously Singh isn't a Buddhist." You say, "Well, why not?" I say, "Well, because he isn't virtuous." Then you would say, "Well, he goes to temple. He reads the scriptures regularly. He calls himself a Buddhist, comes from a Buddhist family. So why isn't he a Buddhist?" You say, "Because he isn't virtuous." That's to beg the question.
4.18: What you have done is take what's the ordinary understanding of what is a Buddhist. Someone who thinks of himself as a Buddhist, goes to the Buddhist temples, read Buddhist scriptures, etc. But you've substituted your definition, which is to say if it doesn't meet your criterion of virtue, any deviation from that, then suddenly that person is not a Buddhist. That's a contentious, slippery way of avoiding having to argue for the issue at stake.
4.19: Now, a more complicated one, aside from these arbitrary definitions being substituted and restated—and this is where one really has to be paying attention and do one's work—is what is more formerly called circular reasoning or arguing in a circle. Now, the crudest form of this is going to be: one says A proves B. You might have some good evidence that A leads to B, and then B proves C. C proves D, but then you find that the argument from D proves A.
4.20: What you've done is you've gone in a circle here. You don't have anything outside of this circle, any facts independently supporting this whole circle of reasoning, and that's illegitimate. Now, what makes this challenging is that in complicatedmatters, particularly cutting edge matters, when one's developing an argument, say, over a whole chapter, it might be that the A proves B part occupies the first page or two.
4.21: You say, "OK, finally, we've got A proves B." Then it takes two or three pages for the person connecting B to C. Four or five pages later, we finally are getting to D. Then, in the wrap up, finally, the person is, in effect, pulling the rabbit out of the hat, but it's there that they make the argument for D proving A. You have to have digested, say, this whole 25-page chapter and be keeping track of the argument as it goes along the major stages at each point.
4.22: Then step back and say, "Oh, wait a minute, we've just gone in a circle over 25 pages." That's hard work. In some cases, of course, this happens over the course of a whole book, which means one's note-taking analysis has to be very diligent in order to catch the begging of the question.
4.23: Let me give you a silly but fun example of this begging the question. Suppose you want to get a loan, so you go to the bank and you're talking with the bank officer and you say, "I would like to take this loan out." And the bank officer says, "Well, OK, fine, but do you have any collateral? So if you don't pay back the loan, we can take something of equivalent financial value to cover the loan." And you say, "Well, no, no, unfortunately I don't have any collateral, but I'm an honest person. I always pay my loans back on time. You can trust me. Give me the loan."
4.24: And the bank officer would then, quite rightly, say, "Well, I don't really know you. I don't know your track record. I don't have any way to know whether you are really a person of character and that I can trust you or not." You say, "Well, that's fine. That's why I brought my friend with me." So you did bring a friend with you. "My friend will vouch for me. He'll tell you what a great guy I am, that I'm trustworthy, that I always do what I say that I'm going to do." This is better. A friend vouches for me as evidence, witness evidence, so to speak, for the bank officer.
4.25: Now, then the bank officer, of course, is going to say, "Well, I don't really know your friend either. So I don't know whether I can trust him when he says that you're a good guy who's going to pay the loan back." And then you say at that point, "Well, that's fine. I can vote for my friend. He's a really good guy. He wouldn't lie about these sorts of things."
4.26: And there I've gone in a circle because my friend is vouching for me and I'm vouching for my friend who's vouching for me. And the bank officer is caught then in a circle. He doesn't have any independent verification of anyone's trustworthiness or integrity on these particular matters. All right, now, again, that's over the course of two minutes.
4.27: Chances are good; you can catch that one, but it's the shorter ones like that that flag the thing to your attention so that when—you start to suspect, when you're dealing with longer things that you've come in a circle, you can slow down and check those things out a little more.
4.28: Now, another example of begging the question is typically called the question-begging epithet, where in the course of your argument, you will slip a word or a phrase that supports, illegitimately, the conclusion that you want to support. The most standard examples involve lawyers trying to manipulate jurors in various ways. I say I'm the lawyer for the state and we are prosecuting someone who is suspected of murder, but we've not yet proved that this person has committed the murder. My job as the prosecutor is to lay out all of the evidence systematically to show that this person is the murderer.
4.29: But suppose in my opening speech to the jury, I say something like this: "Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, I will now proceed to prove to you that this vicious killer is indeed guilty of the crime." Now, that's a question-begging epithet, which is a word or phrase that we've used because I have called this person a vicious killer in my opening statements. But I have not yet provided any evidence for this person being a vicious killer. That's my job. But I'm not allowed to call him a killer until I have proved that he's a killer—much less call him a vicious killer until I have proved that there is viciousness.
4.30: Or a politician might say, in the heat of a debate, "This is a monstrous policy, and I will go on to show why this policy that's proposed is monstrous." Can't call it monstrous until you've proved or given the evidence for its monstrosity, whatever it is. The idea here is that you're trying to cheat because you are smuggling in your conclusion in your opening statements, so to speak, and that's illegitimate.
4.31: Another version, in some ways, this is the most fun version of this, but it's very common, is begging the question by means of what are called complex questions. I will put a question out there, and it's a serious question. Sometimes it has a somewhat rhetorical force to it. Part of the challenge is you have to take the question and turn it into whatever the declarative sentences the person is really meaning, the literal sentences and so on. But it's called a complex question because in the formulation of the question, you again have built in the conclusion that you want just into the formulation of the question.
4.32: Up on the board here, if we approach at some family reunion or high school reunion, I haven't seen you for a while, but I ask you: "Do you still gamble away your paycheck every Friday night?" Now, it might be true and it might not be true, but that formulation, particularly if there's a crowd of people around you and I'm doing something attacking, immediately puts you on the defensive—partly because it is formulated, again, as a yes or no question where you can't really say "yes" without admitting something you don't want to admit, and you can't say no without admitting something that you don't want to admit.
4.33: There's two questions that are built into it. Did you, at one point in the past, gamble away your paycheck every Friday night? That's one question. And now, do you still gamble away your paycheck on Friday night? So there's a question about the past. There's a question about the present. But this person, me in this case, has bundled those two together in a complex question.
4.34: The sign of a complex question will almost be that it's phrased as a yes or no. You have to affirm or deny the question, but you can't, or you find yourself resisting wanting to do so. Because in this case, you want to say, "Yes." Admission? Well, that means I did and I still do. Or you want to say, "No, I don't do it anymore," but you've already then seemingly admitted that you did in the past. Have you stopped beating your wife? Would be another one. Drop that one into a social event. The poor guy doesn't know what's hit him.
4.35: Why should we continue—in a political—why should we continue to be exploited by the greedy capitalists? You see that in social media discussions. It's assuming we are, and why should we continue? Well, we shouldn't. There's a whole set of assumptions built at the end of that one as well. Moms and dads to their kids: "Do you want to be a good boy and go to bed?" " Do you want to be a good girl? Eat your vegetables, etc." Of course, the poor kid has not taken logic yet. He's not in, "Wait a minute, Mom, that's a complex question." But maybe they can pick this one up. This is a part of the training here.
4.36: There's two things here. Do you want to be a good boy? Well, probably the answer to that question is, "Yes." Do you want to go to bed? "No." So one answer to this complex question is inappropriate. The kid doesn't want to say "yes" because then they're saying they want to go to when really the little boy doesn't want to go to bed, and he doesn't want to say "no" because he doesn't want to say he's not a good boy. So it's sneaky parenting. It might be a useful tactic, of course, when you're desperate, but, logically, it is fallacious.
4.37: In politics, you see this fairly regularly. People will assume that their approach to politics embodies all virtue and all goodness, so they will bundle a statement about their politics with morally charged language. "Do you want to be a progressive socialist person?" There the assumption is, socialism has a monopoly on being progressive, so we just lump progressivism in with socialism.
4.38: Do you want to be—religions do this, too. "My religion has a monopoly on proper approaches to morality. Do you want to be an upstanding religious person?" Or "Don't you admire these upstanding religious—" whatever denomination you want to praise? Again, making the association implicitly that being a member of this religion entitles you to use that moral labeling.
4.39: But you need to argue for that. You need to argue, to say, "Here's my religion, here's what it stands for. Here's my morality, here's what it stands for. There is an intimate connection between these two things, and that connection is better than what you find in the other religions." That's a lot of work. It's a question-begging cheap shot to go there.
4.40: So let's say, sometimes this gets piled up together. "Do you want to be a good boy and go to bed?" I mean, suppose your kid had been secretly reading logic books, and said, "Wait a minute, Dad. That's a complex question. That's begging the question. That's an illegitimate fallacy." And you say, "Shut up or I'll smack you. Get to bed." And then the kid would say, "Wait a minute, Dad. That's an appeal to force. That was in the earlier chapter, also illegitimate." So logic can be dangerous for parenting.
4.41: One possibly apocryphal historical example that I like to think about involves one of the King Charleses back in the day, and he suspected that his court intellectuals—this was in the early days of science—were just making up a lot of stuff. They really didn't know what was going on. So he put this question to them as a test, but he put it, not that they knew it was going to be a test. So he put this scientific question to them. He made a little competition associated with it.
4.42: He says, "What's interesting is, if you have observed a fish in a bowl of water, a live fish, but you fill the bowl of water right up to the brim—so if you had a little more water, it would spill over, but just enough so that it doesn't spill over, that the fish can swim around in that water and it won't spill any of the water. But if you have the exact same amount of water and you put a dead fish in it and fill it up to the brim right again, it will spill over. Isn't that weird? Why is this?"
4.43: And so his court intellectuals then get busy and they start to come up with all kinds of explanations and so forth. None of them work. The reason why none of them work is that King Charles has given them a complex question. It is not true that the dead fish in the full body of water will cause it to spill over. But nonetheless, they just took the complex question and then devoted all of this energy to useless intellectualizing, when built into that complex question was something they should have detected and checked.
4.44: In that case, the first thing to do would be not immediately go to the speculation, but go back to the beginning and say, "We have some claims here, some empirical claims. Live fish in that amount of water won't spill. Dead fish in the same amount of water will spill. I need to check that, check the data, and unbundle the question before going on to do the explanations."
4.45: Now, another pair of fallacies that go together, they go by the names equivocation and amphiboly. It's big fancy labels for things that are unclear or or ambiguous in formulation. The only difference is that, in equivocation, we have words that could mean two or more different things. The fallacies typically occur, this is an abstract formulation of it, when you start off in the argument using the word this way, but at some point you shift in the argument to using the word in the other way.
4.46: Or in a social context sometimes the argument will break down because one person has started using a concept in a particular way, but the other person at some point gets away from that and starts using the concept in a different way. Then obviously the reasoning is going to go awry in the course of doing so. Amphiboly is the case of particular words, not them alone, but rather phrases that can be interpreted in different ways.
4.47: Here's a silly one to begin. It's a way of insulting someone. You say your argument is sound, nothing but sound. Now, in that case, sound is one of those words that's a congratulations word in logic. Your argument is very strong, good reasoning. It's sound. But we also use the word sound to talk about ephemeral sound waves. They come and go, and sometimes they're empty and they don't mean anything. So this starts off sounding like it's praise, but quickly switches to an insult. That's an equivocal phrase in action.
4.48: We use the words trunk. This would never happen in an argument, but it's an equivocal phrase. Are you talking about the long protuberance on the front of an elephant? Are you talking about the tail end of a car where you can store stuff? Are you talking about a big wooden chest up in your grandmother's attic where there's stuff stored in it? So trunk is potentially equivocal.
4.49: A fence. Is it a boundary between your property and the next property? Is a fence someone who deals in stolen goods? It's the same words. Now, those are crude and quite distant, so we're not likely to confuse them very often. But as, again, things get complicated, they get more serious, and particularly in cases where we're a little invested in what the issues are, the temptation to equivocate and use words in this slippery way becomes more tempting.
4.50: Let's try this one as an argument here. Voting is a right. The government should enforce rights. Thus, the state should enforce voting. Let me pause for a moment. We have this word thus. It's a formal conclusion indicator. Thus, therefore, hence. So we know the conclusion is, the state should enforce voting. Well, why? What are the premises for this? Well, one premise, voting is a right. The government should enforce rights is another premise. You put those together, the state, therefore, should enforce voting.
4.51: Now, there's an equivocation in here because this can be interpreted in more than one way. When I say that the state, for example, in the conclusion, should enforce voting, what does that mean? It depends on what you also take the right to be. So does voting as a right mean this is your prerogative as a citizen, your choice as a citizen? You have the access to the political power to make your beliefs on political matters heard and counted for something in the decision-making process. You have the right to that.
4.52: But also as a right, it's your choice or not, you can say, "Well, actually, I don't want to vote, so I don't choose to vote." But we have this enforcement issue that comes up in the second sentence and in the conclusion. When we're talking about the government enforcing things, sometimes we mean the government would make you do things. If we take the enforcement in this case to mean that, when probably the other person means enforce the other way, you have this free choice right, and so your right to vote or not vote, that's what the government should be protecting, protecting your choice.
4.53: In the second interpretation, the choice gets taken away. No, the government is supposed to enforce rights. Voting is a right, so therefore it's going to enforce voting. So it goes around and rounds people up on election day and makes sure they go to the voting poll booth and cast their vote. Now, that would then be an equivocation on the nature of a right and the nature of enforcement that's appropriate to the right in this case.
4.54: Again, this is more subtle, stakes are higher. Of course, we do know there are some democratic systems that do enforce voting in the one way. It's just an option, a power that you have. You can exercise it or not. Others that say voting is a right, but in a democratic context, everybody has to participate, and so they make people engage in the voting process.
4.55: Here's another example. I give you this sentence here. People who sell drugs to children are the scum of the earth. Chances are very good you'll say, "Well, yeah, of course. They're awful." But then if I were to give you the rest of an argument that said something like, pharmacists sometimes sell drugs to children, the logical conclusion, it seems, would be that pharmacists are the scum of the earth, and something has gone wrong in that case.
4.56: So when we talk about people who sell drugs to children, that phrase, immediately at the beginning, you were thinking of the grubby people, the illegal people, the people who are callous about kids and so forth, whereas, really, I was wanting you to think about pharmacists. But because this phrase is ambiguous, it's not clear which one is which. The argument works if you assume we're talking about the nasty people, but it doesn't work if we are talking about pharmacists. We're talking about legally or illegally, and there's a whole background context that we need to be attending to.
4.57: Some connections between logic and humor. Again, humorists are very often very good with logical expectations and wordplay and so forth. Equivocation is one of their favorite places to spend some time. The famous comedian George Burns died a few years ago. He actually lived to be well over 100, smoking huge cigars all of the time, constantly. But one of his jokes was, "If you live to the age of 100, you have it made because very few people die past the age of 100."
4.58: Now, where's the equivocation in that? Well, it could be, one interpretation is, very few people die past the age of 100. What that means is, by the time you get to 100, most people are gone. So there's very few who get there in the first place. That's the true interpretation. But the fun interpretation is to take it the other way, to say, well, once you get to 100, very few people die past the age of 100. That means you've got it made in the sense of, you're not going to die or you're not very likely to die, because you've made it to 100. So two different ways of playing with that.
4.59: Psychiatrist joke. One out of four people has a mental illness. So check three of your friends. If they are OK, it's you. That's right. Again, one in three does not necessarily mean in every group of four, it's going to be one of them. Doesn't means if you've sequentially checked one, two, three, the next one is going to be the person. It's the statistical percentage of a large group when we don't know the constituent numbers.
4.60: It used to be popular in some farmers' fields where there was a bull, the farmer would put up a notice saying, "The farmer allows walkers to cross the field for free, but the bull charges." So it's a fun way of saying there's a bull in this field, so beware. But we have free and charge used in two different ways—charge as a monetary cost. Well, the farmer is not charging you in that sense. He's not saying you have to pay in order to cross the field. What bulls do when they come at you, we also call that charging. It's non-monetary. It's something else to worry about altogether.
4.61: Then in the ongoing jokes about men and women and marriages and so forth, a linguist noted, the shortest sentence in the English language, "I am." It's two words, three letters, but then waggishly adds, "Could it be that 'I do' is the longest sentence?" Making a joke about marriage, in this case, I do, can be just taken as a certain number of syllables, certain number of words, short words in both cases, there's only two them, but we also know that I do is a performative in the context of marriage, and marriage is a kind of sentence, but sentence not in the linguistic sense, but sentence in the punishment for your misdeeds, whatever those are.
4.62: Take life with a grain of salt, as we all know that cliché, plus a slice of lemon and a shot of tequila. The equivocation in that case is, life taken with a grain of salt. That little cliché. You put salt on something, the idea is that you moderate the claim to a certain kind of chemical reaction. You neutralize whatever these fiery things are going on. Take it with a grain of salt, calm down, not such a big deal. In this case here, literally take life with alcohol. That will help you get through. And that's the joke formulation of it.
4.63: OK, let's move on to amphiboly. Amphiboly is grammatical constructions, not particular words or phrases. So all those rules about grammar and using commas appropriately, dashes, parentheses, word order, in complex sentences—all of that needs to be attended to by clear writers and clear thinkers, so that you don't set your readers up for an amphibolous formulation. Here's an example here. I'm going to flag this one a couple of times.
4.64: So all that glitters is not gold. Now, it's an old cliché. The cliché is meant to say, just because you find something glittery, glittery things are attractive to you, don't make the mistake of thinking that it's valuable. There's a surface and depth issues, but then also a lot of glittery things, or things that seem valuable, are not valuable over the longer time. Gold is, of course, glittery and valuable, but not everything is like that. So it's meant metaphorically to be a warning against appearances and so forth.
4.65: But if you take this literally, another way of saying it is that all that glitters, we also then take that sometimes to mean everything that is in that category, all of the things that are glittery are not gold. And that's not true because gold is a glittery thing. So is it really saying some things that are glittery are not gold? So be on your guard. Or is it really saying literally all that glitters is not gold? The point is that, for your alert reader, they're going to have to pause and think about it to make sure what is the most likely interpretation in that case.
4.66: Another example of the exact same amphibolous formulation—all married couples do not sleep together. Now, if you take that literally, this is all married couples, they don't sleep together. That sounds a bit harsh, and it also is not true. What this person probably means is, it's not the case that all married couples sleep together. But the positioning of this "not" in this overall formulation has made it amphibolous. Does this mean all married couples don't sleep together? Or does it mean some married couples don't sleep together? And you want to, for the interests of clarity and economy, not have amphibolous formulations like that.
4.67: This one here, a little bit amusing. Woman without her man is lost. This then becomes a lesson in punctuation because that can be interpreted in two different ways, depending on where you put the emphasis in spoken language or where you put the commas in written language. Do I say that the right way to interpret this is to take this as the noun phrase, woman without her man? A woman without her man, comma, is lost. That would then be to say, women who don't have a man, they are lost.
4.68: This is a little bit metaphorical, right? To say she doesn't know what she's doing with her life, et cetera, she's not fulfilled. That's a possibility. But if I put two commas here— Woman, without her, man is lost—and that then is the opposite. That then is to say, man is lost if he's without a woman. Woman, without her, the man is lost. So amphibolous formulations, we want to avoid them. So whichever of those you want to argue for and be popular at the party, make sure you put your commas in the right position.
4.69: Some funny ones, sometimes unintentionally funny. Sometimes when I'm writing letters of recommendations for my students, and of course, you want to praise up your students, but there are some students who are a little bit marginal and in a dark humor mode, you want to play around with the idea of sending a recommendation that's not really a recommendation. If I said, for example, "I cannot recommend this person too highly," well, it's like, it could be praise. I could be saying, "Here's all these recommendations, all this great, high, wonderful stuff, and I just can't say enough high stuff about this person in this recommendation."
4.70: That's one, but the opposite is to say, "I can't recommend this person too highly. So there's high recommendation, and I can't do that." But the formulation all by itself doesn't say which way it would go. Or, "Nobody would be better for the job." Ambiguous on the nobody, in that particular context. Are we saying people who are good for the job, there's this guy and there's nobody else? So nobody would be better than this guy for the job.
4.71: Or, this is rather pathetic, would you say, nobody, nonexistent, not having anybody do that job would be better than this guy. And that's the worst possible interpretation. But chances are good, in the context of a letter of recommendation, the person might give you the benefit of the doubt, but you don't want to leave that up for grabs.
4.72: From an old cookbook, instructions: "Serve the meat when thoroughly stewed." This was an old-fashioned cookbook. Stewed is an old way of talking about having had too much to drink. How do you know when the meat is done? Well, after you've had enough wine or whatever it is during your— you are the one who is stewed. Now, finally, the meat is likely to be ready or whatever. In fact, the cookbook is trying to say, no, it's the meat that has to be thoroughly stewed. It has to be in a certain condition, not you, the cook, in a certain condition.
4.73: Book review, the author, these are real ones now. "The author warns against a number of logical fallacies in his book," the logic book, of all things. Now, is he saying that the author of the logic book says, "Here's a whole bunch of logical fallacies," and is warning you, the reader, about the logical fallacies?
4.74: Or is it, the author has written the logic book and reread it, but now it's been published and says, "Man, there's a lot of logical fallacies in my writing. I made a lot of mistakes here. I'm going to warn you up front that there are these logical fallacies in the book." Now, literally speaking, that's an amphibolous formulation. We probably know which one the person means, but it should be embarrassing that a person reviewing a logic book would use that kind of formulation.
4.75: All right, this is an old newspaper account, a real one. The Graf Zeppelin, I think it was almost exactly a century ago, was it not the big hydrogen-inflated balloons that were sometimes capable of transatlantic transactions? And so back in the day, that was a big deal in the early days of transcontinental flight. And this was a real newspaper clipping from the time.
4.76: "The Graf Zeppelin was leaving the Lakehurst airport." It had come across from Germany, I think, and now it was going to have its return flight to go back to Germany. "Among the last to enter was Mrs. Smith, the lone woman passenger. Slowly, her huge nose was turned into the wind, and then, like some huge beast, she crawled along the grass." I can't even say that with a straight face.
4.77: Now, this is an amphibolous formulation in a relatively short paragraph because, at the beginning, we introduced the Graf Zeppelin, which is a big cumbersome-shaped being. Then we introduced Mrs. Smith, and we don't have any descriptors of what she is like physically. But Mrs. Smith is the most recent thing we were talking about, and then we start using pronouns. Her huge nose. Whose huge nose are we talking about? Who is the beast lumbering across the grass? Hopefully, it's the Graf Zeppelin, but this is embarrassing newspaper writing because of the amphiboly.
4.78: Want ads have always been a source of really fun ones because, in old traditional want ads, you had to pay by the word, so you would try to cut out as many words as you possibly could, and often it would be the clarifying words that get cut out. So, "Selling an antique desk suitable for lady with curved legs and large drawers. Also, mahogany chest." OK, well, very well. We'll skip over the next one and go immediately to appeal to emotion.
4.79: Appeal to emotion. This is a complicated one on both the logic side and the emotion side, because arguing passionately about what one believes in, what one thinks is true, can be perfectly fine, as long as that is built upon a logical foundation. So you've done your homework, you've got your facts, you've got your data, you've checked your logic, and it's an important issue. Having some passion in the presentation of your argument is perfectly legitimate.
4.80: Appeal to emotion is a fallacy when the emotion substitutes for the logic. That is to say, one doesn't really have much by way of facts, data, solid argument. Instead, one appeals to all the language that we know pushes people's buttons easily. There are concepts and issues where we know people are coming in with an emotionally charged state in a particular way, and so we can use language to play on that.
4.81: So a lot of mob psychology and mob rallies in a political context are very good examples of this. People come out for a mass rally, they're already excited, they're energized, whatever the issues of the day are, they're charged up about that. And then you bring in a speaker, often a politician, who knows how to play the crowd, get them whipped up even into more of a frenzy. In many cases, the speaker does not have to have good arguments or make particularly clear points.
4.82: But if you use language well, then people will go away, hopefully, they will go away without destroying stuff. They will go away feeling like they've learned a lot, they've heard a lot, and they are more affirmed in their commitments. So demagoguery, certain kinds of populist politicians, particularly now in the last 100 years or so, since we are much more Democratic and Republican, mass participatory politics, and we have the technology to record a lot of the speeches on sound and video, they're useful to study for people interested in political rhetoric.
4.83: The cases of politicians who use logic integrated with rhetoric very well. Martin Luther King is an outstanding example of that, according to logicians who've done the studies here. Adolf Hitler is typically used as a documented example of the others. Very long speeches. Often there's not very much content to it, but he's very dramatic and very charismatic, and he uses certain kinds of language. Equally, as inspiring as people listening to Dr. King felt, people listening to Adolf Hitler felt. So the outcomes tended to be the same, even though one was more empty.
4.84: Now, menus is an example here. Often we go to fancy restaurants. They want to do two things. They want to let you know what you are ordering off the menu, so they have descriptors. But as we know from reading the menus, they almost always use the most elevated language possible to describe whatever the menu is. So, filet mignon sounds foreign, exotic, and so on. But I could describe this literally as chunk of dead cow. It's what it is.
4.85: This tells you as much or more, but you'll never see this on a restaurant menu. The emotional connotations are wrong. You don't want to think about cow. You don't want to think of things as chunk. You want it to be properly prepared. You don't want to think about dead things. You want to think, "I'm in an exotic, fancy, eating a special meal," and so on.
4.86: Egghead is a pejorative meant for someone who is an intellectual. Talking about the same group of people, people who think a lot about ideas, so forth, calling someone an intellectual here, praise, calling them an egghead, is a mild insult. Same thing with respect to more recent phrases like nerd and geek. You call someone a geek, it typically means someone who has unusual habits and unusual ways of dealing with things that are a little bit outside of the mainstream. Nerds, more interested in intellectual matters or really drilling down into computers or math or whatever it is.
4.87: What is interesting, since language evolves, is that in many cases, what starts off as an insult then comes to be adopted by the group and they will start to wear it as a badge of pride. "Yes, I am a nerd. I'll get a T-shirt, nerds rule. Be nice to nerds. You're going to be working for one, one of these days." All of that sort of stuff. There's an ongoing verbal battle over phrases and the emotional connotations that are associated with them.
4.88: When we are debating complicated issues, to what extent or not should a person's race or sex or gender or religious background and so forth be a factor in making decisions about hiring and promotions and who gets into college and who does not, people who are on the opposite side of that will try to say, "Well, it's a kind of discrimination, but it's just discrimination in the other way." So the most literal true statement should be, it's a reverse discrimination. If we're trying to make up for discriminations that went the other way, we're just reversing it, but it's the same thing.
4.89: And the implication of this phrase is that there's something wrong with it. By contrast, people who are proponents of it are more likely to say, what we are doing is something positive or something affirmative. So discrimination has a kind of a bad taste to us, and just reversing it doesn't sound like progress. But if I can say we're taking action in an affirmative direction, trying to make up for past wrongs, then we use that label. So both of them carry emotive content with it.
4.90: In political issues, when we're dealing with people who are engaged in non-standard ways of protest, violent ways of protest, sometimes organized, sometimes not, that are affecting lots and lots of people negatively, lots and lots of victims, is this person a terrorist or is the person a freedom fighter? Very often people who approve of those tactics in that context will say, "Whatever the person's cause was, I approve of that cause, and there's a freedom component of some sort in that cause, and so this person is fighting for freedom."
4.91: People who disapprove are more likely and more quickly to say this person is a terrorist, because it's hard to find any redeeming qualities in just terrorism for the sake of terrorism itself. Or "Marxists versus commies." This is a more neutral person, in a description of what the person stands for; commies is slang and a little bit derogatory formulation.
4.92: So one thing to attend to is, when you are reading a passage or you hear someone, or of course, also yourself, if you are worked up in the heat of the moment, is the language that you are using, emotional language, which is fine, but is it carrying content, or is the emotiveness of the language doing the work and not actually any logic to it?
4.93: Here's a slightly made-up example, taken from social media. Some of the debates over climate change, and some people believe that oil is the main culprit, and behind the oil, it's oil companies are the main culprit, so they want to attack those guys. Of course, there are issues and arguments to be addressed on this whole complex of issues as well. But this my massageed version of the social media post.
4.94: "The only possible cure for the present climate crisis is the elimination of all oil and coal companies. Finally, my friends, we must put an end to the diabolical conspiracy of the oil profit-mad vultures of Big Oil. Don't let the billionaire tycoons wrap their slimy tentacles around our children's future and squeeze it dead." OK. Now, that's some strong language. Slimy tentacles, profit-mad. In some quarters, Big Oil is taken to be a bad thing, squeezing things dead and so forth.
4.95: But if we take a moment and say, "Is there any content to this?", the conclusion seems to be, we need to completely get rid of oil companies. Why? Well, diabolical conspiracy. What diabolical conspiracy? Why is it diabolical, which has religious overtones? Are they really inspired by the devil in doing so? Oil profit-mad. Well, OK, of course they want to make profits, but does that make you crazy or mad? Is that the only thing that is going on in their minds? Et cetera, et cetera.
4.96: If you unpack each of them, it turns out that there is a neutral way of stating that. But even when you translate it into the neutral language, it's not advancing an argument; it ends up being rather emotional. Now, emotional language, I can't overstate this, has a perfectly good place. It doesn't mean you have to turn yourself into a robot or an unfeeling person making various arguments. You just have to make sure your emotions are tied to the logic.
4.97: We have more legitimate uses for poetry as well. In many cases, poets are very good. The good poets will have something to say, something important and significant to say. They could, of course, say it quite neutrally, but one of the things we do like about poetry is a careful attention to the kind of language that emotionally accentuates whatever the message is that the poet wants to communicate.
4.98: In this case here, this is a title of a famous Romantic poem from about 200 years ago. But suppose, instead of calling it or titling it, the poet had said, instead of "Ode to a Grecian Urn," I said "Poem for a Greek Pot." OK, well, an urn is a type of pot. Grecian, poem, a type of pot, and so on. This is more standard. Grecian sounds, as an adjective, a little more elevated. Poem, a little bit neutral; ode is more precise and a specific type of poem and so on. So this works better in poetry, but it carries this information, but adds the emotive language, and that's perfectly fine.
4.99: Another fun one and a popular one we call a false alternative. As the name suggests, the person presents an alternative to you. It's an either-or, choose this or choose this. But it's a false alternative because there are, in fact, more alternatives. Sometimes those other alternatives are a little more subtle, or they're not immediately present in the context that you are operating in. But the person wants to force a decision in a certain direction, so they will limit the range of alternatives available to your mind and try to get you to adopt one of those.
4.100: I want to start with a joke on this one just because it's a classic joke from the comedian Steve Martin, now older, but one of the comedians of my generation, anyway. So he tells this joke, when he was younger. He comes in at the start of the set and he says, "I'm feeling a little bit sad because my girlfriend's not with me anymore, and I'm a little bit broken up about that." Now, then immediately people are there, "Well, Steve broke up with his girlfriend. Oh, poor guy. That's too bad."
4.101: And then he says, "Actually, she's dead." So you get the elevation from breaking up to dead. Oh, then there's nervous laughter at this point. Then he says, "I'm partly broken up because I feel a little bit responsible for her death." And now we all want to know, what's the story here? He says, "Well, we went to a party together, and I had a couple of drinks, but not too much. But she was really having a good time. And she was drinking a little bit too much and then a lot too much. And then she came up to me and she said, 'Steve, I think I've had too much to drink. I want to go home now.'"
4.102: And then Steve said, "Well, I was having a really good time and I didn't really want to leave at that point. So I said a few minutes. So she went off and had another drink, and I continued to have some fun. Then she came back, 'Steve, I really need to go home now.'" And Steve said, "I really didn't want to leave the party because I was having such a good time, so I shot her."
4.103: And that's the joke, but very dark humor. So what is setting this up, though, is a false alternative. So at that situation in the party, you're thinking, OK, the alternative Steve faces is, take her home, drive her home, be the responsible boyfriend, or maybe call her a cab to send her home. Those are the alternatives that are legitimate to be facing her.
4.104: So out of the blue, apparently in his mind, shooting her is another alternative for the circumstance, and that's the one that he chose. And that is kind of a false alternative, Steve, because you do have all these other options that are a lot less extreme than shooting the person just because you're having a good time at the party. So that's a false alternative, a rather blatant one.
4.105: The example we looked at earlier as a complex question, it also is a false alternative. "Do you want to be a good boy and go to bed?" So the mother or the father is presenting it. Either there is this package, you go to bed, or you're a bad boy. That's the implication. Obviously, there are other options. If you don't go to bed, it doesn't mean you're a bad boy necessarily. It could be that you stayed up for another 30 minutes and you're still a good boy and so forth.
4.106: Often in political contexts or religious contexts, people want to turn things into an either-or, and they don't want to deal with people socially in an inappropriate way. So you're either with us or you're against us. That's the bottom line that is communicated. But often it's not the case that you're either with or [against]. Sometimes, of course, you have to make a choice. What you stand for, you don't have any alternatives. But lots of times, it's an issue and you don't care about that issue. So you're not for or against on this issue. Or you're undecided. Maybe I'll be on your side after I think about this more, but at this point, it's a false alternative to say either-or.
4.107: Suppose this is a class involving testing. We've talked about certain material. You're in the midst of taking a test, you're writing away. At the end of the test, I'm your professor, and I come up to your desk where you're writing, and I take your examination, and I say to you, "You cheated," and I proceed to tear your examination up and deposit it in the trash. You say, "What?" You're surprised. "I didn't cheat." And I say to you, if that went well, "Prove it. Prove to me that you did not cheat."
4.108: In that context, if that's all I've got, I have committed what logicians call the fallacy of appeal to ignorance. Now, you probably at this point would say, "How would I try to prove that I didn't cheat?" You've been sitting there and you're doing your writing, you didn't look right or left, you didn't have secret cheat sheets. None of those things exist. So there's nothing that you can proffer as evidence of your non-cheating. If you didn't cheat, there won't be any evidence of non-cheating, because not cheating is a non- existence.
4.109: By contrast, I am the professor. Maybe I have a responsibility to make sure that student work, or part of my responsibility to make sure the student work is reflective of what the student knows. If I want to make the claim that you cheated, then I can point to evidence, if there is such things as evidence, because cheating requires certain actions taking place.
4.110: I can say, "Here we were videoing. I can see that you were looking at her thing for a certain number of minutes and copying down what she wrote." I can look in your ear and see evidence that you have a remote speaker in there and someone is feeding the answers to you, or you have a cheat sheet. Aha! I pull it out from under your desk, and so on. In that case, if there were certain actions that actually occurred in reality that are cheating actions, there will be evidence for it, and it's my obligation to provide them.
4.111: In that situation, we call it an appeal to ignorance because you are ignorant in this context of not being able to come up with anything to support your side of this disagreement. I am appealing to your ignorance. You can't prove that you didn't cheat. Then I'm going to take that as evidence for you did cheat, and that justifies me throwing your examination away. Appeal to ignorance is an illegitimate mode of reasoning. I want to make a claim something exists, it's up to me to prove it.
4.112: Now, the reason for this is that we all start from a default position of not believing billions and trillions and so forth potential things. Things are not in our heads. We don't have to start off with some sort of obligation to explain why a certain idea is not in my head right now, why I don't believe a certain thing. It goes the other way around.
4.113: For me to justifiably or logically have some idea in my mind, I have to show what led me, what facts of reality or inferences from facts of reality, led me to have that idea in my head. If I just randomly come up with some idea and say, "I want to believe that idea," and you haven't proved why that's a bad idea, you've never considered that idea before, therefore, I'm justified in believing whatever random thing in my head, that's appeal to ignorance.
4.114: A slightly dated example, going back to my mother's generation of college, when colleges were much more ruthlessly segregated between boys' dorms and girls' dorms; and the girls' dorms had very strict policies about times when young men were allowed to be in the dorms, where they could be in the dorms, and when the curfew kicked in and they absolutely had to be out, and these were very strictly, strictly monitored.
4.115: And my mother tells the case of a young woman she knows who was accused of having a boy in her room at the wrong time. And it turns out that this was just a revenge accusation from one of the girl's enemies, but she reported it to the house mom or whoever. "She has boys in her room, or a boy in her room," and the house mother goes up and says, "You had a boy in your room." And she says, "No, I didn't." She said, "Well, prove it. Prove that you didn't have a boy in your room," right, at that.
4.116: Well, how would you do that? This is before video cameras and various sorts of things like that. But if she's correct, and there was no boy in her room at that, there won't be any evidence of that, because non-existing boys don't leave traces of where they have gone in the world. In this situation, the obligation is with probably the first girl who allegedly reported it; but certainly, the house mother, if you're going to prosecute or, that's too strong, if you're going to pursue this, rather, have some actual evidence for why you are putting this person in the hot seat.
4.117: Now, this takes us to an important distinction that we have to insist upon. We call existence claims versus nonexistence claims. There's a difference between saying or thinking or considering that something exists, versus the position of someone who does not consider that something exists, doesn't believe that something exists or things not actually existing. The idea of logic is that we're trying to keep our minds connected to reality, and the only thing that connects our minds to reality is evidence from reality.
4.118: We always start from the position of asking, if you want to say something exists or something is real or something is true, you start from having the obligation to provide that evidence for it being there. If something doesn't exist, then it doesn't leave any traces. It doesn't leave any evidence. Non-existing things don't interact with anything else in the world, so they can't be detected. They can't be detected because they can't exist. So it's just an empty void.
4.119: And so asking for evidence of nonexistence is a very different kind of claim. It's almost impossible to achieve that. That's why we have a closely related principle that we call the burden of proof principle, or sometimes it's called the onus of proof principle. So sometimes this is a rhetorical issue. Whoever starts the discussion, starts the argument, puts something out there—let's talk about this—that person does bear an immediate onus or burden of justifying why we should be talking about that. That can be partly a motivational issue.
