4.120: But if you are going to make a claim, "I think this is true, I think this is reasonable, I think this is a probability," and so forth, you can't immediately say, "This is my claim. Now, you disprove this claim." That would be to shift the burden of evidence to the other person. If you are the one who's making the claim, you start with the burden of putting some evidence behind that claim. Shifting the burden is almost always illegitimate. Particularly, it's illegitimate if you are allowed to just put these things out there, shift the burden to the other person, and then put something else out there that shifts the burden to that person, because you're never going to get anywhere.
4.121: Let me give you an example of that. I will pick on this gentleman here for a moment. Suppose there was some terrible crime that happened last night, and I'm a police detective, and I don't have any evidence, right, one way or the other, and you just happen to be the first person I come across, and I say, "Prove to me that you didn't commit that terrible crime last night." Yeah, exactly. And you're saying, right, your immediate reaction. "What? What terrible? Oh, OK, there was a terrible crime. Well, it wasn't me."
4.122: OK. So personal testimony. Says, "Well, I don't know you. I can't trust you. Prove to me that you are a reliable person and you're not lying." How would you prove that you're not telling a lie? So then you've got another burden, and you have to start to think, right, and so forth. "How could I tell him?" He said, "Oh, well, wait a minute. I just flew back from Switzerland last night when the crime was occurring."
4.123: So you whip out your passport, and there you've got the Zurich stamp on your passport from last night and your Swissair flight ticket and so forth. And so you say, "Aha, see, I can prove that I didn't commit that crime because I've got these other kinds of evidence. I've got a passport with a stamp. The dates are all right," and so forth. I say, "OK, well, that's fine." Now I'm a clever detective. I say, "Well, prove to me that your passport is not a forged passport, that you didn't pay someone a lot of money to make this fake passport so that you could be secretly committing this other crime as well."
4.124: What's going on here is, and I can play this game all day, and maybe you're pretty smart and clever, you can play the game for a pretty long period of time, but you're never going to be able to prove that you did not commit the crime, if that's the game that we are playing. I'm consistently asking you to prove a negative. Prove that you didn't commit the crime, prove that you didn't lie, prove that you didn't have this passport for it. Prove that you didn't run. So that constant negative language is always a clue that something is going on.
4.125: Instead, we say the proper thing is, if I'm going to make an accusation of him in particular, I need to have some glimmer of evidence that ties you, and I can start with that, and then on the basis of that, build a further piece of evidence. That is the burden of proof principle and the appeal to ignorance. Immediately following the burden of proof and the distinction between positive claims and nonexistence claims, and what we then more formally call the appeal to ignorance, is a long, long history. I want to indicate some philosophical issues behind that, ones that have important implications for law and for religion. It's one that has gone deep in human history.
4.126: In Roman jurisprudence for the first time, there was this burden of proof principle, and the claim there was, the necessity of proof always lies with the person who lays charges. You want to sue someone in a civil court, if you're the plaintiff, you have an obligation to present the evidence behind your suit. It's not that the person has an obligation to disprove the charges that are just thrown out against them. In a criminal case, the police and the entire court system have an initial obligation to come up with the evidence.
4.127: So we say, if you are functioning as a police officer, as I was in the earlier example, I have to have some probable cause. That is to say, I have to have some evidence that the cause involved this particular person, and it's probable. It doesn't have to be certain at this point or even particularly compelling, but I have to have something before I can start interacting with the citizenry and subjecting them to further investigations.
4.128: If I, as a police officer, gather a significant amount of evidence, and I take it to the prosecuting attorney, and the prosecuting attorney agrees this is worth taking to court, the person is arrested, we bring the person into a court, we are going to have a defense. We are going to have a prosecution. They both will have a chance of making their case. But the making of their case, the obligation of making the case, is asymmetrical. The burden of proof lies with the prosecution. If the prosecution fails to prove it, the defense does not necessarily have to do anything. If, just on the face of it, the prosecution fails to make the proof, then we are going to consider the person not guilty and let the person go.
4.129: Another way of formulating this, tightly tied into the principle of the burden of proof, is the presumption of innocence. When you enter into civil society, the presumption is you are an innocent person; you are free to go about your business, and police officers can only interfere with you if they have some grounds to think that you are no longer an innocent person. In a courtroom, even though the person has been arrested, the prosecution thinks they've got a case. In the eyes of the court, that person is still innocent until he or she is proven by the prosecution to be guilty.
4.130: We don't want the prosecution to be playing the same kinds of games of shifting the burden of proof over to the defense. I'm the prosecutor. I don't have any evidence. I don't have any logical arguments. You, defense attorney, prove that your client is not guilty of the particular client. That's an illegitimate move. Always, it will be objected to and so forth.
4.131: Now, there is a purely logical reason for this; that is that distinction between existence claims and nonexistence claims. If the person is guilty, that is to say the person did something, something exists in reality, there will be causal interactions and we can get the evidence for that. That's why, logically, we put the burden of proof on the prosecution. If it didn't happen, it's a nonexistent thing. There's no non-evidence that the defense can come up with to bring in. You can't bring nothing into the court and say, "Here, look at the nothing." Because the nothing doesn't do anything for you, it's a completely empty nest.
4.132: But there is another philosophical issue at work. It's one that's often contested, even to this day in some legal jurisdictions, because not all legal jurisdictions around the world now, or certainly historically, have had a presumption of innocence or had a burden of proof principle. In some cases, it has been the opposite, and that was for philosophical reasons. There would be the presumption of guilt. We assume that you are a bad person, and you have to show in some way that you're on the up and up, and then we will perhaps let you go about your business. Then even more formally, when we bring you into a court of law, we will require you to show that you are innocent.
4.133: Now, sometimes this stems from a philosophically very different view of human nature. If, for example, you think human beings are born bad, awful, terrible, we're all little monsters or whatever, that's the default understanding of human condition. Sometimes we might put this in strong religious language and say that everybody is born in sin, in original sin, and we expect that the badness and the wickedness of human beings is going to dominate their thinking and dominate their actions.
4.134: If that's your understanding of what it is to be a human being, then human beings are guilty from the get-go, and the innocent or good behavior is something that's going to be exceptional and rather rare. Then you're more likely, in a judicial system, to say, "Well, why should we presume that this person is innocent? Chances are very good from the get-go, what we know about human nature, that this person is guilty."
4.135: So you're going to much significantly lower the burdens of proof on the prosecution, make it a lot easier for the police to arrest and bring people and charge them. Your standards of proof from the prosecution will be a lot lower, and you will correspondingly elevate the amount of work that the defense has to do to try to show that they were not guilty in this particular case. So this philosophical issue about whether we think people are born basically good, whether we think they are born basically bad, or whether we think they are born neutral, tabula rasa, morally, and might become good or bad, has important implications for legal procedure.
4.136: It's also interesting, if you look at some of the methods that were considered legitimate for hundreds and hundreds of years in Western jurisprudential circles until, in the early modern world, they were gotten rid of, you take, for example, trials by ordeal. Suppose, I don't know, there's something that has happened in the village, and I'll pick on that guy this time. I think that he is the bad guy, so I will bring him up to the court of law. "Did you do this bad thing?" Of course, he's going to say, "No, I did not do that bad thing." But we all know that everybody's a liar because they're all wicked, so he's probably lying.
4.137: But what's my evidence that he did that thing? I don't necessarily have it, but we can figure it out by asking him to undergo a certain ordeal, and you will be willing to undergo this ordeal to try to prove your innocence. So here's the ordeal. We'll pretend that this is an iron bar. We'll take this iron bar and heat it up until it is red-hot. Red-hot means that it will ordinarily burn and damage terribly any human skin that it comes in contact with.
4.138: We will ask him to put his hand out. This will be laid in his hand, and he will voluntarily —so we're asking him to initiate something, to engage in some action here—clasp it and hold it for a certain amount of time, and then unclasp it. Then we will have the evidence of whether he is innocent or guilty. Now, how is this supposed to work?
4.139: Well, the evidence here is going to be based on a certain religious presupposition. If he is an innocent person, if he's not a guilty person, that's kind of unusual, for someone to be innocent, in fact. But God protects the innocent. Does he not? It might be an unusual circumstance that this guy is in fact innocent, but if God really is protecting the innocent, then God will protect him in this particular case. If we, after this certain amount of time, have him release it, and his hand is fine, then he has proved his innocence.
4.140: But of course, if not, he has failed to prove his innocence, and the judicial system takes him away, considers him guilty, and he is gone. So that is the exact opposite, partly driven by different commitments to logic and burden of proof principles, partly driven by understandings about metaphysics and how the world works and our understanding of human nature.
4.141: One more to take with you. If we take that jurisprudential example of this, you can think about this one more on your own time. Burden of proof principles in discussions of religion. Logicians will argue that, obviously, if we're going to believe in the existence of God, we have evidence, we have arguments and so forth, so we pay attention carefully to evaluating the arguments for the existence of God. And the open question is, do I think the arguments work? In which case I believe. If I don't think the arguments work, then I disbelieve until better arguments or better evidence comes along.
4.142: All of that is perfectly legitimate from the perspective of logic. But the logicians will insist that certain tactics that are sometimes used involve shifting the burden of proof inappropriately. So if we want to talk about the existence of God, well, we are making an existence claim. What this then means is, when you start to see the words flying fast and furiously and the phrases are complicated and things are moving along fairly quickly, if you can take some time, slow the process down, and do some quick checks, then that will save you some time.
5.71: Now, I'm going to turn to the Venn diagram method, the graphical method. I like that one the best for the initial stages of learning logic and as you practice more and more becoming very good, because as we know, logic is very abstract. In many cases, you're dealing with abstract issues; or if you are learning them for the first time and reasoning about them, they seem complex and abstract to you, the Venn diagrams are great because they are graphics and trying to capture information in pictorial form helps us learn. It brings things down to Earth, so to speak, in a way that's very useful.
5.72: There are some other methods that have been useful. It is possible to just learn four rules for all good arguments, or at least for all good categorical syllogisms, and you can memorize those rules and apply those. That's fun. Sometimes the rule method is useful as well, but I prefer the Venn diagrams for the visual.
5.73: One thing is, this here violates one of the rules for categorical syllogism, that is to say, the middle term. The middle term is the term that appears both, in both premises. So P is the middle term here. The middle term here is also P. The claim is that, in all valid arguments, the middle term has to appear once as subject and once as predicate, so anytime you see it both right appearing. So one of the rules is, don't have the middle term be in the predicate position both times.
5.74: Another rule is, anytime you have a negative premise, whether it's a none are, or a some are not, then your conclusion has to be negative. If you learn that rule and you look at an argument and it's got a negative premise, one of them is negative and the conclusion is positive, that's going to be an invalid argument, and so on and so forth.
5.75: But let's turn to Venn diagrams. How do we translate the abstract propositional information in the syllogism to a graphical form? We started to play around with that a little bit earlier to set the stage. The first thing that we always want to do is, we look at the argument, or if we're just starting with propositions, and see how many categories are we dealing with, and we will draw a circle to represent each category.
5.76: Initially, abstractly, we don't know if the things in that category overlap or they don't, so we'll leave open both of those possibilities. We'll draw this circle and this circle with some overlap, but also some areas where there's not overlap, and then we'll carry on. There is a way to do one more circle that I know of, in more advanced categorical syllogisms. If you have three premises and then a conclusion, there still is a way graphically to represent it. It gets more difficult after that, just because we have a two- dimensional space and we're trying to capture multiple dimensions. We will stick with the three-dimensional ones right now or the three-category arguments as well.
5.77: In this case, what we would do is, say, take number one. Samantha is here. She's her own category. Here are all of the things that are lean, and here are all of the things that are elegant. You know that, according to this proposition, that we're trying to say that Samantha is both of these things. We want to indicate somehow that, on the diagram, this is where Samantha lives, or this is where Samantha hangs out, so to speak.
5.78: What we could do, and one of the symbols is, is if we're talking about one thing, it's just put an X. The language is going to be that X means that there is something there. To indicate that there is something right there, we could put an X. But this something is a little bit generic. What we typically do then is say is, any time we're dealing with the whole of a category or something that represents the whole category, we're going to use shading. I'll just call that shading. That means nothing is there.
5.79: These will be our two graphical conventions. There's either something there or there isn't something there. Those are the only two options. We have something that indicates the one, something that indicates the other. In this case, what we know about Samantha is that she is both lean and elegant. It's not possible for Samantha to here. There's nothing there, we would say, because that would be Samantha, not lean and not elegant.
5.80: We could consider this. We'd say it was not there either, because that is, would be Samantha, elegant but not lean. We know there is nothing there. Nothing there. Then what about this category here? Well, that would be Samantha being lean but not elegant, but we are told that she is elegant, so we know there is nothing there either. That's been ruled out as a possibility. If we know that Samantha is a real person and not just a made-up one, she would say that's where she is. Samantha is there.
5.81: Now, try the one with John. Things that are funny, things that are sophisticated. What is the relationship asserted by this particular proposition? Well, we know, rough and readily, we want to have John somewhere also in the same as the F circle, but not in the S circle, because the assertion is that he's not sophisticated. All right, so we can't say that John is here. This would be John in the sophisticated circle. This would also be John in the sophisticated circle. We want to say, I want to rule that out. There's nothing there.
5.82: We've got sophisticated things. We got John over here. No overlap between the two. But we do want to say that John is also in the funny things circle. John is not over here. He's an unfunny John. We said that's not the case. There's nothing over here. That means, if John is a real guy, this is the material implication point. He's a material being who actually exists. We'll say this is where that something is, the John stance.
5.83: So Samantha is lean and elegant. John is funny but not sophisticated. The diagrams are similar but importantly different. This carries graphical information that is different from the graphical information of this one here. Someone is a dirty, stinking liar. OK, boy, the language is getting strong here. Dirty, stinking, liar. Now, in this case, I'm speaking vaguely, someone. I don't have John, Samantha's concrete. It's just something, something or other.
5.84: I want to say that it's close to the something that's there. Someone, something, something. We've got vaguer information. But I want to seem to have strong enough information to rule out a whole lot of others. How would we say that there is something that is in the D circle, in the S circle, and in the L circle? Well, the only possibility is to say that it's in there. There's something in there. Maybe you walk into a room, you haven't identified any of the people yet, but you know something's going on really bad.
5.85: All right, all humans are rational and capable of self-agency. All right, this is the one that we did the circles for. Now, let's do the diagramming of the information for it. All humans are capable of rationality. Let's take that part. Well, this here would be a human being that is not capable of rationality. It would be outside of the R circle. Same here, so we're going to cross this out. Nothing here. That's empty.
5.86: And capable of self-agency. Well, these would be humans that we think are not capable of self-agency. We know there's nothing there, either. That gets crossed up. That then is to say, all of the humans have to be in here. If we're just speaking abstractly, maybe we're talking about things we don't really sure that humans exist or just hypothetically, we would not put an X there. That's the material implication. If we stay in the hypothetical mode, we won't make that assumption.
5.87: If we're talking in a context where we know we're talking about real entities, then I would put an X here. If I change this argument, though, to unicorns, suppose, all unicorns are rational and capable of—I've just made up this fictional creature. Well, we would not use material implication in that case for reasons that, when we enter into a fictional space, the metaphysical assumptions are different. We don't want to make those assumptions when we're doing the logic, so we would just leave it with this abstract characterization. As I said, that's an interesting issue, but a little to the side for us right now.
5.88: Now, this, again, something worth practicing. Take individual propositions and diagram them until one becomes fluid with putting the X's where they need to go. Now for the big payoff, once we are comfortable with taking individual categorical propositions and diagramming them, we can then take entire arguments. In this case, we have two propositions and a conclusion. We're going to then say we have three categories, so we can use those same three circles and start down that exercise.
5.89: At the end of engaging in that exercise, we will be able to step back, look at the diagram, and it will tell us whether this is a valid argument or an invalid argument. The thing to be keeping in mind will be the formulation we put out several times before. In a valid argument, if the premises are true, the conclusion has to be true. Or if the premises are taken for granted, the conclusion follows logically.
5.90: What we'll be looking for is, once we take the information from the premises, if it already just follows necessarily that the conclusion is true, then when we diagram the information in the premises, that is to say, we capture visually the abstract information of the premises, we will find that the conclusion is already diagrammed for us. The conclusion in that sense is built into the information already given in the premises.
5.91: Or one way of putting it, another way of putting it, is to say that the conclusion is implicit in the argument's premises, and the purpose of the argument is to make explicit what's already implicit in the premises, or you've got enough information to make that move safely. Let's, with that preamble, do the same thing here.
5.92: So we have humans, mammals, and mortals. So we'll call those the humans. These will be all of the mammals. These will be all of the mortals. All humans are mammals. Well, what's that to say? This would be a human that's not a mammal, so there's nothing there. This would be a human that's not a mammal. It can't be anything there, so we can safely cross this out. Those two possible zones, given this information, must be empty zones.
5.93: All mammals are mortal. So now we look at the mammals and the mortals. We know, well, this would be a mammal that's not mortal. There can't be anything there. This would be a mammal that is not mortal. There can't be anything there either. We can cross those zones out. Those are empty zones. That's the information we get from this second premise. Now we stop, you diagram the premises and no more. We look and we ask, have we already diagrammed the conclusion?
5.94: Now, if we were going to diagram the conclusion, we're not going to, but we would say, all humans are mortal. We would say something like, well, this would be a human that's immortal, and that doesn't exist. This would be a human that's immortal, and that doesn't exist. But we already know that that doesn't possible. It's already been diagrammed for us in the information that we got from the two premises. In this case, our conclusion is already diagrammed. It's represented graphically, based on this abstract information.
5.95: We've not made stuff up. We've not gone beyond the available evidence. We have reasoned well. This now is a valid argument. Having done this exercise, do it with several examples until it becomes obvious. You say, "Oh, yeah, that's great." Then just memorize that one. This always is a good pattern of reasoning.
5.96: By contrast, to show how the diagram will prove to you that something does not follow, that it's an invalid argument, let's use our whipping boy here. This is the one we've used several times. Intuitively or just looking at it, something seems wrong about it, but let's show graphically why this is going to be so. All men here. I guess I need M-E, M-O for all of the mortals, and pigs. We'll put those guys down there. Three categories, three circles, each one labeled.
5.97: We say, all men are mortal. Well, we've done that one before. So this would be a man that isn't mortal, outside the middle space, so there's nothing there. This would be, something that is a man, but also outside the mortal category, so there can't be anything there. Almost typically, the universal positive proposition, you're crossing out those two zones. All the men have to be over here. That's what we know.
5.98: Second piece of information, though, that we're given in the argument, is that all of the pigs are mortal, too. This would be a pig that is not mortal. There's nothing there. That's empty. This also would be something that's a pig. It's in the P circle and not mortal, but it's already crossed out. We just leave that one alone. We've diagrammed this one, we've diagrammed this one. We stop. If the argument is valid, our conclusion is diagrammed for us. If it's not diagrammed, then that would mean we would need more information in the diagram in order to capture the information of the premise.
5.99: If it's not diagrammed, that means it's an invalid argument. We say, all men are pigs. That's the asserted conclusion. We look at the diagram. Well, it could be, as far as we know; there are some men in this category here, but it also could be that there are some men in this category. This is still possible. These are men who are not pigs. That then is to say, this argument is asserting that there's nothing there, that all the men have to be down there. But we don't know that yet, given this information.
5.100: This argument goes beyond the information in the premises. The conclusion does not necessarily follow. This is now an invalid argument. Then the claim is, there's 256 of them. You can go through, and what you will find is, 24 of them work or 16 of them work, depending on the material implication issue. The other ones are going to be invalid, invalid, invalid. It's a useful exercise to do a lot of those because then you start to recognize certain patterns, and things crop up on a regular basis, as well as just becoming really good at doing Venn diagram quite quickly.
5.101: But even so, don't feel obligated to do all of that. Do enough of these to make sure that the Venn diagram works for you and seems a reliable method. Then when necessary, dealing with something complicated or interesting or something you want to double- check, do the diagram for your own reassurance.
5.102: One of the great controversies in the philosophy of the logic has been over the status of logical principles. We develop Venn diagrams, we develop rules, we make distinctions between valid and invalid. In many cases, it gets very abstract very quickly, and logic shades into formal mathematics very quickly. One philosophical tradition has instituted a kind of divide between formal methods of thinking that exist only in the mind and applications in the actual world. For various philosophical reasons, the claim ends up being that these formal abstract principles are just that; they are just empty formal definitions.
5.103: Now, one form of this came to be popular in the early 20th century, where it came out of a philosophy of language that said language is made up of terms that we have defined, but we can define terms any way that we want. Grammar is a matter of a whole bunch of rules, but we can make up, if we want, all kinds of grammatical rules, whatever we want, including grammar and rules for chess and all sorts of games, including logic and mathematics. We start to see them just as games based on rules that we made up.
5.104: But they're not real. They are empty. They are just, we have decided to define terms a certain way and make combinations of symbols in certain ways. They're not actually saying anything about the way the world works. The early Wittgenstein is very close to this position and a work that he called Tractatus: Logico-Philosophicus. There's an arresting quotation. Of course, there's a broader context for all of this. But the point for our purpose is to say that all the propositions of logic say the same thing— that is, nothing.
5.105: So logic is ultimately empty. It's just a formal game that we play. It doesn't tell us anything about the world, the structure of the world, the causal nature of reality, and so on. It is a subjective game. Now, it might be a game that we really like to play. And given my constitution, I might like the idea of defining rules a certain way, and then making sure I can stay within the bounds of those rules and see how far I can go with those rules. But I'm not really saying anything about reality if I'm just using abstract S's and P's and all's and this, that; it's just words and so on.
5.106: Now, another anti-logic position, even more extreme, has been to say, yes, we do have logical principles and so forth, but they also are in subjective origin, not so much because we've decided to define terms, even define terms carefully or rules of grammar, but they have a different kind of subjective source. And Friedrich Nietzsche is one of the big names behind this tradition here. Let me read this quotation from his late work, The Will to Power.
5.107: "Our subjective compulsion to believe in logic indicates merely that long before we became conscious of logic itself, we did nothing but introduce its postulates into events. Now we find them in events we can no longer help. The world seems logical to us because we have already made it logical." The idea is, the world is what it is. For all we know, it could be chaos, then we are just complete randomness and so forth. But something subjective in us doesn't like that. So what we do, even before we start to think about it, is we start to impose structure, impose order, impose logic on the world.
5.108: That, according to his mentor, largely his mentor Schopenhauer, makes us feel more comfortable, which is a subjective emotional state. Nietzsche is not quite so strong in that way, but nonetheless, what we are doing is imposing what we want onto the world. If we happen to want the world to be logical and orderly, then we will construct, even without realizing that we are doing it, a basically logical and orderly way of looking at it. Then the logicians come along and say, "Oh, we will just take that subjective structuring and run with it and be very silly." But really, it says more about us than it does about reality itself.
5.109: Then the third position here is represented by H. W. B. Joseph, early 20th century, in the Aristotelian tradition of logic—that logic is formal, but it's not only formal; that the forms of logic are abstractions on patterns in reality; that we should have a compulsion to be logical, but it's not something that just happens automatically. We know it's possible for us to have a compulsion not to be logical, and we have to choose the right choice, which is to be logical because we want our subject to match objects as they are out there.
5.110: In his formulation, "Unless the primary laws of thought," those are the logical principles, "were laws of things, our thought would be doomed by its very nature to misapprehend the nature of things." And he goes on to argue that, yes, we do have laws of thought, but they're not just arbitrary semantic definitions that we came up with. It's not just emotionalists tidying things up because we want things to be tidied up. Our laws of thought are reflective or mirroring or abstractions on, or drawn in some way from, the structure of reality.
5.111: Things are what they are. They move in various ways and in various abstract ways. That's where we get our logic from. Now, this is just to introduce another deep debate in the philosophy of logic, particularly as we get more and more abstract, as we've seen in this lecture. Where you stand on this issue becomes fundamentally important.
5.112: Is there a way to use logic to deal with the appeal to majority, for instance?
5.113: Yes, or in particular, the appeal to majority? Or, yes. OK. I think the best way is to start with oneself because we all have our individual minds, but we all are also social beings. We typically, to the extent we are social and we like other people, we want to be in agreement with other people. If we are benevolent, we typically like to give people the benefit of the doubt initially. So the first thing would be to recognize that that's all fine and normal and healthy.
5.114: The point would be just to make sure that, when you are thinking about something that matters to you and you know your own mind, make sure you're not letting those social desires influence your thinking. Sometimes that requires just to self-identify. "Oh, I'm dealing with this issue. I really want to say yes, but I'm not sure." Make it your own habit. Then how you do that with other people, I think it depends on how close the relationship is with you, how much time you are spending with someone.
5.115: But if you are, say, the mother, then you're going to spend a lot of time with people just modeling that in your behavior. You want to get along with your kids, you your kids to agree with you, but show them that you're being reasonable in doing so, that you're not just going to agree with them automatically, but you know how to raise gentle criticisms and provide the counter-evidence, and also that you don't expect them to do the same with respect to you and your partner. If you outnumber them, it's going to be, we want you to think for this and come to agreement, but by your own light. So I think it has to be a slow, carefully built-up set of habits.
5.116: If we go back to fallacies, I was thinking about the hot debates that are happening today and, given the abortion debate, so pro-choice or pro-life, the usual argument is, when life begins, that's usually the thing. But nowadays, there's an argument about the bodily autonomy, as far as to say that women should have pro-choice. So is that a logical fallacy, because it's not really centering on the whether or not it's a life, or is it a logical argument?
5.117: Right. Now, that's a good complex set of issues. So one way, and the abortion issue, like all controversial issues, is rife with logical fallacies all over the place. To take the appeal to emotion, for example, people on the pro-life will say, abortion is the murder of tiny, defenseless human beings. Just put that out there really strongly. Tiny, defenseless, and then human beings, and murder—so it's all strong language. And if all you have is that, then that is appeal to emotion.
5.118: On the other side, if the pro-life people will say, well, abortion is just the surgical removal of an unwanted clump of cells, or something like that, so they're going out of their way in that language to dehumanize whatever potential status the fetus has. Both of those are signs that you're dealing with people who are not interested in actually looking at the issue logically and see what the facts on the ground are.
5.119: The second part of your question, I think, is not fallacious because I think you're right to say, part of the abortion argument does involve the status of the fetus. So we do need to spend a certain amount of time looking at embryology and fetal development and figuring out what the significant milestones are, what traits are present, which ones are activated at what point. And all of that has to feed into our decision about what is the status of the fetus, at what point does it become human person rights-bearing.
5.120: And all of those concepts are slightly different. It's one thing to say something has a personality, to say that it's a human personality. Dogs have personalities. So the person language, but human language. Then to be a rights-bearing being is another thing in there. What is the status of the fetus requires, I think, a lot of moral investigation and a lot of biological investigation.
5.121: But the other side of the argument, or the other part of the argument, it's not a side of the argument, is to say that the fetus is in the woman's body, and the woman is a human being. She is a person. She is a rights-bearing being. So what is her status? And then again, we have to do the same sorts of things—attend to her biology, attend to her moral significance. Then once we've got it worked out, the right solution is going to talk about the relationship between those two in the best resolution.
5.122: I don't think it's an unfair thing for one person to say, "Well, look, the fetus has a certain status." They may say a good argument for why the fetus has that status. For the other side to come back immediately and say, "Yes, but the woman also has certain status and rights as well." That's just to put two parts of the overall picture on the table for discussion, and that seems perfectly legitimate to me.
5.123: On the theme of fallacies, what are some factors that make someone more susceptible to fallacies?
5.124: Yes, that's a good question. There are dozens of other commonly committed fallacies. Sometimes, logicians will just use the label non-sequitur, borrowing from the Latin. Just because there's so many of them, you don't want to name all of them. But in many cases, just the conclusion doesn't follow from the premises. It's not even sequenced, it's a non-sequitur.
5.125: So your question, though, is in part a psychological question, I think. So we know that there are people who don't commit fallacies very much. They're clean in their thinking. Other people are, yeah, it's like, whoa. Yeah, so what's going on there? And maybe we don't want to know too much of what's going on in the analysis. But I would say, probably the two biggest ones are laziness. That seems to be common to many of the fallacies, because what the fallacies almost always enable you to do is, there's some complicated or important issue, is just not to have to deal with it, not to have to do the work, and so forth.
5.126: If you can just throw a fallacy out there, it sounds like you've said your two cents worth, you've made an argument, but it's almost like a get-out-of-jail-free card from having to do thinking. In that case, the difference would be between people who are committed to doing work, if it needs to be done, and people who are just lazy.
5.127: I think another bigger one, if I were just to mention another one, is that probably subjectivism is—it could be an own standalone fallacy, but subjectivism often will utilize the other fallacies in self-defense as rhetorical strategy. I want to believe what it is that I want to believe, and someone's giving me a hard time. They're presenting those pesky facts and counterarguments and criticisms and so forth. I don't want to deal with it, because I don't want seriously to consider the possibility that I'm wrong and I need to rethink certain important things in my view.
5.128: Depending on the kind of argument that you are dealing with or the kind of data that you are dealing with, it might be useful as a subjectivist just then to say, "Well, I don't like this person's race." So use an ad hominem to get rid of that person. Or I will be dealing with someone who seems kind of sophisticated and is used to multi-step arguments, so I will argue in a circle and maybe it will track, so you're begging the question in that case.
5.129: If it's someone who is under my power, who's raising difficult questions, I can threaten that kid. And that's the use of appeal to force. So maybe what's really going on is the subjectivism, but the person just has all the fallacies, so to speak, as tools in the toolkit, to be used depending on the circumstance. I think that's the best short answer we can come up with.
5.130: A question about, and I'm going to mispronounce his name, Wittgenstein.
5.132: Wittgenstein, Nietzsche, and Joseph. It seems their relationship to logic is literally the relationship to truth, as in subjective. There is an objective truth, and no, it's all subjective. I mean, Nietzsche practically said that logic is like unconscious bias, that we manifest belief.
5.133: Exactly. Nietzsche is a Kantian, in that respect. We just have these—but a Kantian with a twist. We have these inbuilt structures, is the Kantian idea. Whatever reality is, we have no idea what that is. All we can do is think that our subconscious minds or our unconscious minds structure the data a certain way, and so it's a working-out of subjectivity.
5.134: Nietzsche is a couple of generations later, and he argues that these subjective structures are not constant and universal. They're more relative and subject to change, and so it might be that there are different logics or different subjectivities at work. But you're exactly right. This is the fundamental issue of objectivity versus subjectivity. What sets the terms? The small-O objectivists, Aristotle on down to H. W. B. Joseph in the 20th century, want to say, what's out there objectively in reality sets the terms, and the subject initially has to take its marching orders from reality.
5.135: It might be that we have distinctive methods because of our mental structure about how we process that data. We might devise tools, but nonetheless, those methods that we use have to prove themselves as being capable of keeping us connected objectively to reality. The subjectivists are almost always skeptical; or skeptics, initially, what they find is, they think for various reasons that we can't maintain a connection between our minds and reality. There's a breakdown at some point. Our subjective side is disconnected from reality, and it just takes on a life of its own, and we don't talk about reality at all.
5.136: Now, the concept of truth that you mentioned right along the way, in my conceptual scheme, that is a correlative concept with the concept of fact. All of human cognition is our minds in relationship with reality. It's a relationship. If the relation is a positive relationship, then we say things like, it's an objective relationship. But then we have terms to designate the two sides of the relationship. What's the nature of reality? There we're talking about facts.
5.137: Then we want to get those facts inside our minds in some sense, but then we form concepts and propositions. When we use truth language, we're talking about what's going on on the subject side. So we say, you take these initial data, we're trying to figure out what the facts of the world are, and the result is, we want to have in the mind true propositions about that.
5.138: And so, if we say it's a fact, then in that context, we're emphasizing the object side of the relationship. If we're using the word true, we're emphasizing and stressing the subject side of the relationship. Already, we use, I think, eight or more important cognitive concepts, and all that needs to get sorted out. Very good question, too. Lecture 6: Deduction: Hypothetical & Disjunctive Syllogisms At a glance — Deduction: hypothetical and disjunctive syllogisms.
6.1: All right, let's turn to hypothetical syllogisms. Categorical syllogisms, as we have seen, have all been taking two categories, and it gets complicated because, with two categories, we can say a lot of different things about them. There are 256 possibilities, and we have Venn diagrams and rule methods to sort out the valid from the invalid.
6.2: Hypothetical arguments are much simpler because there's only six possible hypothetical forms. Three of them are valid and three are not valid. We can just talk through them, identify the forms, use a couple of examples. These ones are susceptible to memory. These are ones that you should make a commitment to memorizing the patterns and making it automatic, so that you recognize them, valid/invalid. The red flags go up automatically when they need to do so.
6.3: Now, a hypothetical proposition or a sentence is one that is governed by the if-then structure and connects with our ordinary use of hypothesis. I consider this as a possibility, and if this is possible, then we draw out some implications. Now, as with all other kinds of propositions, English is very rich and varied in how it makes its hypothetical statements. The first thing to do is to get comfortable with recognizing hypothetical statements when you see them.
6.4: One thing is to just, the if-then structure, if-then, start to circle it if you're dealing with something in print and you're comfortable with putting print a circle to it or write it out. But pay attention to the if-then structure. Sometimes people don't say, "If this is true, then this other thing is true." They will say, "This other thing is true, if this other thing is true." So sometimes you will get the "then" part first, and then the "if" part first.
6.5: Just a little piece of language, terminology. The part between the if and the then, we call it the antecedent. The part after the then, we call it the consequent. We'll come back to that because, in naming the arguments, we use this antecedent and consequent language. 6.85: I want to contrast to that with one of his contemporaries. Lecture 7: Propositional Logic At a glance — Propositional (modern symbolic) logic.
7.1: This session, we're going to turn to modern symbolic logic. It's called modern because, while we've been doing logic for well over two millennia, developing very sophisticated methods for handling all kinds of logical arguments and circumstances, early modern logicians started to make connections between logic and mathematics in a more rigorous way, and some of the developments then, over the course of the modern era, including a generalization on what had been accomplished in logic up to that time, and an extension, set the stage for, in the 20th century, programming languages, the development of computers, and all of those amazing technologies.
7.2: There is a continuity at the same time and extension. To see that, let's start with some of the things that we know so far. On the board here, I have some hypothetical arguments and a disjunctive argument. These are four patterns of reasoning, common, and they're all valid patterns of reasoning. Having checked that out for ourselves, practiced it and so forth, we're in a position to automate it. Anytime we want to combine information in any of these patterns, we are comfortable to go ahead and do so.
7.3: So if we have P, then Q, it's a hypothetical statement, and we find out that we have P, then we can infer we must have Q. Now, traditionally, we would call that affirming the antecedent in English, what the second sentence or proposition here is doing, and then we draw the consequent as the conclusion. We call that antecedent. Henceforth, though, I want to start calling this argument modus ponens, or just MP for short, modus ponens.
7.4: The language then will be more uniform with some of the other developments in logical, modern symbolic logic, rather. That's affirming the antecedent or modus ponens, abbreviated with MP. Perfectly good. This one, we know we have our hypothetical statement here. The second sentence is denying or negating the consequent. We call it denying the consequent, and that as a matter of the conclusion means we can logically deny the antecedent. This one we call denying the consequent, but henceforth, we are going to call it modus tollens, or abbreviating it rather MT.
7.5: This one is the pure hypothetical form. All of the proposition constituent elements are hypotheticals. Informally, it's the chain argument. P is linked to Q, Q is linked to R, so we can link P to R, which is what we do in the conclusion. There can be as many links in the chain, as long as the pattern is consistent. This one is a pure hypothetical argument or chain argument. We are going to call it the hypothetical syllogism, henceforth, abbreviating just HS. Perfectly valid.
7.6: Then the fourth form I have here is the disjunctive form, either P or Q. We have two alternatives or two disjuncts. Second proposition denies or negates one of the disjuncts. It can be either one, and that means we can affirm that the other disjunct must be the true one. So if it's either P or Q, and we know it's not P, then it must be Q, and that's a legitimate pattern as well. This is called the disjunctive syllogism, and we will just abbreviate it, shockingly, DS.
7.7: Now, much of the reasoning that we do is isolated arguments, where we do a modus ponens, or we do a disjunctive syllogism. But as sophisticated thinkers, we often will engage in extended arguments, and we will typically mix and match the kinds of arguments that we are putting in the extended arguments that we are doing so.
7.8: I have a couple of introductory examples here, moderately complicated, but the kinds of things that we do routinely on a regular basis, and we want to be able to capture that in the logic. We also want to see if we can start to axiomatize, symbolize, make everything ruthlessly simple and clear with an idea, perhaps, to programming machines, computers, and making logic and mathematics a more tightly integrated set of disciplines. Here's a family vacation planning example of reasoning.
7.9: We should visit either Toronto or Rochester this trip. If we go to Toronto, then we won't see Sylvia, but we have to see either Sylvia or Quincy this trip. I just found out that Quincy isn't available, so Rochester, it is. Now, in a sense, that makes perfectly good sense. We would do this in our heads; we would do it in conversation. And we would then, OK, I guess we're off to Rochester for our family vacation, all of these factors taken into account.
7.10: If we start to do the logical techniques that we have developed so far, we don't see any real premise indicators, but we do see one conclusion indicator. So all of this information must be the premises that support this conclusion, the decision that we are going to go to Rochester on this family trip. When we start to look at the premises, we see this one is an either-or. So at some point, we then know we've done a disjunctive syllogism or disjunctive argument, or we're doing that.
7.11: We have here an if-then, which indicates that we are using hypothetical reasoning at some point. It might be pure, it might be mixed with a straightforward declaration sentence or not. We have some negations, not, not, and so on. We have a combination of either-ors, this and that, not this, and if this, then that. We put it all together, more or less naturally in our reasoning then, to support this final declarative sentence. It makes sense if you think about it, and if you're in the zone, you do all this sort of thing regularly on the basis.
7.12: But how do we show that this is good reasoning, or if there's a mistake in the reasoning somewhere, that there is in fact a mistake in the reasoning? Now, suppose we say, look, let's look at these, and this is what, five sentences all together? Suppose we just look at the last two before the conclusion. I just found out that Quincy isn't available. So that then is to say, not Quincy. The third sentence, though, said, it's either Sylvia or Quincy. So if we just extract that, then what we have is either Sylvia or Quincy, and not Quincy.
7.13: What we can then infer is that it must be Sylvia, and that's to do a disjunctive syllogism on the fly. So now we know Sylvia. We've got to see Sylvia this trip. Then suppose we look at this sentence here, the second sentence. If we go to Toronto, then we won't see Sylvia. That's a hypothetical statement. But if we combine that with this new thing we know—we have to see Sylvia—if we go to Toronto, we won't see Sylvia, but we are going to see Sylvia. So therefore, it makes sense to say, we can't go to Toronto.
7.14: And that is this pattern of reasoning here. We've just done modus tollens. So now we know we're not going to Toronto. Now, if we then look at the very first sentence, the very first sentence said, well, it's either Toronto or Rochester. And now, after a couple of steps of reasoning, we have eliminated Toronto as an option. So if it's either Toronto or Rochester, and we know not Toronto, then it must be Rochester. That then is to use this pattern of reasoning, the disjunctive syllogism, again. Then we are in a position to draw our conclusion.
7.15: Now, the point of that then is to say, we have initially five sentences, but more or less on the fly, or if we slow down and notice what we are doing, we are adding three more steps of the inference. We end up with eight propositions altogether, and we're pretty confident that this conclusion follows. But can we show that systematically, that in fact that follows? We can't, and that's what we want to work toward.
7.16: Here's another example, artificial party planning example. Just A, B, C, D, and then F. Just the first letter. This is not a real example. But if Alice comes to the party, then Bob will. We now definitely know, given this information, Fred is not coming.
7.17: This is our conclusion indicator. This is what all of this reasoning is supporting. Again, if we then notice what we have in terms of the logical techniques we've developed so far, we have an if-then, so there's a hypothetical statement. Then we have another if-then statement here. This one's a little different because we've got a semicolon, and often when we use semicolons in our grammar, we're implicating a somewhat tight connection between two things, rather than having them as standalone sentences.
7.18: We have this other "and", this other connection. The idea is, if this, then that, and, keep this in mind very tightly, closely, if this, then that. We have an either-or, so a disjunctive sentence in there. But immediately before this either, we have an "if", so it's like a combined hypothetical disjunctive statement. That's a more sophisticated mental construction. If either of these things happens, then something else is going to happen.
7.19: And we have a negation built in here and another negation down there. We're looking at some of the logical operator concepts. Again, we've got a combination of if-thens and either-ors, and this one seems a little bit more sophisticated. But if we pause again, we try to work it through in our heads, we can say, we're either getting Alice or Carl. Suppose we focus our attention on this one. We don't know which one, say, but we're going to get at least one of them, either Alice or Carl.
7.20: Now, suppose we then say, well, if it's that one, that's the Alice part, then we're going to get Bob. If it's the other one that turns out to be the case, if it's Carl, then we're going to get Darlene. So doesn't it make sense then to say, if we're either going to get Alice or Carl, we know that, then we're also either going to get Bob or Darlene, even though we don't know which one yet? We know something definite, but we're still in hypothetical mode with some options, and that's a little bit harder to hold in your head.
7.21: Now, if we know that we're either going to get Bob or Darlene, but we're not sure which one, maybe both, then we get either of those ones, Fred's not coming. And so the person then says, at this point then, I'd say, well, even though we don't know which one, Alice or Bob, Carl or Darlene, we're still in that uncertainty with respect to all of that, nonetheless, we definitely know Fred, rather, is not coming. It could or should make sense, but can we show that clearly, so that we could say, explain it to a computer, that this is a valid piece of reasoning, however much the complexity is there? The answer is yes. That's what we want to work up to in this session.
7.22: Now, some housekeeping, notation matters. We want to, in symbolic logic, start to, more systematically and ruthlessly, symbolize things. What we want to do is, say we have this argument pattern, and we're going to just abbreviate that and assign names, modus ponens, modus tollens, hypothetical syllogism, disjunctive syllogism. There are other good patterns that we can learn as well, and we're going to work our way up to that as well.
7.23: But we also have some language in here, the if-then and the either-or and the word not. One of the first things we want to do is, partly just for saving ink and saving time, is to symbolize those as well. Our conventions are going to be the following. We'll say any if-then statement. We are going to replace that with a horseshoe. I would take this argument and just say P, sorry, this proposition, P ⊃ Q. So any time you see the horseshoe, it's just that.
7.24: The not, not, the negation, we will use the tilde sign. Very close to the mathematical negation negative sign, but in logic, the convention is mostly that we use the tilde. Soin this one, we would say P ⊃ Q, and then ~ Q, not Q. This one, we have no more operators, so we'll just, so the final symbolized form of that argument would look like that. This argument here, the modus tollens, the inference that's drawn is therefore not P, so we abbreviate that argument that way.
7.25: The either-or, we'll use a hard v symbol. That one has the nice, it's like pointing forks in the road. What we would do with this one is say P v Q. That's the symbolization. We know this not symbolizes with the tilde. It's ~ P. Then we bring down the conclusion, Q. This one would just be P ⊃ Q, Q ⊃ R, so P ⊃ R. We're still using the line as a convention to indicate the divide between the premises and the conclusions.
7.26: I want to add one more connective, as they're calling it. We call these connectives because they take constituent elements and connect them in various ways. That one is the word "and." "But" is another conjunction as well, but we use the word "and" a lot to take elements and combine them. Sometimes we will say, if you have fire, then you must have oxygen. Or we might say, if you have oxygen and a combustible, then you can get fire. That is an if-then statement, but the antecedent has a conjunction in it. You have to have oxygen and something to burn, then you can get the fire.
7.27: We will just use a dot, usually not like a period dot, not like the upper colon part of the colon dot, just kind of in the, in the middle. The idea then is going to be, we can take all of the propositions that we use, and we combine propositions in various ways to draw various sorts of conclusions. We will take the propositions and symbolize them. When we're thinking through all of these things abstractly, we'll use letters P, Q, R, just to symbolize all of the propositions.
7.28: But then the initial claim is that there are only four basic ways to combine propositions. You can speak hypothetically. If you have this one, then you get that. You can speak disjunctively. It's either this or that, or this and that, or we can negate things. Now, that is a claim, I think, for further research and thinking. We do have lots of other words that we use, but most of those end up being one of the four basic combinations in various ways.
7.29: So, "and", for example, is a connection, but we also have the word "but." "But" is a kind of conjunction, but it usually indicates also a negation is coming. It's really conjunction with some warning of negation at work there. Either-or, we have neither-nor, but that is either-or, and you are adding negations to both of them. I might say, if and only if, and there's that word "only" in there, and that's making some really strong claims, if and only if.
7.30: It's more than if this happens, then that happens. If and only if. When we work that one out, it turns out you're saying, if it's, if P, if and only if Q, then what you're saying is, if you have P, then you get Q, and if you have Q, then you get P. It's a combination of a couple of hypotheticals with a connective, and we can work all of that. The idea, though, is spend some time with the English or whatever your language is, and see if the constituent propositions have any other ways of being put together, logically, other than these four.
7.31: If you discover a new one, that's great. We'll find a way to work that into the logic, but we're going to work with this assumption here. We have five things, a basic proposition, P. We might connect the P with a Q. We might do a disjunct P or Q. We might say the P is not true, the P is negated. We might speak hypothetically, if we have P, then Q.
7.32: Now, as ordinary language speakers, we know what all of these things mean, and we use them fluidly. But what we want to try to do is axiomatize. If we're going to axiomatize, take things very basic, strip them down as far as we possibly can, then what we we need to do is define them in an axiomatic way. So all of those issues about concept formation, here we're doing concept formation about logical connectives, how we're going to connect things in various ways. Can we define the connectives rigorously and ruthlessly?
7.33: So this is what we devise what we call truth tables for. Truth tables for the connective. What do we mean when we are using this connective? Under what circumstances will we say that using that connective is being done truly or falsely? Now, one way in which this is axiomatizing is that we start with the claim that, for any given proposition that we are talking about, it is either true or it is false.
7.34: We go all the way back to Aristotle and what was called the law of excluded middle. Every proposition, we might not know if it is true or false, but ultimately, it either is true or it is false. We're going to use the words, the symbol T for truth, and the symbol F for false. Defining those terms, we've got our propositional variables and all of the connectors indicated there.
7.35: Now, in that case, if we know that a proposition is true or false, then I can say P. But we don't know what P is, but we do know that P is either true or false, whatever P turns out to be. When I say P and Q, I don't know what Q is, I don't know what P is. But if I make the assertion P and Q, under what circumstances would that sentence, rather, be true or false? We know there's how many possibilities? Well, it could be that P is true and Q is also true. It could be, though, that P is true and Q is false. It could be that P is false and Q is true, or it could be that they're both false.
7.36: So we have two propositional variables, and each of them has two possible states, true or false. So, there's four possibilities. So the idea of a table then is to say, let's diagram that in a table. So what we will then first do is, I'll start over here, I think, to say, well, let's take P, and let's take Q, and make a table. What do we know about P or Q?
7.37: Well, it could be that this one is true and this one is true. It could be that this one is true, but this one is false. It could be, this one is false and this one is true, or it could be that both of them are false. But since we are speaking abstractly, we've just symbolized and abstracted everything, we don't actually know what the P is and its connection to reality or not.
7.38: What we mean, though, and here we are defining carefully P and Q. Now we're defining that connective "and". If I say P and Q, I'm making a kind of commitment. Under what circumstances am I speaking truly with that compound proposition? Under what circumstances would I be speaking falsely? Well, if it turns out that P is true and Q is true, then saying P and Q is true. So we will put the true here.
7.39: Suppose I'd said, Peter and Quincy are coming to the party, and Peter comes to the party, and Quincy comes to the party. Then what I said was true. Now, suppose, though, I say Peter is coming to the party and Quincy is coming to the party, but Peter comes and Quincy does not come. Then what I said was false. I said both of them are coming, but only one came. So in that circumstance, the "and" statement is false. Both of the conjuncts have to be true for the whole thing to be true.
7.40: And the same thing is going to hold here. If I said Peter and Quincy are coming to the party, Quincy shows up, but Peter doesn't, then what I said was false. So that is false. If I said Peter and Quincy are coming to the party, but neither one of them shows up, then my statement was false. What we are doing, working from basics all the way up, is now we have a definition, a truth table definition, of exactly what we mean when we use the "and" statement and the circumstances under which it is true.
7.41: Now, let's do the same thing for the disjunctive proposition. As I say, well, I've got P, I've got Q. Those are my propositional variables. What I do know is that they could both be true, could be true here, false here, false here, true here, or both of them false. The compound that we are interested in is P or Q. To say P or Q is different from saying P and Q, what's the difference graphically? Well, under what circumstances is this compound statement true? We can stick with the party example.
7.42: If I say, well, either Peter or Quincy is coming to the party, and they both show up, this first situation here, well, what I said was true. Suppose Peter shows up at the party, but Quincy doesn't. What I said was still true. I said either-or, I got at least one, so that's still true. Same thing here. Quincy shows up, Peter doesn't. It was true. But suppose I said, either Peter or Quincy is going to show up at the party, and neither of them shows, then in that case, what I said was false.
7.43: And this comparison now will indicate what makes sense to us in common speaking, that it's a lot harder for an "and" statement to be true than for an either-or statement to be true. You have more wiggle room, so to speak, with the either-or statement, but you're making a stronger claim with an "and" statement. There are fewer circumstances under which it is true.
7.44: OK, let's do the same thing for the negation. This one in a way is simpler. We have P, make our truth table. What do we know about P? Not much. We only know that it's either true or it's false. How do we define negation, not P? Just the opposite. If P is true, then not P is false. And if P is false, then not P is true. OK.
7.45: What about the fourth one? Now we have P and Q, and we are interested in—let me put one more line in here for consistency— the hypothetical statement. P ⊃ Q. Same for possibilities. If P, then Q. We'll help with our English. I suppose we say, if Peter comes to the party, then Quincy will come to the party. I make that statement. And what happens is, Peter comes to the party and Quincy comes to the party. I said, well, if Peter comes, Quincy will come. They both came. So that is true.
7.46: So as I say, if Peter comes to the party, then Quincy will come to the party. Peter comes to the party, but Quincy doesn't show up. Then my hypothetical claim was false. Now, in the assignment of these next two, it's a little bit more complicated, and sometimes it's a little counterintuitive. I'm just going to say that what we have shown, we being logicians collectively, is that the right answer here is to put a T and a T there.
7.47: As long as, in any other circumstance, no matter what, if the antecedent is false, the corresponding consequent is true. We might then say, well, if I said, if Peter comes to the party, then Quincy is going to come to the party, and Peter doesn't show up, but Quincy does, what does that say about my initial statement? The controversy is, you might say, well, that should leave that undefined or unknown. I understand that. Think about that.
7.48: Or suppose neither Peter nor Quincy show up at the party. This should be undefined. Now, this will require one more lecture than we are going to get into today. But what you can show is there are various equivalences. You can show that P ⊃ Q is equivalent to other formulations. When you take those other equivalent formulations and you do the truth table for those ones, this is the array that you get. Right now, take that as a promissory note. You can work on that on your own time or check in your logic textbooks. But this is what we are going to go with.
7.49: Now what we have done is, we have symbolized and essentialized the propositions, P's and Q's, maybe there will be R's. We've taken all of the ways that we can connect pieces of language together. If, then, either-or, and so forth. We've defined exactly what they mean. What can we do next with these things? That's where we want to say, what we did in discussing hypothetical syllogisms and disjunctive syllogisms before, where we went in a somewhat intuitive sense—this makes sense, this doesn't make sense, this seems valid, this seems not valid— lots of examples, and they all work to illustrate the point.
7.50: Now we can axiomatically, from these axioms, prove that the valid forms are in fact valid and that the invalid forms are in fact invalid. I want to keep all of this in mind and now go and work on some examples. Let's start with, as our first example, one of the forms, the modus tollens. We know what modus tollens is, is, if P, then Q. We have P, therefore Q.
7.51: What if we tried to make a really big truth table? In this case, we have two propositions. I'm going to draw a line here. P, and we have Q. Again, we know there's four possibilities. In this case, what we have is one proposition, P ⊃ Q. We're going to diagram the circumstances under which that would be true. We have another proposition, which is P.
