But if you're born into these economic circumstances, you come to think about the world a certain way, including your logic.
7.124: If you're born into this class, it's the same. You have a different understanding of the world and a different logic. Those two classes cannot really understand and/or communicate with each other. Hence, things are going to be solved not through argumentation, diplomacy, but rather by means of violent method.
7.125: Adolf Hitler and his theoreticians represent just another variation on this poly-logist theme, which is to say that it's not your nationality, it's not your class membership economically, but rather your race. Different races construct their worlds differently, think and have actually different logics as well. For his preferred races, there's no point in trying to accommodate, understand, or work with members of other races. Again, we're into a violence with respect to sociability.
7.126: The point then is, this is a deep issue in the philosophy of logic. Hegel was a deep thinker, Marx was a deep thinker. Many of the theoreticians behind Adolf Hitler were PhDs in philosophy who had a lot training in what they thought was the outmoded non- Aryan logic that they wanted to reject, but they were smart people who knew what they were doing. This is another deeper issue in the philosophy of logic, just to attend to for further thinking. Lecture 8: Induction & Open-Ended Discovery At a glance — Induction and open-ended discovery.
8.1: So far in this course, we have been focusing on what we call deductive reasoning, and that's already very complicated. Working out the methodologies for handling all of the different kinds of deductive arguments takes a certain amount of time. There's a standard contrast between deductive reasoning and inductive reasoning. In this session, I want to turn to induction, which in many ways is even more complicated than deduction, but to stake out some basic territory for inductive reasoning.
8.2: Now, on the board here, I have four arguments, and the idea is to contrast the black ones with the ones that are in blue. We take this one here. All plants contain chlorophyll. Fuchsias are a type of plant. Fuchsias contain chlorophyll, is the conclusion there. We recognize that as a categorical argument. We're talking about all plants. Here's a particular kind of plant. We apply the generalization about all plants to this particular plant and draw the conclusion. Perfectly valid form of reasoning.
8.3: Here we have a disjunctive argument. He's either stupid or lazy. You know he's not stupid, and you conclude, therefore, it must be that he is being lazy. Again, we recognize this as a valid form, and it follows necessarily. If those are our two only options, you rule one out, it's got to be absolutely the other one. Now, I'm emphasizing in my tone some language that will be different when we read these other arguments here. Go to this one here.
8.4: We examined 280 chronic liars. We're psychologists or social psychologists, and we're doing a systematic study. 280 chronic liars, all of them suffered from low self-esteem. Our discovery. So, now, here's our conclusion. Probably all chronic liars have weak self- esteem. Now, a couple of things are interesting here, is that we started with an "all" statement about an entire class, and then started to focus on an element within that class or a type within that broader class, all plants, applying it to two particulars.
8.5: Our intellectual move is different here. Here we are talking initially about 280 individuals, but then we are generalizing to the entire class of people who are chronic liars, and that's a lot more than 280 individuals. Here we're going from all to a particular, or from a generalization to a particular. Here we're starting with a number of particulars and generalizing to the universal statement, and that's a different intellectual direction.
8.6: The other thing is that we are, say, well, it has to be that fuchsias contain chlorophyll. It follows necessarily as a result of this piece of information here. But this person is being careful and puts the word "probably" in there. From the fact that we've studied 280 chronic liars, that's pretty good. But if we're talking about potentially thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions of people who are chronic liars, do you feel super confident that your study of 280 of them applies more universally? Maybe there's a difference between reasoning deductively, which enables us to feel certainty, it's a valid argument or it isn't, versus less certain, more probabilistic or possibilistic kinds of reasoning.
8.7: In this example here, a magazine did a survey. 90% of those who responded were against free love. Therefore, 90% of the general population are opposed to free love. Now, in this case, we have a particular magazine, the particular individuals who responded to the magazine, and then we're going to a more general, the general population, which is much more. How confident are we about the nature of that generalization? There is some discretion and judgment that is called for, as well as there being this issue about how we do these generalizations in the first place.
8.8: Now, that we do generalizations, and also lots of other animals seem to do generalizations, is important and it's powerful. So you take kids, for example, and you tell them, "Don't touch the hot stove, don't stick your hand in the fire," and so forth. But at some point, they are going to experiment, and we hope it's only one experiment. So they might touch the hot stove one time, suffer the pain, but they don't then say, "I should probably run that experiment again." No, one-time generalization, never touch the hot stove, negatively speaking.
8.9: We do generalizations all over the case. I'm stuck in the burn mode. You go out in the sun one or two times, you stay out too long, you get a sunburn, you learn your lesson. Never engage in too much sun exposure, whatever that's going to be. Generalization is very handy in lots of cooking. For example, you're cooking pasta. I expect you do the same thing that I do. You put the pasta in the bowl or in the pot, you boil it for a certain amount of time. Is all of the pasta in the pot cooked as much as I would like it to do?
8.10: You take a device and you take one piece of pasta out. You let it cool off a little bit, you taste it, that's good, and then you generalize. All of the pasta in the pot is cooked. And so that again is going from particular. I don't have to test each piece of pasta individually to do so. The question, though, about why we do that and under what circumstances we can feel that we are doing so legitimately, there's an immediate philosophical puzzle that we can raise because we can say, "Well, look, the pasta in the pot, they are all the same."
8.11: They're the same product. They're subject to the same manufacturing process. We're putting them in the same conditions. Water, the water is uniform all around the pot. If all of the same antecedent factors are the same, then we should have the same effect on all of the individuals. I only need to test one piece of pasta and then I can make the assumption.
8.12: What makes that assumption legitimate is the broader assumption that we are living in a cause-and-effect world. If you have the same cause, you'll get the same effect, or if you have the same set of causes, you will get the same effect as well, because the world as a whole is cause and effect. Now, the interesting question philosophically comes in, because that right there is a generalization that justifies our saying the same causal processes are working in this case, this case, and so forth, deductively.
8.13: But that very big generalization about the world as a whole, where did we get that from? The idea that all of reality is cause and effect? I might then say, well, I was looking at reality over and doing with this part, and it was all cause and effect operating here. I was looking at reality over here, and it was cause and effect in various ways, and it's also cause and effect over here. I've checked all of these areas, and therefore I'm generalizing.
8.14: But that's exactly the thing that we have in question here. Under what circumstances is it legitimate to generalize, and how do we do so? How do we get to great big whopping generalizations, like all of reality is cause and effect, when we know reality is a pretty big place and we have not experienced all of reality? At the same time, we do feel quite confident, fire burning, pasta cooking, and lots of other examples.
8.15: But where we have to start being cautionary is that we know lots of times we do generalizations, and the generalization is just way off bat. I might, for example, maybe a thousand years ago, I walk under a ladder, and then within a few steps, I trip and I fall off the curb and twist my ankle, and I say, "Oh, cause and effect. Walking under a ladder causes bad luck." There I've got a superstition, and I'm generalizing to a certain causal understanding of the universe, but that's just wrong.
8.16: And lots of times we know we might meet individuals who are members of certain ethnic groups or whatever. I go to Manhattan and I ask someone for directions, and he gives me a certain hand sign and says he's not interested. I say, "Whoa, New Yorkers are so rude." And so immediately from this example, I'm going up to the big generalization. And it might, of course, be that that generalization, I've just soaked it up from osmosis listening to other people and their experiences, but that's not very systematic at all.
8.17: Of course, we can go the other way. Canadians have a reputation for being nice and polite. You meet a Canadian who comes to visit and say, "Oh, boy, that's such nice people. Those Canadians are just so wonderful." Well, let me tell you, many are, some aren't. So that's an inductive generalization that remains to be put to the test.
8.18: More amusingly, there's a famous example from Bertrand Russell, who was, wrote on, a famous philosopher from about 100 years ago now, who gave the example of the chicken. And the chicken in the barnyard, and every morning the rooster crows, the chickens come out. The farmer comes by with a bucket of feed and throws the feed down and the chickens, happily—if it happens the next day, happens the next day.
8.19: So you imagine from the chicken's perspective, say, "Wow, this farmer is such a great guy, every day without fail, blah, blah, blah." And it's now been dozens and dozens of days. "The farmer is looking after us. He's feeding us." And then, of course, one morning, sun comes up, rooster crows, the chickens come out, farmer grabs the guy by the neck, takes him over to the chopping block, whack. So that generalization, if we can imagine the chickens are engaging in generalization, that the farmer is benevolent and looking after you, that that is going to extend, is obviously faulty.
8.20: So generalizations are enormously powerful to us in our thinking, but at the same time they are fraught with danger and there's lots of false generalizations. You think about what scientists are doing for most of their career. They're looking at particular examples, trying to find decisive experiments to run, to generalize to a whole class of whatever it is that they are studying, and to come up something they want to call a law or a principle. We then use those laws. In many cases, we stake our lives on the basis of those scientific discoveries and the experiments that they've been done at the time. It's extraordinarily fraught.
8.21: Not only in science per se, one of the most famous examples of the power of generalizations comes from Adam Smith, writing in 1776, when he published On the Wealth of Nations. There's a famous example that he opens with, of a pin factory. Now human beings have been around for tens of thousands of years, working, making stuff, and we're always concerned with, "How can I make stuff more efficiently, lower cost, and increase my productivity and so on?"
8.22: But Smith, as a social scientist, happened to go and study a pin factory that makes pins that we use in clothing and so forth. He had studied or looked at a certain number of pin factories, and he was blown away by how productive this pin factory was. Because up until the early modern world, the standard was that one person would have an area of expertise and would do all of the functions in that area of expertise.
8.23: If you want to make pins, then you buy your metals, and then you hammer it out and make it into wires and you cut it, and then you shape it into long strands. Then you take some snips and you cut it to length, and then you put it in a device, and you tap it on the end with a hammer. So you have a little bit of a cap at the end of your pin. You sharpen the edges, then you put it in the box and you wrap up the box. And so if you're really good in practice, you can make a certain number of pins per day. Maybe you can make 500 pins in a given day.
8.24: But he went to this factory, and it turned out this factory was cranking out 50,000 pins a day, and it only had about 10 people working at the factory. But 10 independent craftsmen, each of them, if they were very productive, would only be making about 5,000 pins per day. And so what he noticed was that they had divided the labor. They had one person who was responsible for shaping the metal, pounding out the metal. Then the next guy would cut it, the next guy would shape it, the next guy would cut it to length, the next guy would sharpen, the next guy would tap on the pin.
8.25: And for whatever reason, this is what he was interested in, that method of division of labor made each of them more efficient. Now, a lot of it has to do with transition times. If you are doing this part of the operation and you're going to do the next part of the operation, well, then you have to put down your tools for that part of the operation, get your tools, practice a little bit until you get into a flow, then you put the tools down. That might explain a lot of it.
8.26: But Smith wants to say, they have divided the labor into parts, and then each individual person is specializing in that part of the labor, and that's adding up to enormous productivity gains in this particular case. Now, this is pins. Does it also work for other things, not just pins? What if we're talking about clothing manufacturing, even to stay within that territory as well? And so he said, yes, it does, in fact. And so at a certain point, he's ready to generalize through this principle of division of labor.
8.27: And the idea then is, this is an enormously powerful generalization for those of us in business. If we're interested in business productivity, whatever it is that I'm doing 100 years, 200 years later, I can take that generalization, apply it to my business, and chances are good, I will be more productive as well. That is social science using generalizations and so on. How do we do this?
8.28: Now, we know there are all of the fraught cases, all of the superstitions that typically, and all the stereotypes and so on. At the same time, there are very good generalizations that we've engaged in. Now, the challenge is that when we think about evaluating inductive arguments, we use criteria that are different from the criteria we use in deductive arguments.
8.29: One thing we say in the case of deductive arguments is, say the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises. If it's going to be a valid argument, the conclusion follows necessarily. But it doesn't seem the case that the conclusion follows necessarily from an inductive argument. Instead of using necessity language, we start switching to possibility language, probability language, likely, maybe, and we're more cautious, particularly in cases like this about many of our generations.
8.30: We can't be looking for immediately. We might get to certainty, but we can't be expecting certainty in all inductive arguments. Sometimes it's a process where we generalize cautiously, then we generalize more certainly, we have studied, and so forth. The other thing we sometimes do is to say, well, in a deductive argument, really the conclusion is contained in the premises, and all we're doing is making explicit the information that's contained in the premises.
8.31: We saw that, for example, when we were doing the Venn diagrams for categorical syllogisms. We take the information that we get in the premises and the categorical syllogism, and we diagram it. Then we stop and we look and we see already we have diagrammed our conclusion, if it's a valid argument. In a way, the conclusion was already in the premises and we're just making explicit the information that's already there.
8.32: In this case, we might say, in the first premise, we're talking about all plants, and then we're already applying that in a particular case to fuchsias. But fuchsias are a plant, so already implicitly we've been talking about fuchsias because they're in the category that we established initially, and we're just drawing out information. Now, that then is to say, we're not expanding the range of our knowledge, we're not amplifying anything, we're not going beyond the available evidence.
8.33: But all of that does not apply in the case of inductive arguments, because that is exactly what it seems like we're doing in the case of the inductive arguments. We're going beyond the initial 280 people that we studied here to all of them. It is an amplification. It is a generalization, is the word that we use, or even a universalization. In this case here, we're saying, well, 90% of those who responded, we didn't even have a full response rate. We're against free love, so therefore we are going beyond, we're amplifying and making a claim about the general audience. We need different evaluative standards.
8.34: Now, what has been developed over the course of time as logicians and philosophical scientists especially, who are studying the methods that they are using, is to say, what we have are five rules of thumb. Initially, we will call them rules of thumb for evaluating inductive arguments. Sometimes it's going to be a matter of more or less, depending on how well you satisfy these criteria.
8.35: So, one of the obvious criteria is to ask, how big is your sample? So the more instances you have initially in your sample, the more credence will reside. So you go to New York, you've never been to New York, you've never heard about New York, you don't have any preconceptions about New Yorkers. You meet one, and maybe the person is rude. You ask for directions, and he blows you off. All right, that's one. To generalize to that, all New Yorkers are rude. Based on one, that's too much.
8.36: On the other hand, if you had five New Yorkers in a row, that's more. But still, probably not enough for all New Yorkers are rude. Maybe it was rush hour. Maybe it was a super hot day. Maybe everybody was crowded in the subway. So there can be other factors at work. But still, five rude New Yorkers in a row, that's better than one. So that's one thing to check. Partly this is, don't generalize too hastily or too quickly. If you have more instances available, look for them and bring them into your survey sample.
8.37: Another one close is the diversity of your sample. In the case of pasta in a pot, it's hard to get diverse samples because they are all the same. But when you're dealing with more complicated things than pasta, say, like human beings or plants that are actually growing out in the wood, you know there's a lot of diversity among plants, compared to strands of pasta. So chances are good, before you make generalizations about plants, you'll need to consciously check a number of different types of plants.
8.38: And then in the case of human beings who are even more complicated than plants and much more variable, you have to pay attention to all of the ways in which human beings are diverse amongst themselves. It might be relevant to whatever it is that you are talking about and get samples there. If you're at a very basic biological level, and you sense that humans have all of the same kinds of cells, whatever cells are in the skin, for example, it's all pretty much the same. That might be one thing. On the other hand, if you're talking about human beings' psychology, psychology is a lot more variable among human beings than their skin cells, then your project has to be a lot more diverse.
8.39: A third thing is a self-check. That one of the things that we know that we have a problem within our reasoning is looking for things that support the thing that we want to believe or the thing that we want to investigate, and not to as easily pay attention to things that might go against our hypothesis. So the rule of thumb in this case is to go out of your way to try to find examples that don't fit the pattern. Try to find cases where there's an element in the group, but it doesn't have the same trace, and see if you can disprove your generalization.
8.40: This is a psychological check. Basically, it's a variation on the diversity point, but you're looking for a diverse factor that might, instead of just looking for diverse factors that might confirm and still fit your hypothesis. So, a standard example here is, we might take something relatively simple like water and want to know what the temperature water boils at. We might have 10 pots of water, and we might boil them, say, in pots that are made out of different metals.
8.41: We have the thermometers in there and we find, well, all 10 of them, it doesn't matter what kind of pot they are in, they all boil at 212 degrees Fahrenheit or 100 degrees Celsius. Then we're ready to generalize. Water boils at—but then it might be that we have set ourselves to the project of looking for diverse circumstances and find that, if we were, for example, already up in the mountains, that it might not be 212 degrees. The temperature might be a little bit different.
8.42: If we went down sea level, the temperature of boiling seems to be the same, if we went even up higher in elevation. If we were consciously setting our minds to looking for that as a possible factor, as we know, for example, that we are affected by, say, changes in elevations, maybe the water is affected by changes in elevations, but we're looking for something that might disconfirm our example.
8.43: Another important one is to make sure whatever it is that you study, that it fits with all of your previous background knowledge. Partly, this is the thing that helps you in figuring out what number of diversity factors might be relevant. But it's also important to say, on any important thing, before I get too much into the generalization range, to make sure that this general hypothesis fits with other important things that I know by analogy.
8.44: For example, this is in the history of sciences, the history of zoology, actually, for a long time, people in the West thought that swans were white, and that's a reasonable thing to believe. Because if you are in England or you're in Western Europe and you are among the first people to start doing systematic biology, all of the swans that you encounter are white. It might be the case that all of the cardinals that you have encountered, the males are reddish and the females are a more mixture of olive greens and browns and tans and so forth.
8.45: And so even though you've studied, say, all of North American cardinals or you've studied all European swans, you're comfortable with a generalization that swans are white. But even before you travel to other parts of the world—and there are other parts of the world where the swans are not white, there are native black swans in various parts of the world—but you can reason and say, well, one of the things I do know about birds is that birds are a kind of animal species. And animal species like dogs and cows and horses and so forth are much more varied in their external coloring.
8.46: Human beings, I also know, are much more varied in their external covering. So before I get too locked into this idea that all swans are white, their external covering of the feathers, that also might be subject, or something that is subject to high variation depending upon where one is in the world, by analogy to human beings and other animals. So make that a formal part of one's check.
8.47: It's also in a social context where this part is useful. So you run your ideas by someone else who has different experience, different background knowledge. Often they can point out things that you need to pay attention to. And then the next one, and this is where the science really gets down to business, is to say, if you can find underlying causal mechanisms that explain whatever it is that you are talking about.
8.48: So you have the pasta in the pot, and you can do the chemical analysis of the pasta. You can see, say at the microscopic level, that the pasta's molecular structures are all the same and all identical, then you know the underlying process and how it's interacting with the heated water, and you're in a safer position to generalize about surface matters like texture and how soft or hard it is.
8.49: If you can, as we all know, fish need to stay in water in order to stay alive, we can learn that, we can be quite comfortable in that generalization, but if we can start doing the science and figure out that the way fish process their oxygen, the way that we process the oxygen, the mechanisms are different underlying. We know what our lung structure is like. We know what their gill and underlying causal structures are like. They are different. They work differently. Therefore, we can explain the effect, fish needing to be in water, by appeal to a deeper mechanism. That makes the inductive generalization stronger.
8.50: Now, let me run a couple of examples by you and just ask for your reaction on them. Suppose I gave you this one. The barber did a good job cutting Rick's, Bill's, and Larry's hair. Those are my premises. Good job on Bill, good job on Rick, good job on Larry. He will do a good job on mine. That's the generalization. He's a good barber. I can plug myself into that mix. We will get the same effect.
8.51: So, what would we think in this case? Well, we would say, Rick, Bill, Larry, and I, we are all human beings. Those are all male-sounding names. So same general style of haircut. I'm a male, I'm going to get the same general style of haircut. Any other factors that we should think about? Well, is it that they all go first thing in the morning? Maybe there are morning people and I'm an afternoon person. He's good in the morning, but as he gets tired, he gets worse and worse. Maybe I should think about this as a factor.
8.52: Is it that Rick, Bill, and Larry are all friends of his? But he doesn't really know me, and maybe he pays extra attention with friends, and maybe he's not quite so good with strangers. We would think through all of that. We'd say, well, this is only three people. Is that a big enough sample? And so forth. But those are the kinds of questions you would ask. I would say this is a weak generalization, but there's probably something. If it's only one haircut, maybe it's worth the risk.
8.53: Out of 20 letters to the editor, 18 complained of the inconvenience caused by the strike. The public is clearly antagonized by the strike. We got 20 letters to the editor, 18 were complaining about the strike. Therefore, the general public is antagonized by the strike. How strong is that? Well, it's 9 out of 10, or 90%. That's pretty high.
8.54: On the other hand, we might say there's a difference between people who write letters to the editor and people who don't write letters to the editor. People who are really worked up about something are more likely to write a letter to an editor. Maybe the majority of people are not particularly excited by the issue, so they're not writing. I'm drawing only from a much smaller pool of people who are worked up about it.
8.55: We might also bring in some background knowledge. We also know that if things are going fine, people don't typically say anything. But when something is going wrong, that's when people start to complain, and the squeaky wheel gets the grease. It might be that we have a disproportionate sample toward not only people who are worked up about the issue, but people who are on the negative side of that issue. So I would say this is a weak generalization. You've got something to go on here. Clearly, there's enough people maybe to pay attention to, but this generalization seems to be much too strong.
8.56: Buster, assuming he's a young guy, maybe he's in his teens, should prove to be an excellent batter. He plays just like Babe Ruth, one of the most famous baseball players of all time. He has the same stance. He stays low and has a real good eye. He should do really well in baseball. OK, so some optimistic thinking about the prospects of this individual. In this case, what would we say?
8.57: Well, we're making a comparison between someone who was a great baseball player and someone who is a young and developing baseball player. We are pointing out some similarities— stance, his eye-hand coordination, and so forth. But this one, I would say, seems to be weak because, given our background knowledge about human beings, there's a great deal of variation.
8.58: If we have more specialized knowledge about baseball, we know that to become a very good hitter, much less the best hitter in the history, that there are dozens and dozens of factors, not only a dozen physical factors, lots of psychological factors, and we don't have any information about any of those. So predicting that this teenager is going to turn into Babe Ruth or something close is relatively weak.
8.59: All right, now suppose we are getting past wanting to be accomplished thinkers as we go about our lives. We're going to be engaging with particulars, learning all sorts of new things, informing all kinds of generalizations ourselves. Sometimes we're going to be hearing generalizations from other people, and we want to know whether we should accept them provisionally or wholeheartedly, so we know how to think through them for ourselves and for the ones we're hearing from other people.
8.60: Is it a big sample? Is it a diverse sample? Did they go out of their way to find disconfirming examples? Are they looking for underlying causal mechanisms, et cetera? Then in a rough and ready but sophisticated way, we're ready to take on the complicated world and navigate it with all sorts of generalizations. If we upgrade and we want to do that process more systematically, we want to be scientists, social scientists of various sorts, then there have been developed methods that are called inductive methods.
8.61: More historically, credit-wise, they are sometimes called Mill's methods, because John Stuart Mill, the great 1800s British philosopher who wrote significantly on logic, was among the first to systematically identify four inductive methods that scientists can and should regularly use, depending on what they're studying, in order to make more rigorous their approaches and their findings.
8.62: Let's take this first case, and I've got a schematic of it here, and it's just this upper left quadrant on the board. You are a scientist, and what you have is, all right, I'm studying four different cases. I'm looking for a cause and effect explanation here. I noticed beforehand, we had A, B, C, and G, and as a result of that, E happened. In the second case, we had A, B, D, and G, and E also happened. In this case, A, C, F, and G happened. Then we also got the effect. In this case, it was B, C, F, and G, and we also got the same effect.
8.63: Having gathered all of that data, put it in this table to structure the data, we start to analyze. One of the things we are thinking is, well, we're trying to find the cause of the effect. A principle of cause and effect says you will get the same cause leading to the same effect. Something that isn't present can't be a cause. The thing that is the cause has to be present in all of the cases.
8.64: We can start going through and sorting, and we say, well, in this case, C was not present. We had D. In this case, D was not present. So C can't be the cause, D can't be the cause. In this case, we had F. In this case, we also had F, but we didn't have F in these cases, but we still got the effect, so it can't be that F is the cause as well. So the only thing that is in common in all of these cases, or the only thing that is, that agrees in all cases, is the presence of G. Every time we got the effect, G was present, and that's the only thing that was present every single time. Then we can draw a conclusion from these four cases. G was the cause of E.
8.65: Now, a homey example would be, suppose you and—how many people would it be? Three friends. You went to a party, you all ate and drank a bunch of stuff, and then the next morning, everybody has a terrible stomachache, all four of you. And so you start to do the postmortem, so to speak. You're still alive, so postmortem is a bit harsh in this case. But you say, "You, what did you eat and drink? You, what did you eat and drink?" And someone says, "Well, I had a burger, I had a Diet Coke, I had some salad, and I had some lemonade." And then someone says, "Well, I had a burger and some Diet Coke and some pretzels." And then the third person had a different array of things.
8.66: But it turns out, lemonade is the only thing that all four of you had. Everybody had different combinations of everything. Then it's quite reasonable to say it has to be the lemonade. Now, I said that pretty strongly. It has to be the lemonade. Now, this is where we might start and say this is good science. We're being systematic and we're probably isolating something important, but it might be something else.
8.67: It could be that you all went on a little expedition in the same car, and someone had left something rotten in the car, and there was some sort of mold in the air that you all breathed in. If we're going to be really serious about it, we would have to control for that variable as well. But presumably then we would just add that to the list, and we would see another kind of test, to see if we can differentiate the lemonade from, say, that mold. But this is a perfectly strong, powerful, commonly used method.
8.68: This is, as Mill labeled it, the method of agreement. It's one of the basic elements of scientific method to learn. This one here, two cases, in any case it's simpler. In initial conditions, you have A, B, C, and F, and you consciously make sure people in this group are exposed to F, whatever that is, and you get the effect. In the second case, you make sure that people are exposed to not all of those factors, you explicitly withhold F, so they're not exposed to it, and you don't get the effect.
8.69: Then on the basis of that, it's reasonable to conclude, F is the cause. F is present, it happens. F is not present, it doesn't happen. This is the standard for initial rounds of drug testing, for example, among many things. You have a new experimental drug. You want to know, does it work? You get a certain number of volunteers, say, 200 people. You divide them into two groups, and hopefully you can divide them into, the groups are more or less homogeneously.
8.70: If you want to be super controlled, you will say, let's all get the same amount of sleep, have the same amount of food, drink the same sorts of things. Those might be the A, B, and C. They both slept sufficiently. They ate the same breakfast. They had the same amount of coffee. One control group, you give them your experimental drug. The other group, you give them a pill that's a placebo pill. It doesn't have any active ingredients whatsoever.
8.71: In one case, you get the effect. Hopefully, it's the effect that you want. In the other case, it doesn't make any difference. Therefore, you can include positively in this case, there is something to your new pill. Now, how big do your human groups need to be? How many of these variables do you need to be controlling? That is an art, as well as a science. This John Stuart Mill labeled the method of difference. As in the method of agreement, you're looking for the thing that agrees or is common in all cases. In this case, you're looking for the one differentiating factor, and we label it so accordingly.
8.72: Now, there are other cases in science, though, where the factors, the causal factors and the effects, we're not able to isolate them independently from each other. We have to figure out methods in order to be able to test for one, even while the other ones might be changing. Sometimes we can hold them constant in varying degrees, but we can't separate them out. It's not, we will give you the pill or we won't give you the pill. We will drink the lemonade or we won't drink the lemonade. Those are either-or, off-on sorts of things.
8.73: An example to think through this would be something we know in reality, and that is that pressure, temperature, and volume, say, when we are studying physics. I can take a flask or a container of some sort, and suppose I have a sealed container with a certain amount of oxygen or some gas that is inside that container. I know I have a volume, I know I have it at a certain pressure, and the whole thing might be at a certain temperature. But we want to know what's the relationship between pressure and volume and temperature.
8.74: We can't just say, well, let's just take the volume away. We'll have things that have no volume and we'll test them against things that have volume, or things that have no pressure and things that have some pressure and so forth. We can't get things down to really absolute zero. I think we can get pretty close, but we just can't say, let's have no temperature and compare that to things with temperature. Instead, what we know is that these things vary with respect to each other. In order to come up with laws like Boyle's law, we have to then hold what we can hold constant and notice the variations in the others.
8.75: One thing we might then do is to say, well, we have this container. Let's keep the size of the container the same. That then is to say, we are going to hold the volume constant. We're not going to change that. We have a gas inside the volume, and right now it is at a certain temperature. We know what the volume is, and maybe we can measure the pressure that it is at. Now, one thing we can control the variation on is temperature. I might take a heat source and apply it to the container. I'm going to add heat into this container, and then the volume is going to stay the same, but my pressure measuring is going to change.
8.76: Then I can then say, as my temperature changes, say at this rate, the pressure is going to change at this rate. It might be also that we have an experimental device, where we have our volume is expandable or not, say, like a balloon or whatever. We might then be able to say, well, we have a certain volume of gas in there at a certain pressure. What happens as we increase heat? Well, the volume of the balloon will expand. The volume will change with the temperature.
8.77: If we can measure each of these things carefully, then we can form precise mathematical laws about the relationship, without being able to do either of these methods over here. In this case, it might be pressure, temperature, and volume, and we get a certain effect. But we say, as we increase this factor, whatever the effect is that we are measuring, it also increases. Or it might be, as we lessen this factor, the effect that we're trying to measure also lessens. And so Mill called this one, this has the most fun British name, the method of concomitant variations. It is variations, but the variations are concomitant with each other. That is to say, they match each other. Concomitant.
8.78: And a fourth one that Mill emphasizes, and it's one that's very commonly used, also involves not being able to separate out factors and measure them independently. In many cases, we're dealing with compounds, and they are separate, but not necessarily separable in the case of experiment. We can use what he called, and I'll give you the name first, the method of residue. That's to say, whatever's leftover, the leftover, and trying to identify the leftover.
8.79: Now, my favorite homey example of this, this is something that I used to do, is suppose you want to know how much your dog weighs. You have a little tiny bathroom scale and you have a big dog, and you say to your dog, "Please get on the scale and stay motionless for 30 seconds, so that it can stabilize and I can find out how much you weigh." You know that experiment is never going to succeed because your dog is not going to stand still on the scale for that amount of time.
8.80: What you can do, though, is you can scoop up your dog and then you, with your dog, go and stand on the scale. Everything is stable for a certain amount of time. You look down and you say, "Oh, 235 pounds," just to make up a number. Then you step off the scale. Now what I know is, this is me, this is my clothes, this is my dog, and I get A plus B plus C is the entire weight altogether. Suppose that, for sake of example, ends up being 235.
8.81: Then what I can do is, I can put the dog over there, come over, step on the scale, weigh myself, and suppose it comes out to 175 or whatever. Then I can step off, I can take my clothes off, I can weigh them or I can weigh myself, and I can say something like, "Well, I know I am, say, 175. Maybe my clothes are five, if I'm wearing heavy shoes or whatever. Therefore the residue," and here I do the math, "is my dog weighs, what would it be, 50 pounds, 45 pounds? Something like that."
8.82: So that is a scientific method. It applies obviously to beyond just measuring dogs and so forth. One very interesting example from the history of science is the discovery of Pluto as a planet. So for many centuries on up until the 1600s, we thought there was only seven bodies up in the sky, sun, moon, and a certain number of planets. I don't know that they had even gotten to Saturn at that point, maybe. But certainly, Pluto, Uranus came along 1700s, 1800s. And then finally, Pluto was discovered.
8.83: But the discovery of Pluto was not by direct observation with a powerful telescope. Instead, the scientists were using the method of residue. So what they were doing is, they were able to figure out where Uranus was and what its gravitational attraction was on the various other planets, where Neptune was and what its gravitational attraction was, and then the various other planets and all of the effects on each of them.
8.84: You can't ask the planets to stop moving, so you can measure these effects. They're using a lot of concomitant variations in order to tease out the contribution of the gravitational attractions of each planet on the others. Then what they noticed with one of the planets, I can't remember right now whether it was Neptune or Uranus, I think it was Neptune, that if they had taken into account all of the gravitational forces exerted by all of the other planets, then Neptune should be here.
8.85: We will predict that Neptune, as it continues its path, will go here. But it turned out that Neptune was there, just a little bit off. But they were very sure about the calculations they had done for all of the other planets. And so the inference was, well, there must be something else out there exerting a certain amount of gravitational attraction, something that we haven't seen yet. And it has to be probably in this position, and it probably has to be about this big in order to alter what we think Neptune's planet should be.
8.86: So at that point, they had the telescope technologies. They could train them on that part of the sky and wait. Sure enough, Pluto pops into the picture and we have a discovery of a new planet. That is a lot of concomitant variations in the background. In this case, it's the residue. It's what's left over in the math, and we need to figure out that there's something there that accounts for that.
8.87: This is an introduction to inductive logic, and it's very complicated and very open- ended. As we are reaching to the end of this eighth session, this introduction to logic course, I want to do one more cumulative example, but rehearse, before we get to that cumulative example, how far we have come so far just in eight lectures and how much more interesting stuff there is to do.
8.88: We started off talking about basic argument analysis, sorting premises and conclusions, filling in missing pieces, attuning ourselves to indicators, and all of that requires working with our ordinary English or whatever our language's facility, to become very good at the grammar and the parsing of sentences. We talked a lot about the importance of definition and concept formation, and forming hierarchies of concepts in our mind, and being able to position things well and clearly.
8.89: And then the precision of definition in doing so, being absolutely essential to anything that we do later, building on, we've decided that we are using these words as meaning certain things. But there's a lot more work still to be done with concept formation, how we do this, and psychology is the discipline that is going to work out more understanding of how we do these amazing abstractions that we do with the sophistication that we do. So logic has a lot of work to do, not only with linguistics, but ongoing with psychology.
8.90: Prior to all of that, the initial data seems to come from our senses. We are bodily beings, and learning how to use our senses well so that we can notice the similarities and notice the differences that are going to feed into our conceptual structure; and hopefully in an ongoing way, let us finetune or change when we need to our conceptual structures. Logic has to work hand in hand with the empirical evidence that comes along.
8.91: As we started then to look at deductive arguments with increasing abstraction, increasing sophistication, we start to develop all of these methods for dealing with categorical argumentations. Are we now, with better graphical methods, able to have better diagramming techniques, so that with categorical syllogisms right now, we know how to diagram and model on a two-dimensional surface, three-term arguments? But what about four-term arguments and five-term arguments? And so, will the new graphical programs and sophistication enable us to do better with even more complicated such arguments?
8.92: And then, as we saw in the last session, the link between hypothetical arguments and disjunctive arguments and the various combinations of those and truth tables and all of the exciting things that come out of that with respect to integrations with mathematics, integrations with machines that can do our calculations for us. There also are ways, as we progress further down in that road, to integrate in categorical syllogisms into a more broader symbolic logic framework. All of that is cutting-edge and still a work in progress.
8.93: The example that I want to work through in closing, though, is an example of how all of that fits together. To my mind, it is a beautiful example from the history of medicine, when something absolutely important was discovered, but it was only discovered because the person responsible, his name was Ignaz Semmelweis, he was a medical doctor working at University of Vienna Hospital. But for him to figure out this important medical discovery, he had to be doing everything and everything very well that we have been studying in this course so far.
8.94: Let's go back to the 1840s. We are well into the modern world, well into the scientific world. Medicine also is being revolutionized, starting in the 1700s on into the 1800s. 1840s, though, we do not yet have germ theory. The idea that there are little tiny microorganisms, that some of them are good for us and some of them are bad for us, that was all perhaps wild abstract speculation, but we did not have that germ theory. We also did not have any antiseptic theory. That's something that's going to be developed in the next generation.
8.95: Ignaz Semmelweis was originally from what we now think of as Hungary, but he had come to the University of Vienna as a young medical doctor, and Vienna was one of the great centers of medicine, medical research, and the associated sciences at the time, and so he was in a very prestigious position. This is a picture of Vienna Hospital in the 1840s, and Semmelweis was working with maternal issues.
8.96: Women who arrived at Vienna Hospital, pregnant, who sometimes stayed at Vienna Hospital to give birth, and then they would be in recovery from birth for a certain amount of time. As it happened at Vienna Hospital, you can see it's a very large establishment. Vienna is a pretty large city. They had two different divisions for maternity. One was in one part of the hospital and another was in another part of the hospital. They called them Division One and Division Two.
8.97: In these two divisions, women would come to Vienna Hospital. Some would be assigned to the first division, some would be assigned to the second division. Semmelweis shows up. He's making his rounds, checking in on the women in the first division, some of them are still pregnant, close to delivery, some have given birth and are in recovery, and same thing happens over in the other division as well.
8.98: As he's going around, he's an alert guy; he's learning on the job and practicing, but he notices something. And he notices that it seems like in the first division, women who have given birth are dying at a much higher rate than women are dying after having given birth in this division. Now, in one sense, this is not particularly remarkable because giving birth to children had been the number one killer of women throughout human history, prior to the modern world and the medical innovations.
8.99: But nonetheless, even so, Semmelweis was alert enough. He was observing and he was keeping track. There's a woman who died. Here's another woman who died in the first division. There's a woman who died in the second division. This woman, fine, this woman fine, and so on. In a rough and ready way, he is observing the difference between life and death, rather obviously, but a whole bunch of other things. But he has a category scheme. First division, second division, and he's starting to categorize deaths according to that geographical location.
8.100: Now, one might say, "Well, women die in childbirth. That's just the way things go. I'm a busy guy, got a lot of things to do," but Semmelweis cared. He took some extra time to check. And so he made a point of consulting his own records. He consulted the hospital's general records, including from before he was there, and he did the math. And what he found was, this is 1840-something, say '41, 1842, 1843, going back a certain way. Then we count up all of the deaths in the first division. We put the numbers in there. Second division, we put all of the numbers in there.
8.101: So he's making an effort to do all of the previous observations of women dying. All of the record-keeping has been categorically organized. He can use it with his own, and he comes up with a table. It turns out that his initial sense was right, that in fact, women in the first division were dying at almost four times the rate of women dying in the second division. That would not have happened without lots of observation, lots of record- keeping, lots of good categorization, and someone who cares enough to pay attention to all of that, to come and do so. And then the basic math that's involved in calculating those numbers.
8.102: So he now knows there is a problem here. Now, again, I might say, "Well, it's a mystery. Who knows why? The world is chaos," etc. Or I could say, "No, there's cause and effect operative in the world. There has to be something going on in the first division that is not happening in the second division, and I think I can figure this out. So I'm going to," and he takes this on then as a research project.
8.103: Now, he starts then to consider hypotheses. What could it possibly be? Well, childbirth is complicated. People are complicated. The number of people who are involved in the hospital, there's all sorts of factors. What could it possibly be? So one of his initial hypotheses then was to say, maybe it has something to do with whether the women voluntarily are coming into the hospital or whether they are brought in against their will, as is sometimes the case. So that might be a relevant factor, something to do with their psychological state. Are they there under coercion or not?
8.104: Then he goes through the records and see the terms under which the women were admitted. If it was that, then I should find a difference in the two divisions. Notice I'm making a prediction. Then when I examine the records, I don't get that predicted result. It doesn't seem to matter whether they came voluntarily or whether they were brought under some duress. Therefore, that hypothesis is false. Now, we now know that is denying the consequent. That's modus tollens, and he more or less effortlessly is doing so.
8.105: Then he says, well, maybe it has something to do with overcrowding. It turns out, when he was looking around, there seemed like a lot more women were packed into the first division than were in the second division. So now we have a new hypothesis. Overpopulation is the cause of the childbirth fever, the death.
8.106: Now, I should mention that when he was looking at the deaths more closely, he started to notice some other factors. It wasn't just that they were dying. They seemed to have certain common symptoms, many, many, many of them involving certain blotches on their skin, certain kinds of anemia. He noticed that, as a result of paying more careful attention to the women, particularly now that he knows that he has a problem on his hands. So, increased observation to noticing something relatively subtle that might have escaped the gaze of other physicians as well.
8.107: Then he starts to say, well, OK, if it's not the overcrowding, because that one then gets disproved by the data, another modus tollens, what could it be? Now, months are going by, more months are going by, because it takes time to come up with a new idea, to consult all the records, to do the calculations, and so forth. One thing he notices is that the attending physicians in the first delivery seemed to prefer that the women deliver their children while lying on their backs, whereas in the second division, the attending physicians seemed to prefer women in a side position. You put the woman on her side, raise her leg, and you deliver the baby that way.
8.108: So then he's thinking, maybe it has something to do with this position of delivery. And so let's run the experiment, and we gather all of the data that's now hopefully in the, in our records. How many women in the first division over here did back delivery, how many did side delivery, and what was the death rate for each of them? Same thing for the second division. Crunch all of the numbers, and it turns out, not the delivery position. It makes absolutely no difference. Another modus tollens, another rejected hypothesis.
8.109: Now, a year has gone by, two years has gone by, and what you might think is, well, a lot of people would say, "I'm out of ideas, I give up." But Semmelweis does not. He wants to solve this problem. There has to be something. There has to be an explanation. Now, he's starting to get desperate because a couple of years have gone by and he doesn't seem to be any closer to getting the explanation or the causal explanation.
8.110: So, one day he's hanging out in the first division, scratching his head, wondering what he can do next. And he notices that a priest walks in one part of the first division, crosses through the first division and out the door and into another part of the hospital. And so he starts to wonder about this priest. He says, "Could it be that the priest is the problem?" Because he goes and talks to the priest and he investigates the priest, and the priest is a good guy. "Why is this guy asking me all of these suspicious questions?"
8.111: It does turn out that the priest has his office close to the first division in the hospital, and that whenever he is called to do last rites anywhere in the hospital, the easiest way for him to get anywhere in the hospital is just to cross through the first division, and then he has access to pretty much everything. But he very rarely goes to the second division. So Semmelweis thinks about this, and he says, well, maybe it's not primarily a physical cause. It's not birth position. It's not overcrowding. Maybe it's a psychological cause. Maybe it's something like this.
8.112: Women who are giving birth are stressed. They're physically tired, they're physically exhausted. Then they go through the process of birth. That just is draining, physically very difficult. Their emotions are all up and down, new life, and so forth. At the same time, they are psychologically drained. There are often physical things that have happened, tearings that have happened, and they need time to recover from all of that. What we have is women who are really at the outer reaches of what a human being can endure. That seems like a pretty good description of much of childbirth historically.
8.113: Then what happens in the first division is this priest comes in. From the psychological perspective of someone who's maybe this close to death, you see a priest and you know that someone is dying, and this priest is going to give last rites. Maybe you add, maybe this person is going to heaven, but maybe they're going to hell. And all of these increasingly stressful thoughts are happening inside the women, and it's just that little bit too much that pushes them over the edge.
8.114: And so we have a new hypothesis. The priest is the cause of the death in combination with, of course, all of the other stuff that's going on. It's the straw that broke the camel's back, metaphorically speaking. All right, well, it's out there, but we're desperate and we really want a cause, so we check this out.
8.115: We go to the priest, and Semmelweis says to the priest, "Look, I'm working on this hypothesis. Don't look at me like that, but would you please do me a favor. Whenever, for the next little while you are called to give last rites anywhere in the hospital, take the long way around. Please just avoid the first division. Also, stay out of the second division as much as you possibly can." We're trying to control this variable, the priest. The priest is a good guy. He says, "Yes, absolutely."
8.116: For the next month, the next two months, the priest goes the long route, and Semmelweis is monitoring very carefully the death rates in the two wards. If it's the priest, then the death rate in the first division should go down because we've taken out the causal factor. And unfortunately, the death rate stays the same. It's still four times as many women dying as in the second division. Another modus tollens, it's not the priest. We have to eliminate that hypothesis.
8.117: Semmelweis is very close to being out of ideas. He doesn't know what to do. Then a lucky accident occurs. Lucky for Semmelweis, that is, lucky for women and people who care about women. Not so lucky for Semmelweis' colleague, another medical doctor named Kolletschka. Dr. Kolletschka was working with students. This is a hospital, but it's also a teaching hospital working with the University of Vienna medical school.
8.118: What typically happens then is, credentialed physicians will, of course, lecture to their students, but they will also take the students on rounds through various parts of the hospital, so the students can learn what the practice of real medicine looks like. Professor Kolletschka was working with a group of students, and as part of their routines, they had anatomy lab. In the anatomy lab, what they would do is they would have corpses, and they would do dissections on the corpses. This is the way that students can learn anatomy, physiology, and all sorts of things.
8.119: What had happened was that, in the course of doing dissection, one of the students was holding a scalpel and doing various things, and Professor Kolletschka wanted to point to something inside the body, but the timing was bad. He pointed just as the student's scalpel was going to do something, and he got a cut on his pointing finger right there. Now, OK, you get cuts, these things happen, but the next day, Professor Kolletschka was sick, and then the day after that, he was very sick.
8.120: And Semmelweis comes to see his colleague who is sick, and he sees that Kolletschka has exactly the same symptoms as the women who have been dying at very high rates, particularly in the first ward, the discolorings, the various kinds of discomforts, and so on. And so this is an observation point within a certain categorical scheme that Semmelweis is operating in turn. He sees those symptoms in the women. He sees the exact same symptoms in Kolletschka, even though Kolletschka is a male, even though Kolletschka has not given birth recently, and probably never will give birth.
8.121: Different categorical schemes, but nonetheless, strong overlap on the symptoms, and he observes those and is willing then to form a category adjustment. Whatever kills Kolletschka—and it did kill him the next day, he was done—is the same thing that kills the women. We know what killed Kolletschka. We put it in archaic language. We would say it was the cadaveric material or some blood on skin tissues, or whatever on the scalpel from doing the dissection had punctured his skin, gotten into his blood stream, and gone into the rest of his body and done whatever nasty things that thing does to people's bodies.
8.122: Now, that's what killed Kolletschka. How might it be that that is also killing the pregnant women? Because that's the anatomy lab. Here we have the women. Then we find out, and this is where it gets dark, that after anatomy lab, it was the practice of Professor Kolletschka and the other teaching professors to go to other parts of the hospital. But no germ theory, no antiseptic theory. They would perfunctorily wash their hands, but not in a very serious fashion. Then they would go and be handling patients in the other parts of their rounds.
8.123: In this case, we know they're going into the maternity ward, because it turns out the anatomy lab is pretty close to the first division, rather far afield from the second division. In many cases, they would go from anatomy lab into the first division, and the professors and the students would be handling the women who had recently just given birth. They have cadaveric material on their hands and fingers. The women have abrasions and lesions and so forth. That then gets introduced into their bloodstream. So now we have also a causal transmission measure. We know now what caused puerperal fever.
8.124: Now, Semmelweis, this is a great scientific discovery, and as a result of that, we then know what we can start to do. We can introduce more rigorous hygiene regimes and thereby save thousands and thousands of women who otherwise ordinarily would die. Now, that's a great value, but my point as a logic teacher is to say, this would not have happened without someone raised in an environment in which commitment to logic and all of the constituent elements are praised, practiced, and internalized, not only as part of his intellectual furniture, but as part of his moral character as a professional practicing medicine person.
8.125: Excellent sensory skills, use of categorization schemes, precise definitions, whether we're willing to alter the conceptual schemes when new data comes along, a commitment to generating abstract hypotheses and predictions from them, and doing logical and mathematical operations on them to sort the good ones from the bad ones. Then in his case, not simply to do this as a matter of a five-minute exercise on the whiteboard or even a month's work or a year's work, but to stick with it, consistently applying those methods for several years, then and only then we get the ultimate discovery.
8.126: Now, this is Semmelweis, and he is a great hero in the history of medicine, from my perspective, not only as a human being, but especially as a logic professor. But there's an additional challenge that I want to add to it here. It's not enough that only individuals isolated here and there be able to do this. A sad part of the story is that Professor Semmelweis, then having engaged in this stupendous amount of research yielding these results, had a very difficult time, almost impossible time, getting anything changed at Vienna Hospital.
8.127: He would go to the other physicians, explain his data, if they would listen to him, and suggest that they change their procedures. And many of them would say, "I'm not interested in doing so. I read my textbook, I listened to my professors, I'm going to carry on them. Who are you, Semmelweis, to tell me that we need to do something different germ theory, I've heard about that, but that's just weird speculation. I'm not in that particular scientific school, and I'm not really open to discussion on it."
8.128: In some cases, it was an issue of age. Semmelweis is relatively young or an early middle career at this point. I may be an older doctor, and I have a certain reputation, and who is this young whippersnapper to come along and tell me? Certainly, Semmelweis doesn't have power on the hospital boards that make the policy decisions and so on. Those are all occupied by other people. Sometimes there's religious prejudice, and sometimes there's political prejudice, and sometimes there's personal animosities. And so many of those people just don't like Semmelweis for various reasons, and so they're not willing to pay attention to his argument.
8.129: So the personal commitment matters, but also part of the lesson of logic is a social. The more we have more people who are able to do these things, appreciate them, and have internalized them, the better we are going to succeed. Wonderful intellectual heights, I think, still to scale, and logic will help us do so, but also wonderful improvements to life that logic, as part of the package, will also enable. We'll stop there.
8.130: When we are trying to find cause and effect, there's a lot of studies that have come out that have been debunked now because they took correlation as causation. We know that correlation doesn't always equal causation. Is that a fault in our methods, or is that merely human error or maybe a moral issue with the scientists?
8.131: Sometimes correlation is causation, and sometimes correlation is not causation. That's exactly what we need to figure out. That's precisely why we're developing these methods and using them in increasingly sophisticated ways to do so. I think the quickest thing I can say in response to that is that the problem is going to be human error. That the person is too quick to think that they've used the methods, and so they generalize too hastily.
8.132: In many cases, it might just be that they want to get to a conclusion, or they already have had that hypothesis in mind and they're somewhat invested in it, so they do the other hard work rather hastily. But I don't think it's even in a majority of cases in scientists, it's that, because I think scientists, by and large, have good training and good ethics for the most part.
